posts.title: AUGUST CHALLENGE INFO: PIXEL PICASSO 🎨
posts.content:
🎁 Reward: 3 people get a private call with me! And featured across my socials.

Sup guys! Exciting news....

We're running something new this month, and I'm pumped about it!!!

We're calling it the Pixel Picasso Competition 🎨 We run this competition weekly already in my company... giving cash rewards to the team that creates the BEST email across the whole company.

Now, we are carrying it over to the community here!

👉 How It Works / Rules:
[ol:1][li]Every week in August, you must post in this community one fully written/designed email in the community \(under the "Email Feedback" category\). Agency owner or brand, doesn't matter. You must send at least 1 per week \(4 by end of month\) to qualify.[li]You also must respond to at least one other person's email once per week to qualify. Give feedback. share your thoughts, eyc [li]At the end of the month, we will gather all of the emails and you guys will vote for your top 3 favorite emails! The "Pixel Picassos" 👨‍🎨[li]The 3 winners get a private call session with me AND featured across my socials 

‼️ QUESTIONS / LOGISTICS
[ul][li]How to submit your emails? -> Post in the community under category "Email Feedback" with the title "August Pixel Picasso Challenge" [li]What if I don't think my emails are good? -> Totally fine... this is your opportunity to get feedback and tips from everyone in the community. People will be responding to each other so it's a great way for you to get tips![li]How many emails can you submit? -> Unlimited! Post as many as you want. But you need to do at minimum 1x per week to qualify for the final rewards. [li]What makes a good email that can win? -> Strategy behind the email, the copy, and the design. This is NOT a design challenge... we will be looking at all parts of the email.[li]What happens if you don't meet requirements of 1x post per week and 1x response to another post per week? -> Well, then you won't qualify. We are running this to boost engagement, so be sure to participate! :\) 

Winners get announced on the last Thursday call, so pull up for that.

First designs go up TODAY...

So START POSTING and getting feedback!

Let's see what you got!

posts.title: July 30th Mastermind: Tools + Email Reviews
posts.content:
Banger mastermind call today.

We covered:

[ul][li]August email design challenge. Three winners, private call with Max, featured on all socials. Post one email per week to qualify. Full details dropping in the community shortly.

[ul][li]Top tools stack. The full breakdown of every tool Well Copy uses internally — Meta Ads Library for campaign angles, Milled for email inspo, Magnific for AI images, Hyros for analytics, Maverick for inbox optimisation, OpenSend for abandonment recovery, Zemo for subscription brands, Alia for pop-ups, Fondue for cashback offers, and the Claude MX Skill for copy and ideation.

[ul][li]Gate-kept tools revealed. Maverick and OpenSend — two tools Max doesn't usually talk about publicly — both covered in full with context on when they make sense and how to get set up.[li]SMS platform breakdown. Which platforms to use, why Klaviyo and Omnisend are kicking peptide brands off, and why Max doesn't recommend AI conversational SMS flows.

[ul][li]Live email reviews. Testimonial welcome email, a word search engagement campaign, free gift flows, new product launch emails, and clothing brand campaigns — covering discount code placement, urgency framing, photo galleries, Klaviyo dynamic blocks, and spacing.

Link to recording and full summary in classroom here: [https://www.skool.com/email-marketerz/classroom/ce66996f?md=7e5a9dd964d14b6fa09a90bf958b8abe](https://www.skool.com/email-marketerz/classroom/ce66996f?md=7e5a9dd964d14b6fa09a90bf958b8abe)

posts.title: #1 Pixel Picasso Challenge
posts.content:
For context if you're not familiar, MBway is basically the #1 way people send money to friends/family in Portugal \(think Venmo/PayPal but even more universal here, everyone has it\). So the notification format isn't just "generic bank app" to a Portuguese audience, it's instantly recognizable, everyone's seen this exact "you have money waiting" notification pop up on their phone.

Used that recognition to hijack attention, then flipped the "twist" into a discount code reveal instead of an actual transfer. This angle \(real-life notification style, tied to something hyper-local/familiar\) is one I keep coming back to for CASEOVER because it consistently performs

posts.content:
Hey, here's some work i thought deserved some spotlight.

I love a good fashion brand, especially one with good photoshoots. This is a trendy new brand in Romania, started by an influencer so of course they had cool shoots, but also they have a very cool and fun sort of energy on social platforms, i just wanted to showcase that in the emails as well.

Most of their posts are collabs and a lot of comments started as "What brand is this?" so of course i had to include this somehow with the "where did you get that?" product section.

Then, we just let the photos do the work, fashion is visual, lots of white space.

Only thing i look back on is that hero headline that contrast is a bit off.

Feedback is much appreciated.

posts.title: AGENCY MASTERMIND CALL RECORDING AUG 4TH
posts.content:
Epic agency call today led by [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5) & [@Ben Saunders](obj://user/9d3ab72326574b2b96da874b833f59a6)

We covered:

[ul][li]Referral acquisition strategy. Charlie's method of paying external people $1,000 per closed referral — cold DM'd across Twitter and ecom Discords, got six leads, three converted. A low-effort, high-ROI acquisition channel most agencies aren't using.

[ul][li]The scaling playbook. Max's full framework for going from one man band to a systemised team — the four stages of agency scale, when to hire, who to hire, where to find them, and why hiring alone changes nothing without proper training.

[ul][li]Hiring for hunger, not experience. Why inexperienced people with dog mentality consistently outperform experienced hires at the small agency stage, and how to find them.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
Hey, found myself in a very similar position recently.

I actually disagree with your statement. You don't have to charge the new referrals the same low retainer, even if the current client has told them what they pay you.

If they push back and say "But but my friend only pays you X amount", I would reply with something like "You're right they do pay X amount and I understand that our new price feels a lot higher. However your friend started working with us over a year a go when the team was much smaller and our margins were wider. Now we've grown as an agency and are no longer in a position to offer those lower rates. The only reason some clients are still on them is because we respect their loyalty over the last 12 months." Then if you can ensure you client their is still a very strong ROI you should be all good.

Also if you want to increase the retainer of your current clients I would recommend using the same angle of "we've grown and our margins have shrunk" but then anchor it down with something like "we appreciate you for working with us for a long time so won't be pushing you all the way up to the prices we're charging new clients, \(then state a really high price which you know would burn them\) instead we're happy to offer you X amount to continue working with us". That makes them feel like they're still getting a great deal.

I recently did exactly that to increase ALL of my client retainers and NONE of them left me :\)

posts.title: Question for agency owners who charge based on a percentage of email revenue:
posts.content:
I manage email marketing for a client through a white-label partnership, and our compensation is based on a percentage of the revenue generated from email.

The problem is not the payment. The client simply wants a reliable way to identify the actual revenue generated by email without counting the same order across multiple channels.

For example, a customer might:
[ol:1][li]Click an email.[li]Later click a Meta or Google ad.[li]Purchase using an affiliate’s discount code.

In this situation, the email platform, ad platform, and affiliate platform may all claim the same order because they use different attribution windows and tracking methods.

The client currently gives commission to the affiliate whose code was used, but that does not always tell the complete story because the email may still have influenced or converted the customer.

Most emails also do not contain unique discount codes, so using codes alone would significantly underreport email revenue.

For those managing rev-share or performance-based email accounts:
[ul][li]What do you use as the final source of truth?[li]Do affiliate codes automatically take priority over email attribution?[li]Do you use first-click, last-click, last non-direct click, or another attribution model?[li]Do you reconcile everything manually using individual order IDs?[li]What tools or reporting systems do you use to prevent duplicate commissions?[li]How do you define “payable email revenue” in your client agreements?

I’m not looking for a way to inflate email revenue. I’m looking for the fairest system that gives each channel credit without paying multiple commissions on the same sale.

Would appreciate hearing how other agencies structure and track this.

posts.title: Updating Segmentation To Deliver Insights
posts.content:
I'm tired of seeing just one basic 120 day engaged segment sent in campaigns...

With Klaviyo's new-ish "Audience Breakdown" tab this leaves a huge opportunity on the table...

Instead, split your engaged list into useful customer groups for better campaign analysis,.

In the attached example we used a 160 day engaged but split into 4 segments:
[ul][li]Churned subs[li]Non-buyers[li]One-time buyers[li]Repeat one-time buyers.

It's the same thing as sending to a broad 160 day engaged list... but now we get data we can use on our different customers.

Once you're sending to these split segments, Klaviyo's Audience Breakdown tab on any campaign shows you performance broken out by each one automatically. You instantly know which customer type is responding to that specific send.

Set this up for EVERY SEND going forward to get customer-level insight instead of one flat number that hides who's actually buying.

comments.content:
Hi [@Kate Koel](obj://user/e036e14866ec4129b27efdd6d9c1a3fb) this is a really strong first email! The visuals and brand voice are pretty strong imo, so have to give credit where it's due.

However, there is room for improvement. Honest feedback will be below:

Your angle doesn't rlly read like a hook. "A little garden romance that blooms all year" is poetic but doesn't make someone stop scrolling. The actual hook is buried in your body copy: "They will not brown. They will not fold. They will not be swept off a table in September." Real flowers that never die, preserved in jewelry. That evokes emotion out of somebody, so I'd lead with it.

The CTAs need more contrast too. "SHOP NEW ARRIVALS" is above the fold which is good, but it kind of blends into the muted aesthetic. Even in an elegant design like yours, the button needs to pop on a quick mobile scroll.

One thing I also don't see rn is a product section. So u have beautiful images throughout but zero product names, prices, or individual buttons linking to specific product pages. That blue flower ring looks great but I can't click to buy that specific ring. Every product shown should have an image, name, price, and a direct link.

The body copy could be more visual as well. The paragraph is well written but your "Summer, kept alive" section with the circular images is def a more effective format. More of that, with less text blocks.

But you do have a ton of stuff that's working well! Like I think ur founder note adds real personality and the Judge me review is a good trust signal. Ur foundation is strong, and the angle and product section are your two biggest fixes imo.

posts.title: How To Be A Better Communicator & Leader Mini Course 📕
posts.content:
Different sort of post today because I get asked about this quite a bit... We talk about email a lot but email is only a part of our job. And what's more important is running a team and having proper communication.

You've probably heard me say it before, but Leila Hormozi is the best person out there to learn leadership, communication, and team management from. Pulling together some of my favorite older videos of hers here, stuff anybody on this team can learn from regardless of what role you're in.

Highly, highly, highly recommend picking at least a few of these and actually watching them, not just skimming the summary...

[1. The Key To Getting Your Team To Do Good Work](https://youtu.be/PNP_emcQoVA?si=t5DtgaYSawlMLpuS)
Recognition is one of the most underused management levers there is... and it's the key for human motivation. Breaks it into when, who, what, and how to recognize people.

[2. How To Communicate With Your Team](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ErKqopYErdk)
Good communication is trading assumptions for curiosity. Nobody ever quits because you over-communicated. Introduces three leader archetypes and the energy, engagement, exploration framework for how teams actually communicate well.

[3. 3 Things To Get Team Members To Do What You Want (Alex Hormozi)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=wdZ9kd5jH8vrZ_c8&v=IMowPVgcWbA&feature=youtu.be)
When someone isn't doing what you want, it's always one of three things... they don't know you want it, they don't know how, or they're not motivated. Gives you playbook and examples in practice.

[4. How To Run Meetings Without Wanting To Kill Yourself](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gumrYK5BLWY&t=195s&pp=ygUWbGVpbGEgaG9ybW96aSBtZWV0aW5ncw%3D%3D)
Your culture gets built in your meetings, since that's the most actual time you spend with your team, so bad meetings mean bad culture, full stop. Five questions to ask before any meeting... who really needs to attend, do you need to attend, do you need to attend the whole thing, who owns the pre-work, and what's the actual outcome.

[5. Recognition & Reward vs. Punishment -> Team Motivation Framework](https://youtu.be/X2y2AAhTK9I?si=qL_8tTv1x5kqt-5d)
Punishment breeds compliance and avoidance, not real effort, while praise actually reinforces behavior. Same core stats as the recognition video, but hammers home why instant, in-the-moment recognition is the most powerful version.

[6. How To Become A Leader People Respect](https://youtu.be/7q6rYu6wVqU?si=uEe0cwN5JS1FYxgr)
Self-doubt never fully goes away, even at her level, the goal is just to not let it stall you. Most new leaders swing too far toward fear or too far toward coddling instead of balancing accountability with kindness.

[7. How To Give Effective Feedback](https://youtu.be/DAY3WQsHXlY?si=6E6DQ65D0tQk8C4l)
People can't grow without proper feedback. It's on you as the leader to make sure you give good feedback and you do it the right way. Introduces the 5 A's... Ask, Acknowledge, Appreciate, Accept, Act.

If you watch any of these, drop here in the thread what you learn. I would also love to discuss it with you in the DMs because I find this stuff fascinating and it has changed how we run the company.

You'll probably see a lot of these principles internally haha because this is the stuff I repeat!

comments.content:
Feel like the segments you built are correct, they're just kind of early for a brand new list.

30/60/90 day engagement segments need a certain amount of sending history to mean anything. At 15 days old i don't think anybody's had time to show an engagement pattern yet tbh.

That's why your suppressed segment shows 4,500.

It's catching profiles with no engagement data, not profiles that disengaged. They haven't received enough emails to show a pattern yet, so I would NOT exclude them.

Also, where did the 6.5k come from? If they signed up organically through your popup then you're in good shape. But if any were imported from an old list or another platform, run those through some sort of validation tool first \(DeBounce, or any other\).

For the first 30 days, your full subscribed list is gonna be your campaign audience. But if the sending domain is new, then I'd still ramp gradually. Would start with smaller batches \(1-2k\), and watch open rates and spam complaints. Then just scale up as metrics stay healthy.

I always see shit like this as just a data collection phase fr. The segments are the infrastructure and engagement data is the fuel. Just let the data accumulate my guy!

posts.title: Steal Angles From Meta Ads Library
posts.content:
Hard but honest truth... Most of our emails aren't actually good.

The only reason our emails make money is because the leads are already warm and would've bought anyway, not because our email actually did real work.

Notice how almost every campaign generates roughly the same amount of money? But every once in a while you get some banger that just has double the performance of the average campaign? We need to work harder to find those emails every time. Those are the banger angles.

If you want emails that actually perform instead of just converting on warm intent, you need banger angles.

The easiest way to find them is by looking at the ads getting tens of thousands of spend behind them a day in the Meta Ads Library \(literally you can look up any brand running ads and all their ads show up here\).

Go to the Meta Ads Library: [https://www.facebook.com/ads/library](https://www.facebook.com/ads/library)
Search your brand or your competitors or any big brand to take inspo
Read the ad copy, the hooks, and the video scripts.

Ad teams spend crazy money finding what actually stops someone mid-scroll, and that same angle will convert just as well in an email.

I went to Mars Men's ad library. Took 5 minutes. Here's some BANGER angles I pulled straight off their ads:

"Man boobs gone or your money back. Three months from now, you're either shirtless and confident, or reaching for the cover-up again."
"We want five men who realize that 'I'm just tired' isn't a personality."
"Please accept our apology."
"I divorced my 'manopause' symptoms..."
"Dear future self, this day will mean as much as the day you took your oath, the day you took your life back."

Every one of those is a headline that could carry an entire email or SMS

Steal steal steal.

posts.title: Klaviyo SMS verification Failed
posts.content:
Our toll-free number verification was rejected with the following message:

“Your toll-free number verification was rejected because the business registration number is invalid or missing.”

Our business is registered in Hong Kong, and our target audience is primarily located in the United States and Europe. We carefully reviewed the information submitted and believe that all business registration details were entered correctly.

Wondering where it went wrong? does anyone have idea abou it

user.name: Femail Marketerrr
user.bio: Call me sizi

comments.content:
Hi [@Femail Marketerrr](obj://user/143f98dad26648bea1b4e7f2ca6eb448) so from what you've shared so far this is most likely a format recognition issue with your Hong Kong registration number, not necessarily wrong information.

US toll-free verification requires business registration number, type, and country. The verification is handled by carrier partners, not Klaviyo, and those systems are mostly built around US EINs. A Hong Kong BR number prob won't match the format their validation expects even if it's 100% legit.

Make sure u double check if the registration type entered correctly for Hong Kong, if the business address exactly as registered, if the phone number valid, and if the email uses a person's name \(so it can't be like an info@ email or something\). Also make sure the website live and accessible bc any of those can trigger rejection.

If it still rejects after checking those then I'd just escalate to Klaviyo support tbh.

One thing worth knowing that goes a level deeper:

US carriers really want a US business identity behind any number sending to US recipients. A Hong Kong BR number will keep hitting friction because their validation is built around US EINs. So even after you fix the field formatting, you may keep running into this.

if you have any US entity or EIN, register the SMS under that, it clears verification way more smoothly. If you don't, you could look into an SMS provider that specifically supports international sender registration into the US, since some handle the carrier paperwork that Klaviyo can't.

user.name: Danie Ortiz
user.bio: Danie

comments.content: Hi [@Danie Ortiz](obj://user/025afa959ae840eaa2524b8915aa974f) ! I would keep it off for flows, specifically because flows like the abandon checkout/cart, welcome, winback, post-purchase, etc are all purposefully set up to send at the time when it's most relevant for the subscriber. let's say a subscriber receives a regular campaign email at 5pm, then they go to the website and add an item to cart, they are technically supposed to receive an abandon cart email 30-60min later, however they will never enter that abandon cart email flow if the smart sending is enabled since they had already received that regular campaign email at 5pm. typically you will want a subscriber to receive the flows always because the messaging is the most relevant to where the subscriber is at in the buying journey at that time

posts.title: Easy Way To Increase Opt-Ins
posts.content:
If you're running pop-ups on [Alia](https://www.aliapopups.com/), there's a feature called Smart Trigger that many brands aren't using that 100% should, and it's basically free upside on your existing pop-up design with no extra work.

Here's what it does:
[ul][li]Normally your pop-up shows once per session and that's it. If someone closes out of the form the pop-up won't fire again[li]Smart Trigger uses an AI model to identify visitors who look high-intent based on their behavior, and shows the pop-up to THEM a second time in the same session, at whatever moment the model thinks is best. [li]This makes it not spammy, not random, and just re-triggering for the people most likely to actually convert.

Alia says it can add up to 20-40% more signups with zero changes to the actual pop-up design...

Proof in results in first image attached for one of our brands... in just the past 5 DAYS we have gotten 2,481 more emails and $95k more sales.

Setup is really easy: Open your pop-up editor, toggle "Smart Trigger" on in the right sidebar, hit publish. That's the whole thing.

Pair it with your normal page-load trigger \(say, a 2-second delay\) so you're capturing first-touch signups AND re-engaging qualified visitors in that same session.

One important catch. Smart Trigger can fire before your paired time delay finishes. So if a brand has a hard rule like "never show the pop-up before X seconds no matter what," Smart Trigger can't guarantee that, there's currently no way to enforce a strict minimum delay while it's enabled. Keep that in mind for any client with a locked-in delay requirement.

Go check every client running Alia and see if this is off. Easy win sitting right there.

posts.title: Couple small questions
posts.content: [ul][li]Is it best for revenue to send at 12pm recipient time or at a certain time zone for a US based company?[li]Which exact Shopify notifications do you replace with Klayvio emails in post purchase to reduce churn?[li]I'm having trouble inboxing designed emails and plaintext works fine. How do you make sure a design is optimized to inbox?

user.name: Florian Ruhstaller
user.bio: Email list manager with big dreams

comments.content:
[@Florian Ruhstaller](obj://user/25feaa3355334940a0919731e28915d7) good questions brother! Let me hit all three:

[ol:1][li]Recipient-local time is usually the safe bet. I'd just pick a set window in ET/CT and test between morning and afternoon, then work off what your own data shows. The best general windows I've seen are 10am EST, 1pm EST, or 6-7pm EST, but seriously just test them on your list and go from there.

2. The main one worth replacing is the order confirmation. It's the single highest open rate email a customer ever gets, so rebuilding it in Klaviyo lets you brand it, set expectations, and drop a soft cross-sell. One important thing though is you need Shopify Plus to override the native order confirmation. Without Plus you can't swap it out, so if your client isn't on Plus, focus on the shipping notifications and your post-purchase flow instead.

[ol:1][li]That's almost always a text-to-image ratio problem. If your designed emails are heavy on images with little live text, spam filters get suspicious. So you cake sure there's a healthy amount of real text \(like a section or two with it\), always add alt text to images, and make sure your code isn't bloated. Basically the more your designed email looks structurally like a normal text email under the hood, the better it inboxes.

Curious how you guys handle copywriting internally. How do your copywriters and AMs collaborate so everyone has the same context for each client?

Every account manager is paired with their copywriter, and that pair works closely on the same set of clients so they're always on the same page. We also do regular meetings where we run down each brand, any changes, client feedback, etc.

The AM owns the content calendar, briefs, and strategy, and the copywriter handles the copy. So it's a clear scope of work that way nobody's stepping on each others toes and whatnot.

For keeping everyone's context aligned, we use a custom platform built called MX for our workflow. It houses copy, calendars, flows, and brand notes all in one place.

But the biggest thing is just communication brother. If a client tells the AM they don't like something, the AM passes it to the copywriter, and it gets logged in the brand notes. Figma is a big one too since copywriters review and edit there and that's where a lot of client feedback lives as well. Our team uses that to actually learn the brand over time.

posts.title: Preference page worth it?
posts.content:
Most big brands I checked barely do anything there. No frequency options, no topic toggles, just unsubscribe. Which makes me think the whole "let them choose fewer emails" thing is more theory than practice.
So curious:
[ol:1][li]Do you even have a preference page, or just straight unsubscribe?[li]If you have one, what options do you offer \(less frequent, pause, topics\)?[li]Does it actually save a meaningful number of unsubs, or is it just there?
My gut says unsubs are a content/frequency problem, not a page problem. But happy to be proven wrong before I skip it.

comments.content:
[@Fred Schneider](obj://user/54459b850d52433fa942e02e8362ea4e) your gut is mostly right. Unsubs are primarily a content and frequency problem, and a preference page won't save someone who's getting blasted with emails they don't care about, so I'd fix that first.

But where the page earns its keep is giving people a step down instead of a step out. Some people don't want to leave, and just want fewer emails. So if their only options are "keep getting everything" or "unsubscribe," a chunk of them will just unsubscribe. So we have our preference pages catch people in different segments who want our emails "once a month" or "only during sales". Have found it keep them a bigger % on the list instead of losing them.

I'm going to attach two SOPs we use for this, one on building and customizing the custom unsubscribe/preference page, and one on activating it and setting up the exclusion segments 💪

Part 1: [https://www.loom.com/share/0ede8dd63ad649fda1050dd6baac62e8](https://www.loom.com/share/0ede8dd63ad649fda1050dd6baac62e8)

posts.title: SMS Abandonment Flows Optimized Setup & Copy 💬
posts.content:
Most brands treat SMS as an afterthought bolted onto email abandonment... Done right, SMS abandonment can make you more money than the email version.

Here's the setup and copy that works:

Sequencing: Email first, wait 5 minutes, then SMS. If someone converts off the email, that is ideal because SMS costs more money to send. And critically, make sure people on both channels get BOTH messages. Don't skip someone to receive SMS-only just because they're subscribed to it \(common mistake\).

The One-Message Rule: In the US, you're legally limited to ONE SMS message per abandonment flow. You cannot send a second follow-up text in the same flow. This is the law, don't build a 3-text SMS sequence for US contacts. Europe is different and multiple messages are fine there, so if you're running international, add 1-2 more messages.

Split By Buyers and Non-Buyers: Exactly like you do in email. Same logic applies here. For non-buyers, remind them of the welcome discount they already have. For past buyers, don't include it \(however you can test adding a new offer here\).

A Few Copy Patterns \(Cart/Checkout, Browse/Site\):
[ul][li]For cart and checkout abandon, buyers get straightforward momentum copy \("your order is packed and ready, you're one click away"\), non-buyers get the discount stacked right into the same message \("your order is ready to ship, use code XY786H for $10 credit"\).[li]For browse and site abandon, buyers get soft "pick up where you left off" framing, non-buyers get the same soft framing PLUS the credit reminder, with urgency added at the end \("expires soon"\).

Use these... and don't forget to test! 🫡

posts.title: 1 day opens, 2 day clicks?
posts.content:
I know we chat about this a lot on the agency calls but I'm thinking about tightening our standard attribution window for clients. I've always stuck to default but now I'm starting to pay more and more attention analytics, I'm considering going down to a 1 day open and 2 day click.

Thoughts? Do you guys stick to default for agency clients? Only tighten when asked to?

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
My guyy [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5). I would just tighten proactively, and wouldn't wait for the clients to ask. If they find the gap themselves then there's a chance ur credibility takes a hit imo. But if you're the one who finds the gap and then fixes it, you become the most trustworthy partner they've had.

1-day open and 2-day click is a solid middle ground. On opens, 1-day is better than default but post-MPP, and any open window still credits phantom Apple opens. I run 0-day personally and just strip opens entirely. But I do think a 1-day is a reasonable compromise tbh. On clicks, 2-day is smart bc someone clicks, browses, and comes back the next day and buys, and that is email-influenced and defensible. For higher-AOV clients with longer consideration cycles, a slightly wider click window can make sense too, so the key is having a rationale not just defaulting.

Will say tho that Klaviyo doesn't change historical data retroactively. Past reports stay at whatever window was set when those campaigns sent, and month-over-month will show a drop that's actually a measurement change, not performance. Note the switch date and tell your clients upfront so nobody panics lol.

The most important thing isn't the exact window. It's that you chose intentionally and can explain why.

posts.title: How Would You Set Klaviyo Attribution for a YouTube and Drop-Driven Brand?
posts.content:
Hey everyone! This is my first post, so I wanted to introduce myself. I’m Lucas Pruss, Head of Email and Marketing at BeefCake Jerky.

This account is under Andrew Flair, BeefCake’s owner, but I’ll be the one posting and learning in here.

I’m trying to determine the most accurate Klaviyo attribution setup for our brand. A large percentage of our revenue comes from limited product drops. Andrew is a YouTuber, and his videos often generate major traffic and revenue spikes when those drops launch.

The issue is that if someone recently opened or clicked one of our emails, Klaviyo may credit the purchase to email even when Andrew’s YouTube video was likely what drove them to buy. This can make Klaviyo-attributed revenue look much higher than email’s actual contribution.

Our current windows are:
Model: Linear
[ul][li]Email open: 1 day[li]Email click: 5 days[li]SMS delivered: 12 hours[li]SMS click: 3 days[li]Non-Klaviyo site activity: 1 day[li]Email and SMS bot interactions excluded[li]Apple MPP opens excluded[li]Transactional messages currently included

For a brand driven by YouTube traffic and major product drops, would you shorten these windows further or focus primarily on click-attributed revenue?

How would you separate the revenue actually driven by email and SMS from revenue driven by Andrew’s videos? Would you use a different attribution model, UTMs, post-purchase surveys, or another reporting method?

I want to give Klaviyo proper credit without letting it claim revenue that likely would have happened from the YouTube video anyway.

user.name: Andrew Flair
user.bio: Jerky lover

comments.content:
Welcome in [@Andrew Flair](obj://user/95a830e01ff846ee83a2999d936c709b) !

The hard truth is Klaviyo attribution will always overclaim when you have a strong external channel like YouTube, so there's no perfect way to separate it in-platform, but your current windows are already pretty tight which is good...

I would probably focus more on click-attributed revenue as your north star because opens are just too fuzzy. ALSO, I'd probably run a post-purchase survey asking "how did you hear about this drop?" and use that as a gut check against Klaviyo's numbers.

Over time you'll get a feel for how inflated Klaviyo's attribution actually is for your brand... might be 20% or 50% depending on how big Andrew's videos are relative to your email sends.

posts.title: Clothing vs CPG Repeat Purchase Data 👀
posts.content:
Pulled repeat purchase timing from WelLTV \(our internal, client only analytics platform\) across niches and the shapes are VERY different. Worth knowing because it should be driving your post-purchase strategy...

Clothing / accessories
[ul][li]Big spike in second orders 4-7 days after the first purchase. That's right around delivery, when the new brand and new product are still exciting and top of mind.[li]Think about a new shirt... you wear it a few times in the first couple weeks because it's still novel.Then it tails off hard after day 21, once it's just another shirt in the closet.[li]How to apply this: don't cool off after someone buys... go aggressive with upsells and cross-sells around delivery of the item. Don't excclude recent buyers from campaigns... keep them in! 

CPG \(beverage, supplement, etc\)
[ul][li]Very different shape. [li]Very low repeat orders in the first 5-7 days, because people are still waiting to actually taste the product and decide if it's worth reordering. [li]Then a long, consistent stretch of high repeat orders from roughly day 10 to 35, since everyone's consumption pace is different. [li]After day 35 it tails off a good amount... if someone hasn't repeated by then, they're probably not in love with the product.[li]How to apply this: Don't try to upsells or cross-sells days 2-7 before they get the product... just focus on education and consumption. Then, days 7-35, have consistent messaging pushing for more orders

Near the tail end of each curve for both, where repeats start dropping off, consider adding an incentive to pull one more order out before that window closes for good.

Match your post-purchase intensity to when people are actually ready to buy again, not to some generic one-size-fits-all cadence 🫡

posts.content:
[@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)

One of my clients just started a new supplement brand, so far he is relying purely on paid traffic and told me to build our email retention.

My question is, since I'm starting from scratch, where do you think I should start.

I'm thinking to go with this order:

[ol:1][li]Pop-up forms[li]Welcome Forms [li]Abandoned Flows [li]Segmentation[li]Campaigns

comments.content:
I agree with the order.
I would first set the basic flows live, see what engagement you get and then send the first campaigns. But this should all not take long we are talking days to set up the core flows with 1-2 mails. So the first campaigns can go out in 7-10 days.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
You're pretty on point here brother, with just a few adjustments:

First, domain authentication. SPF, DKIM, DMARC before you send anything.

Second: Popup + welcome flow simultaneously. The welcome flow needs to be live with the popup, otherwise someone submits and hears nothing. Since the brand runs purely on paid traffic, the popup is doing double duty. Every submit turns a paid visitor who would've bounced into a retargetable profile.

Third: Abandoned cart and checkout.

Fourth should be post-purchase. For supplements it's critical because if someone buys a 30-day supply and doesn't know how to take it or see results, they're gone.

Fifth can be the replenishment flow, and this can tigger when they're running low \(day 25 for a 30-day supply\). Also worth letting ur client know if they don't have subscribe-and-save, supplements are one of the best categories for it. Solves the replenishment problem automatically.

Sixth should be the browse abandonment flow.

And lastly, you'll have campaigns. Once the core flows are live and you have list to send to, that is.

Segmentation isn't a separate step at all bc it's just built into everything through conditional splits from the start. You also def want to start campaigns while building flows. They're independent and actually help build sender reputation. Just ramp things up gradually on a new domain [@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703).

posts.title: Redesign + Content Feedback
posts.content:
I'm trying out this organic strategy with the same kind of redesign thing that Max is doing, and they're for brands I like to use on the daily. Here's my script, and then here's my email redesign. Let me know if you guys have any comments.

Hook: Welcome to part 1 of redesigning emails for brands until they hire me.

Today: Santa Cruz Paleo, owned by the world's healthiest man himself, Mr. Brendan Ruh.
And this one's special. I've been using Santa Cruz's products every single day since the brand started. Brendan's the reason I went all in on organic, whole-food eating four years ago.

\[popups of me with his products + my meals\]

So yeah — this one's personal.
\[old email on screen\]

And this email? It does not do this brand justice.
3 things I noticed off the rip:
One: the copy and the buttons are way too small. Most people read email on their phone, walking around, half-distracted — nobody's stopping to squint and scroll. In an attention economy, if they can't get it in a glance, you've lost them.
Two: there's this random gap at the very end. I have no idea what that's doing there.
Three: there's basically no footer. So if someone scrolls all the way down, they'd never even know Santa Cruz has skincare and sleep products too.

Alright, world's healthiest man. Let's see what I can do.

Now, the brand is so founder-led that instead of a generic best-seller email, I went with a Morning Routine angle — put Brendan front and center and show people exactly how he actually uses these products every single day. When the founder is the proof, you don't have to hard-sell. The routine does the selling for you.

So first, a dopamine-grabbing hero section: logo, headline, a little body copy, and one big fat CTA — because big CTAs equal more clicks.

Then the bridge: the full routine. People don't lie down and read emails the way they doomscroll social. So instead of dense paragraphs, each step is a few skimmable points that deliver the same value — with a CTA for every product. Then it loops back to a "shop the routine" bundle so nobody has to scroll all the way up.

And the footer — where around 50% of email clicks happen — now shows the other categories: skin and healthy-fat products, and sleep.

Brendan, if you're watching: this is part 1 of my series to become the Santa Cruz Paleo email and SMS marketer.
And if you own an ecom brand and want one completely free email plus an audit of your email strategy — DM me "audit" or book a call. I'll find you at least 5 things to optimize, guaranteed.
Peace out.

posts.title: Customizing Your Order / Shipment Notifications
posts.content:
Most brands never touch their order confirmation, shipped, and delivered emails... They just leave the generic Shopify or fulfillment app transactional message running.

That's a massive missed opportunity, because these are some of the highest-engagement emails you'll ever send. People WANT to know where their order is. And for subscription brands specifically, these are also some of your highest-risk cancel moments.

Here's the setup...

1. Order Confirmation, triggered off "Placed Order" in Klaviyo. You can only turn off the basic Shopify order confirmation if you are on Shopify plus, If it's their first order ever, this is where you go deep, welcome messaging, founder note, what to expect, community invite. This is the only one of the three that needs to show shipping info and price paid, since it's the actual receipt. Make sure to customize if this is someone's first order, second, third, etc! The more you can tailor it, then better

2. Order Shipped, triggered off "Fulfilled Order" in Klaviyo. No pricing or receipt info, just a Track My Shipment button and content that builds the brand and educates on the product.

3. Order Delivered, triggered off "Delivered Shipment" in Klaviyo. Same rule, no price shown, just tracking plus more brand experience. This is where you want to go harder on how to use the product. You can also time further educational messaging off of this by having follow up emails off of this trigger.

Important to turn off the basic emails and replace them with these... don't double send. And reminder, for Order Confirmation you must be on Shopify Plus to turn off the email and you have to do it through the support team.

Everyday Dose does this exceptionally well \(attached\). They fill these emails with founder story, how-to-use education, a gamified rewards system, SMS opt-in, community invite, and more. Doing onboarding work in an email people are already excited to open.

posts.title: The "Secret Page" Trick For Email/SMS Welcome 👀
posts.content:
True Sea Moss does something simple and clever...

Their email and SMS flows for non-buyers link to a special landing page instead of the normal PDP.

The page itself is identical. Literally same product, same discount, and same offer they'd get anywhere. But the headline at the top says "Secret Deal For Email & SMS Subscribers... You Found Our Secret Page!"

A discount on a normal PDP feels like something everyone gets... The same discount behind a "secret page" feels like insider access, like you get this because you're on the list. It reframes the exact same math into a reward for being a subscriber instead of just another sale banner.

Costs basically nothing to build. Duplicate your PDP, change the top headline to something like "You Found Our Secret Page" or "Secret Deal For Subscribers Only," and route your email/SMS non-buyer flows there instead of the normal product page.

Here's their page: [https://trueseamoss.com/products/sea-moss-gel-superfood-surprise](https://trueseamoss.com/products/sea-moss-gel-superfood-surprise)

posts.title: Winback Flow Sauce
posts.content:
The winback flow targets people who bought in the past but haven't bought in awhile...

We need to understand that these users gotten 3-4+ campaigns a week from us for months and still haven't bought. They've seen big sales, big launches, and big promos.. and STILL haven't bought. We need to understand this.

Here's what you should do...

Don't Do The "We Miss You" Messaging
If months of campaigns with sales and drops didn't convert them, a soft sentimental email won't either. These people need a real reason... The offer is the entire strategy here.

Testing Offers Is All That Matters
The only way people will buy is with an offer... but not just any offer. Different offers will convert at completley different rates, so your biggest lever in your winback flow is to test them. Store credit with a random specific number like $7.14, BOGO, bundles, free gift with purchase, percentage off, dollar off. All your time in the winback flow should be testing these.

Timing Should Be Average Repeat Purchase Day × 3
Multiply when people usually come back times 3 and that should be the trigger for people entering the winback. 45-day repeat window means winback triggers around day 135. I've found this to be the safest and makes the most sense.

Build It On A Segment, Not A Time Delay
Don't trigger off "placed order" + 120-day delay, or the flow sits active for 120 days before anyone enters the first email. Instead trigger from a segment: placed an order in the last 121 days AND not in the last 119. That captures everyone who hit day 120 today, refreshes daily, and starts generating revenue immediately. Add a time delay before Email 1 so it fires around 11 AM local instead of at midnight when the segment refreshes.

The 4-Email Structure
Email 1 \(Day 1\): Text-based, genuine check-in \("hey, is everything okay?"\), first offer introduced immediately, feeling like a personal message
Email 2 \(~2-3 days later\): Graphic, winback energy, reinforce the same offer with visual impact.
Email 3 \(~1 week later\): Different offer entirely if they haven't converted. Maybe store credit instead of percent off, or bundle instead of BOGO.
Email 4 \(~3 days later\): Final push on the second offer, with urgency

The whole flow hinges on the OFFER. Test test test test.

posts.title: How to double opt in?
posts.content:
I know we shouldn´t use it, but since im in germany and my clients use it \(because they have to\), i was wondering how to optimize double opt in. I set up a Popup with alia and the first a/b test winner had 13.8% submit rate but only 8.82% after double opt in. And the opt-in is trending downwards. So we lose 40% of people here. Which feels like a lot, but what are target numbers here? I made sure to communicate it clearly in the final step of the popup that they are "almost done". They just have to:
1. open their mail app
2. look for our mail
3. get their discount
4. And if no email comes, look into spam and promotions tab.
I also checked the doi-mail, but it gets in the primary inbox for all main providers instantly. So it might be about people beeing not exited enough? So im testing the mystery offer right now. Anyways, what are you thoughts, tipps and tricks?

comments.content:
You're fighting an uphill battle here brother... so I would optimize what you can but don't beat yourself up over the drop. 40% drop on double opt-in is actually pretty normal.

You can make the confirmation email itself more engaging. You can add a reason to click beyond just "confirm" and pivot the messaging to "confirm to unlock your mystery discount" or "confirm to reveal your gift.".. Whatever your offer actually is just hype it up more.

In the first welcome email, I'd also get engagement signals early and add in deliverability boosters \(starring the email, replying with an emoji, having them moving to primary, etc..\) I added an inspo for what we use for teasers before a big drop / announcement but the same principles still apply here too.

comments.content:
Hi [@Tjure Lohse](obj://user/1a5394d0c5c24bc3a31531d5f3d0f9e9) MailTimers is already pretty solid imo. So if ur already using it and just need the watermark gone, then the paid plan is worth it. Sendtric and CountdownMail are good alternatives too that I've tried. The tools all do the same thing so it's more about just picking one and rolling with it.

What's more important is how you're using them strategically.

For campaigns \(like flash sales and promos\), I'd use a fixed-date timer counting down to a specific deadline. For flows \(like abandonment, welcome offer expiration\), use an evergreen timer that starts when the email is opened bc everyone enters flows at different times so a fixed deadline doesn't work.

Don't put timers on everything though.

If every email has a countdown, the urgency will def lose its impact. Reserve them for sends where the deadline is real and the offer actually expires. A timer on a static code that never expires is fake urgency and customers figure ts out quick.

posts.title: Subscription Offers + Pop-Up Offers, Done Right
posts.content:
Ran a first order subscription offer test for a client and first order subscription take rate jumped from 30% to 60%... First-order subscribers have double the 6-month LTV of one-time buyers, so doubling the first order subscriber take rate is massive. Offers are the biggest driver of this, so here's how to do subscription and pop-up offers RIGHT.

⭐️ The First Order Subscription Offer

10% off recurring isn't enough to justify the commitment to susbcription in someone's head... You need an offer that makes subscription the clear winner.

Instead, you should have a front-loaded discount offer.

We do not want to do 20% OFF subscription forever... it has nothing special for the first order and giving 20% off margin forever is tough.

Instead, you should do something like 30% OFF first order, 10% OFF recurring. Get people to subscriber with a front-loaded large first order discount... then drop the recurring charge to save on margin and let the quality of your product keep people subscribed.

Add strategic gifts if you can, but make them functional. Stuff they'd buy anyway to use with the product that contributed to the experience... frother for coffee, shaker for supplements, applicator for skincare. These are great and really make an impact... just make sure they are low cost to fulfill.

⭐️ Pop-Up Offer

Most common mistake I see: brands have a subscription offer, then run a pop-up discount that only works on one-time purchase... Someone signs up for 15% off on the pop-up, tries to stack it on a subscription order which gives 15% off as well, then they gets an error saying the code isn't valid there. They rage-leave or ditch subscription and buy one-time instead. You just lost a subscriber worth 2x+ over a discount code issue.

Fix your pop-up offer in one of three ways:
[ul][li]Make the pop-up your subscription offer, no extra discount. Just highlight the offer you already give. "You've Got 46% Off + 3 Free Gifts," auto-applied. This is what Gruns, IM8, and Everyday Dose do... literally no extra discount code or anything, just highlight what you already give. [li]Give an extra discount on subscription only, stacked into one number. 20% off subscription you already give on PDP pages plus an extra 10% via pop-up code. Just make sure your pop-up doesn't say 10% off... it becomes "30% Off First Order," becuase of 20%+10%. One-time orders pay full price.[li]Give an extra discount that works on both sub and one time, framed as "Up To 30% Off" so the stacked number still leads. For example, if you give 20% off for subscription and give an extra 10% off in your pop-up or welcome flow that works subscription and one time... don't have your pop-up say 10%... have it say "Up To 30% Off" because that sounds better than 10% and will convert better. Your messaging in welcome flow becomes 30% off if you subscribe, 10% off if you place a one time order

In Summary:
[ul][li]Subscription Offer: Every brand should have a front-loaded subscription discount with higher discount on first subscriptuion order... such as 30% OFF your first order and 10% OFF recurring
Add functional and strategic free gifts that contribute to the customer experience and are low cost to fulfill.
[ul][li]Pop-Up Offer: Ideally, just give no extra discount and highlight your subscription offer if it's already a banger \(for example IM8 organically gives 30% OFF + 4 free gifts... so their pop-up form just highlights that\). If you give an extra discount, make sure the code works on subscription and stack the offer. If you give 20% off subscription and are giving an extra 10% for email, your pop-up form should say "30% OFF", not 10%. 

Offers are king!! Get this right and take rate will skyrocket and LTV will skyrocket.

posts.title: Apparel - Flows vs Campaigns
posts.content:
I have my own take but would love to hear how others are thinking about this. When you are working with a brand that has a bunch of SKUS and different personas living within 1 brand, what's your take on how niching down vs going generic on flows vs campaigns?

Example - Sunglass brand sells sunglasses, eye glasses, swim goggles, ski goggles, and red light glasses. How are you segmenting/speaking to each of these audiences in flows vs campaigns?

user.name: Chad Ross
user.bio: Head of Retention @ Hollow Socks

comments.content:
Yooo what's up bro [@Chad Ross](obj://user/45eb6e82bafc44aa8b26e775e4ad09bc) good to learn from you earlier on today's call!

In terms of this, the move here is lowkey somewhere in between "build 5x of everything" and "keep it all generic" tbh.

If we wanna go through this in depth here, we gotta start with the flows. I believe it should be one flow per type, with conditional splits inside. Post-purchase is prob gonna matter the most here bc someone who bought ski goggles would need different content AND a different tone than someone who just bought red light glasses.

So it should be one post-purchase flow, split by product category, with different branches. Abandoned cart handles itself through Klaviyo's dynamic product blocks. The welcome flow stays mostly universal, and just personalize product recs in Email 2-3 based on browsing. A micro-commit popup that reads along the lines of "what are you shopping for" makes that personalization way sharper from the first email.

Then for campaigns, I would run three tiers.

Universal for brand story, site-wide sales, seasonal, with a full engaged list. Should also be segmented for category launches \(like maybe new ski goggle drop goes to ski goggle buyers and browsers, not everyone\). And u could have one campaign with dynamic content blocks showing different products to different segments.

Now, the mistake is 5x of everything, which we know would be unsustainable 😂. The other mistake is keeping everything generic when ski goggle buyers and red light therapy users have different motivations for buying and staying engaged. So having smart splits in the flows, with a mix of universal and dynamic campaigns would be the sweet spot for me imo but lmk ur thoughts!

posts.title: Gamifying More Clicks 👀
posts.content:
Most emails could be getting 50% higher clicks just by using some tricks here and there... let's highlight a few of them

1. Click to activate the discount.
Anytime you do an offer, tell people they have to click the email to activate their offer and then update the link to include the discount at the end so it is auto-applied. Very important for welcome emails and I highly recommend using this framing in your sale emails.

2. The gamified tap.
"Tap for good luck,"... "tap for good mojo before your next round," whatever fits the brand. This football brand does "click for good luck" for the upcming match. Works for literally any brand... like for a golf brand, you could say tap for good mojo before your round. Skincare brand, tap for good skin today.

3. Magic button.
Throw in a magic button here and there in your emails. Just link them to wherever you want on the website but the curiosity gets people to click

4. Click to reveal.
Offer or product hidden until they click. You could do this with a new product release or some sort of product recommendation where you blur it out and you say "click to reveal". You can also do it with some sort of mystery offer, such as "click to reveal your mystery offer", and you use a discount code that they then have to use at checkout.

5. Click for early access.
If you have something new coming up, you can do something like "Click for early access" or "Click for VIP" or "Click to be added to this exclusive list." Make it seem exclusive and you'll get a lot of clicks. Like this example, which is "Click to be the first to know." You don't necessarily have to segment off of this but it's a good way to get extra clicks.

What other ones have you guys seen?

posts.title: Open rates dropped from ~50% to ~32% despite a much larger engaged audience
posts.content:
Hi everyone,

I'm hoping some experienced retention marketers can help me think through this.
I'm managing email marketing for a fashion eCommerce brand, and I'm running into something I can't fully explain.

Our 30-day engaged segment has almost tripled in size compared to our best-performing month.
At the same time, the business itself is growing very quickly through paid ads and is on pace to roughly double its monthly revenue.
However, our campaign performance has steadily declined.

Compared to our strongest month:
[ul][li]Open rates have dropped from around 50% to the low 30% range.[li]Click rates have declined.[li]Revenue per recipient has declined.[li]Overall campaign performance is much weaker.

I've attached screenshots of the campaign data.
The left screenshot shows our recent campaign performance \(July\), while the right screenshot shows our strongest period \(May\). Both are based on campaigns sent to the same 30-day engaged segment.

One thing worth mentioning is that I don't think this is a deliverability issue. Our deliverability is still healthy overall, bounce rates are low, and we're not seeing unusual spam folder placement. Of course there's always room for improvement, but there are no obvious deliverability problems.

My question is: where would you focus first?

At the moment, my flows continue to perform very well, but my campaigns have become significantly weaker, and that's what I'm trying to solve.
I'd really appreciate hearing how you would approach this and what you would prioritize first.

comments.content:
whats up [@Cyril Sudepally](obj://user/2bc1024eb8f54f6e855befbd937f7e04) here are some of my thoughts. I used whispr flow and had Chatgpt clean up my text so forgive the ai slop... but its my actual thoughs.

Really like the design overall—it looks clean and visually appealing.

One thing I'd change is the first question. Since it's a quiz popup, I'd make it about the customer rather than the brand. Instead of asking their favorite flavor, ask something like "What do you need energy for?" \(Work, gym, studying, etc.\). It makes the quiz feel more personalized and gives you useful segmentation data.
From there, I'd have the flow go:

Quiz → Email → SMS → Success page.
On the SMS step, I'd tweak the copy. Instead of positioning it as "early access," keep the messaging centered around the discount since that's why they're signing up. Something like "You're almost there—enter your phone number to reveal your mystery discount." Make it really clear what they get in exchange for their information.

I'd also have the success page tell them to check their email for the discount code instead of revealing it immediately. That encourages people to open the email, which helps build positive engagement and can improve deliverability over time.

Overall, I like how simple and easy the popup is to read. I'd also test making it a full-screen popup and have it appear around 3–6 seconds after someone lands on the site.

One last thing I'd A/B test is the product image at the bottom. It looks nice, but I'd be curious to see if removing it gives the CTA and copy more focus. I wouldn't be surprised if the version without the image converted a little better—the data will tell you.

posts.title: "Free" Beats % OFF Every Time
posts.content:
Was auditing a large brand who frequently runs 25% OFF off site-wide or a specific prodcut.

Their campaigns leading with 25% off never do crazy numbers...

Then I looked at their actual top performing campaigns... they were all buy 3, get 1 free offers.

Let's think about that... that is literally the SAME EXACT OFFER... 25% off is literally buy 3 get 1 free...

But one converts way better AND gets you a higher AOV.

The human brain is so funny.

Because people don't shop with a calculator, they shop with gut reaction and emotion. And "get one free" hits harder than "25% off"...

Free is a magic word and feels like a gift.

So... I'm pushing this brand to ditch percent off everywhere and reframe every flow offer AND their acquisition offer on ads as buy 3 get 1 free instead.

And when you do these offers make sure you properly visualize and let people see exactly what they're getting free!

:point_right: Go look at your clients' offers... Anywhere you're running a percent off that maps cleanly to a free item or free unit, test the free framing instead. Whenever you can turn a percent into a free, try it and do it!

posts.title: How I Audit Email Accounts
posts.content:
People always ask if I have some template or checklist I fill out when I audit... I don't but I've done over a thousand of these, so it's mostly feel now. But there IS an order I move in every single time and the main things I'm looking for.

Here's the exact framework.

1. Funnel context
Before I touch the email account, I look at how the business actually acquires customers... Pull up the website, dig through the Meta ad library, and see what pages and what products they're driving traffic to. Are they sending everyone to the homepage, a PDP, a listicle, a quiz? What's the hero product they're spending to push? What offers are they using. This gives me a sense of what our email strategy should be.

2. Quick sweep on the account
A few minutes, just context, before diving deep. I want to know:
[ul][li]How many campaigns a week are they sending to their engaged list?[li]What's their total email-attributed revenue?[li]What's the flow vs campaign split?[li]Do they have all the core flows, or are they missing bases?[li]How's deliverability at a glance?
Everything's connected, so I need this before I judge anything. You can't evaluate flows without knowing what campaigns are doing...

3. List growth
Top of the funnel, so I look here first. New subs vs unsubs, shooting for at least 3:1, if any less than that we have a serious problem. Then the pop-up form, which is usually where the single biggest lever is. I look at the trigger \(making sure it's a 2-8 second delay\), the format, and most importantly the offer. What's the submit rate, and do I think I can beat it?

4. Flows
In the order the customer hits them:
[ul][li]Welcome: one email every single day, offer highlighted in every email, text-based mixed in. Urgency at end. Ideally increase offer at end.[li]Abandonments: 4+ emails, text-based mixed in, split by buyers vs non-buyers, enticing offers front and center.[li]Post-purchase: immediate upsells and cross-sells, plus real education, not just a transactional thank you.[li]Win-back: make sure it's actually live and running offers.

5. Campaigns
Two things here:
[ul][li]Frequency: how many campaigns a week to the wide engaged segment? I want at least 3-4.[li]Strategy: what content are they sending, can it be better, and how optimized are the creatives?

6. Deliverability
Last pass. Make sure nothing looks off on opens, clicks, and spam complaint rates. If something's out of the ordinary, that's when I dig into inbox placement.

You start with how they acquire, get your context, then move top-down through the funnel, list growth into flows into campaigns.

Watch me literally do this all LIVE in this video... probably the most valuable training I have made: [https://youtu.be/Olt1rwjhS6o?si=_l7_3sNT9zAC1ld7](https://youtu.be/Olt1rwjhS6o?si=_l7_3sNT9zAC1ld7)

comments.content:
Also Max posted this on X about this \(I am such a fanboy 🤓\):

The "it's too expensive" objection is a LIE.

Whether it's someone cancelling their subscription in your ecom brand or you are an agency on a sales call, "it's too expensive" isn’t what it actually means.

It just means they didn't see or get the value they thought they signed up for.

You could call a $50,000 Toyota Camry expensive. But if that same $50,000 got you a Lamborghini, suddenly it's a steal, and most people would figure out how to find the money for it.

When you hear "it's too expensive," that's not really feedback on your price… it's feedback on the value.

> You didn't make the outcome feel worth the price.
> You didn't show them the ROI they'd actually get.
> You didn't dig into what they're really after.

I've stopped letting brands \(and myself\) hide behind "it's too expensive," because it covers up the real question underneath.

Was it the price they had a problem with? or was the value too low in their head?

posts.title: ~6.5K list, barely emailed for a year — how do I restart without nuking my deliverability?
posts.content:
Hi Max and everyone,
I run a fashion brand that's almost a year old. Up until now I've barely done any email — just 1–2 basic flows \(welcome + abandoned cart\), no regular campaigns at all.
The list has now grown to ~6.5K profiles and I want to finally get serious about email. My questions:
[ol:1][li]What should I do with these 6.5K subscribers first? I'm guessing blasting a campaign to all of them at once is a bad idea, since most haven't heard from me in months — but what's the right way to warm them back up?[li]Should I clean the list before doing anything? If so, how do you decide who to cut — and is there any way to try re-engaging them before deleting?
I'm pretty newbie at this, so any help is much appreciated. Thanks!

user.name: Thong Chu
user.bio: Entrepreneur - Solo Investor

comments.content:
Hi [@Thong Chu](obj://user/1b94cfbf3f73430fa0266c1d35ab4398)! So the good news is that your welcome and abandoned cart flows have been running, so your domain isn't fully cold. ISPs have seen emails from you, and you can ramp faster than starting from zero. Still shouldn't blast 6.5k on day one though 😅.

What I would do is validate first and run the list through a platform like DeBounce or one similar to get rid of invalid addresses. A year of growth with minimal sending means some have gone bad and any hard bounces on a ramp-up will hurt.

Then I would segment by engagement, and start with people who've engaged with my flows recently \(conditions like opened or clicked in the last 30-60 days should do the trick for you\) plus recent subscribers. These ppl know your brand and will engage positively.

Finally, I'd simply just ramp over 2-3 weeks. Week 1 should be the first campaign to 30-day engaged only. I'd make it something re-introductory since you've never sent campaigns before, so something along the lines of "we're getting serious about email, here's what to expect." Watch open rates and spam complaints on that first campaign. Then for week 2 you could expand to 60-90 day. Expand further for week 3 if ur metrics are healthy.

Would also suppress profiles, and not actually delete them. Suppressed profiles stop counting toward billing but the data stays whole. Before suppressing anyone though, send lapsed subscribers a 2-3 email re-engagement sequence. Anyone who doesn't respond to that gets suppressed, and that's a fair chance given tbh.

Make sure you keep your existing flows running too. Once the ramp-up is rolling, ur gonna want to build out post-purchase and browse abandonment. For fashion specifically, I'd prioritize a consistent new arrivals campaign cadence. I say this because fashion retention is driven by newness, and your repeat buyers come back for what just dropped, not to replenish. That campaign rhythm is probably your highest-value move once warmup is done. LMK your thoughts!

replies.content:
[@Alice Roberts](obj://user/8f6323726f7e4c2ca2f1271d9c652ff5) In this case you'd follow the same framework as above, but at 100k the ramp needs to be much more careful.

Would def still validate before un-suppressing, and just export the list and run it through DeBounce or a similar platform. With 100k dormant profiles, ur gonna have a chunk that are invalid and hard bounces at that volume can get your domain blacklisted. Also check that SPF, DKIM, DMARC are still configured since it's been a while.

Make sure u don't un-suppress everyone at once too. 100k profiles going active overnight is a spam signal no matter how good the emails are so I'd simply do it in small batches. You could segment by recency, with the most recent activity first, as they're most likely to remember you.

Still remember to ramp up slowly as well. Week 1 should be ur most recent segment, at 500-1000 sends per day. Monitor everything, and then for week 2 go for the next recency tier and increase volume. Expand for weeks 3-4 if ur metrics are healthy. Week 5 can be the older segments \(carefully tho\).

You took time getting the design and brand right so I'd lead with that honestly. You could frame it as "We've been heads down building something we're proud of." That's way better imo than just pretending the gap didn't happen tbh.

But lastly, set realistic expectations! How much you recover depends on how long they've been dormant. So realistically you're reactivating a portion, not all 100k, which is honestly fine. 25-40k genuinely engaged subscribers is a strong list, and trying to force all 100k back hurts deliverability for the ones who actually want to hear from you. Anyone who doesn't engage should def stay suppressed.

replies.content:
[@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) Nice info [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) , mad props for all the knowledge you're bring up

I previously managed the deliverability team @ Klaviyo for APAC in Sydney Australia :\)

[@Alice Roberts](obj://user/8f6323726f7e4c2ca2f1271d9c652ff5) I checked your ecomm site on your profile and I cna see all your DNS records are properly set up

Here's a step by step guide if anyone else is interested on how to warm up 100k profiles:

DO NOW, before any send
[ul][li]Check DKIM, SPF and DMARC records are all set up on the domain for maximum deliverability. Ask Claude how to do this.[li]Verify Google Postmaster Tools on your domain too. It's your only ground truth for Gmail spam rate and reputation, and you want the graphs running from day 1.[li]Run the list through Debounce/Kickbox and expect 10-40% to fail and be removed. Suppress them, don't delete.[li]Keep your flows running the entire time. They're doing warmup work in the background every day.[li]Send 2 campaigns a week, same days. Tuesday/Friday works. Consistency itself is a ranking signal.

Week 1 \(5k-10k profiles\)

Segment: Clicked or bought in the past 90 days. Aim for ~5k. If it's more, shrink the day window until it dips just under.

Subject: you get first look, if you want it
Personal plain-text message from the founder. Ask them to REPLY with "YES!" to get exclusive shots of the new collection days before anyone else. You could even set up a waitlist so they order first. Zero links, zero images. The replies REALLY set up your deliverability, so reply to every single one personally with a link and a message \(links in a 1:1 reply are free, links in the campaign aren't\).

Friday: same email, fresh subject line, to the rest of the segment, but only if Tuesday ran green.

What to look for: opens 50%+, replies 2-10%, bounces under 1%, spam complaints under 0.05%. Bounce over 2% means your list cleaning had a gap. Stop expanding and re-verify before the next send. Tag everyone who replies into a "First Look" segment if you'd like- they're keen.

Week 2 \(10k-25k profiles\)

Segment expands: Opened/clicked past 90 days OR placed order past 180 days.

Tue: First Look segment only. Show one upcoming piece 24-48h before anyone else. Promise kept, habit formed. One image, one link is good.

Fri: the expansion send to the new, cooler profiles. Founder re-introduction: "we went quiet, here's what's changing, about one email a week, and the unsubscribe below works fine if it's not for you."

What to look for: opens 40%+, clicks 1.5%+, complaints under 0.08%. Check opens split by Gmail vs Outlook vs Yahoo. If one provider is 15+ points behind the others, hold that group at current volume while the rest keep scaling.

Week 3 \(25k-50k\), first commercial send
Segment expands again: opened/clicked/ordered in the past 365 days.
Tue: First Look gets the actual drop, 24h early.

Fri: same drop to everyone you've warmed so far. Story-first: why you made it, one detail that proves you sweated it, "First Look saw it yesterday, here's your window." NO discount or sales language in the email.

Week 4 \(full engaged list\)
Tue: normal campaign to everyone engaged in the last 12 months. First Look still goes 24h early. That's permanent now.

Fri: dormants \(12-24 months\) in 5-10k chunks. Soft re-permission: "you bought from us in \[year\], we sent you nothing, that changes now. Here's what's coming." One button if they want in on early access.

Week 5, cleanup + steady state
Anyone older than 24 months \(that survived verification\): one re-permission email, single button, "keep me on the list." No click after 2 attempts = suppressed. That's a fair chance.

Then steady state: at leat one consistent weekly new-arrivals/drop campaign.

The rule underneath all of it: after every send, green metrics = double the audience next send, borderline = repeat the same size, bad = halve it and tighten the segment.

Easy!

posts.title: Using CHARACTERS To Improve Conversions
posts.content:
People want to buy from people... not faceless corporations. So put real people behind your emails instead of sending everything from the faceless brand.

These are character emails, text-based sends written from a specific named person on the team, and they work for a few reasons.

[ol:1][li]They humanize the brand. "Alex from the warehouse team" or "Daniel, Founder" feels like a human reaching out, and people buy from humans they like more than from a logo.[li]They're a pattern interrupt. Change the sender name to a new person and it stands out cold in the inbox. "Megan, Customer Success" stands out more than the same brand name they've seen 50 times.[li]And they unlock messaging you can't do from the brand voice. A person can hijack the account, share a personal story, give you a heads up, be cheeky in a way the corporate brand never could...

Look at the range across these...
[ul][li]Alex from the warehouse team gives a "we're almost sold out" scarcity heads up.[li]Austin from the product team talking about a new release coming out[li]Daniel the founder tells a three-generations-in-a-garage Father's Day story, then slips the sale into a P.S.[li]Megan from customer success plays the helpful gift-guide angle before a shipping cutoff.[li]Alice from marketing "hijacks" the account for a cheeky discount.[li]Clark, the owner's dog, sending an appreciation email

Pick a few real \(or fake\) people/characters on the team, give them a sender name and a personality, and let emails come from them.

Easy fun thing to do!

posts.title: 🤖 AI copy vs human copy

So Max posted the below on X and I am curious how you guys are handling this...

I personally have AI write things out for me, then go in and make edits. So I have a hybrid approach.

My unpopular opinion is that AI has officially hit a plateau.

We're at a point now where we're actively DECREASING our AI usage.

We've basically moved off AI for copy because it's just bad at it lol…

Our best copywriters end up spending more time editing the AI than if they'd just written it from scratch.

The second somebody senses AI in your copy… alarm bells go off and you lose all chance of converting.

It comes across as non-genuine and that you are lazy marketer…

But on the flip side, our AI usage for tools and systems has gone way up…

We built our own analytics tool with AI and it's been a huge differentiator.

AI has always been great at some things and bad at others.

Less AI copy… more AI systems.

posts.title: Post-quiz email flow (product recommendation quiz) — best practices?
posts.content:
Running an ads → quiz funnel where the quiz gives customers a personalized product recommendation. Want to tighten up the email side after that.

Curious what's worked for you guys:
[ul][li]Frequency — how many emails after the quiz, and how spaced out?[li]Angles — do you lead with the recommended product, or mix in other hooks too?[li]Omnichannel — email-only, or are you stacking SMS in there too?[li]Results — any benchmarks or wins you're cool sharing?

Would love to hear what's actually working for your mates. TY!

user.name: Biel Boada
user.bio: Scaling E-commerce Through Email Marketing | Klaviyo Expert 📨

comments.content:
I used a voice note and spoke my thoughts into AI, and then it helped me format it, so ignore it if it sounds a little like AI. These are all my thoughts, lol:

So really this is just your welcome flow with the quiz recommendation baked in... I'd treat it the same way rather than building some separate thing.

Frequency... for most brands I'd run the normal 4 to 5 emails, one a day, first one firing immediately after they finish the quiz. If it's a subscription-first brand or the type where leads go cold fast, you can push harder, two on day one \(immediate + a few hours later\) then daily, 7+ emails. That's because those brands only need the one purchase and getting cold is the real risk. So it depends on the brand... don't go crazy aggressive if you don't need to.

Angles... lead with the recommended product, that personalization is the whole hook, so email 1 is "based on your answers, here's your match" and why it's right for them. But I wouldn't make every email just "buy your rec" or it gets stale. After that, mix in the usual welcome beats framed around their result... social proof from people with the same problem, a bit of education/objection handling on that product, then urgency/last chance and a text-based founder email near the end. One thing that quietly kills these funnels: make sure the offer in the flow matches whatever the quiz or landing page promised.

I also wouldn't overbuild the segmentation. You don't need ten separate flows per quiz outcome unless you're a big brand... one flow that dynamically shows their recommended product based on their answers is the minimum viable version and does most of the work.

Omnichannel... yeah I'd stack SMS if you can. These ads to quiz funnels are usually aggressive acquisition so SMS earns its spot. Daily SMS through the welcome and abandonment, keep it mostly plain text \(like 80/20\) and only drop an image in when it actually adds something, like a before/after or a comparison. That said, if your email side isn't fully dialled yet, get that right first.

Benchmarks... honestly I'd judge it against your own numbers more than anyone else's, too many variables differ between brands. Rough target for a welcome/quiz flow is 10%+ placed order rate. Test it and compare against what you were doing before.
