posts.title: QUICK PATTERN INTERRUPTS
posts.content:
Every email looks the same...

Branded hero, bridge, product section, branded images, repeat...

Your customer's whole inbox is that same layout over and over, yours included...

So, break that pattern!

These are quick pattern interrupt emails. Just a hero section with a direct call to action.

\[OPTIONAL\] They mimic something familiar from your phone, an incoming call, an AirDrop, a notes app, so it stops feeling like an email and starts feeling like a notification you actually check.

Look at these three...
[ul][li]Willie's Remedy: subject line "Incoming call," open it and it's a full slide-to-answer lock screen.[li]hope&plum: "Incoming AirDrop: accept or decline," open it and there's the AirDrop prompt for a new product.[li]HOPR: "Leaked notes app," open it and it's a screenshot of a Friday night checklist.

Nothing else in the inbox looks like any of these...

Two reasons they work:
[ol:1][li]They stand out twice, once with the subject line to get the open, once with the visual to hold it. [li]And they cut cognitive load... one idea, one action, no wall of copy or ten products to wade through... just hey here's what's happening click here 

Mix these in and they'll regularly be some of your best performers of the month.

Just don't overdo it, the whole power is the novelty.

Every email a pattern interrupt and it stops interrupting anything.

posts.title: How do you guys determine campaign frequency?
posts.content:
It's my understanding that deliverability/list growth/engaged segments play a big role in if you send everyday, 2x, or 3-4x a week.

user.name: Mahad Abdi
user.bio: Committed to learning, improving, and being better than yesterday.

comments.content:
Yo yo. At minimum, 2x per week. Ideally, every other day that would be 3-4x per week.

And that's to our base-wide engaged list 90-day engaged.

However, we have a lot of brands where we send every single day, usually the eight nine-figure brands.

It is all based, in my opinion, on subscribers compared to unsubscribers. You want to be at around 3x the amount of people joining your list compared to unsubscribing and leaving your list. If you have 10x the amount of people joining than leaving, you can probably increase your campaign frequency and risk higher unsubscribes with sending more. If you're sitting at even list growth \(the same amount of people joining as leaving\), either your pop-up form sucks and you're not getting people to join the list, or you're sending too much and getting crazy unsubscribes. Usually, that 3:1 is the best ratio. If you're anything higher, send more. If you're anything lower, focus on list growth and send less.

posts.title: Two Post Purchase Myths 👀
posts.content:
Two post-purchase myths that may be impacting your results...

[WATCH MY VIDEO EXPLANATION >>](https://supercut.ai/share/well-copy/fM5iLhweYZXKou962Vv9CO)

Pulled data from a nine-figure apparel brand that flips two things most people believe about post-purchase...

Myth 1:
"Exclude recent buyers... they just bought so they won't buy again for a bit"

Most brands do not do intricate purchase flows AND/OR they exclude fresh buyers from campaigns for the first 21-30 days to "give them space to rebuy."

Look at the data... 50% of all repeat orders in a 90-day window came within the first 21 days. And this brand was sending them near nothing during that exact window. Imagine if they actually pushed rebuying...

Think about where the customer's head is right after buying... Warm, excited, honeymoon phase with a brand they already like. Send with frequency, upsell early, and ride the excitement before they get excited about the next new brand they see!

Myth 2:
"Cross-sell everything!"

Brands obsess over mapping the perfect cross-sell... for example if someone bought a t-shirt, push them to beach bags, then pants etc.

This brand's agency poured effort into these paths.

The data says the opposite! Over half of repeat orders bought the same product again, just a different style. Someone who buys a t-shirt is telling you they're a t-shirt buyer. Sell them more t-shirts in new styles, don't drag them into a category they never signaled.

Same reason supplement brands chasing new SKUs often get it wrong... they sell creatine, so they launch protein trying to cross-sell... The better play is usually more of what's working... new flavors, new formats, gummies vs powder, etc

So two changes for your post-purchase:
[ul][li]Sell early and aggressively in those first few weeks instead of backing off[li]Lead with more of the same before you ever reach for a cross-sell

comments.content:
ai is great for deciding whether tests are meaningful. ChatGPT had this to say:

What this means
[ul][li]Subject B appears to perform a bit better on opens \(+3.1 percentage points\).[li]It also appears better on clicks \(+1.7 percentage points\).[li]However, with only about 1,100 recipients per variant, those differences are well within what could happen by chance.
Revenue
Variant A generated €1,995 vs €1,207 for B.
That looks like a large difference, but you can't test statistical significance from this screenshot alone because revenue per recipient is highly skewed. We'd need recipient-level data \(or at least the distribution of order values\) to perform a proper significance test.
Interestingly:
[ul][li]A: 22 orders[li]B: 17 orders
That's only a difference of 5 customers, and that is far from statistically significant. The revenue gap is mainly explained by:
[ul][li]more purchasers in A, and/or[li]a higher average order value \(€91 vs €71\).
Overall conclusion
If this were my A/B test, I would call it inconclusive. There is no statistically significant winner based on the available data.
If this is a Klaviyo subject line test, I'd probably collect at least 3,000–5,000 recipients per variant \(or more, depending on the effect size you're trying to detect\) before making a decision. With only ~1,100 per variant, you typically only detect fairly large improvements.

posts.title: The RIGHT Way To Run Giveaways
posts.content:
Most brands run giveaways completely wrong and cause more HARM than good...

They run a giveaway, look at the number of opt-ins they get, see thousands of new emails flood in, and assume it crushed. The problem is opt-ins are NOT buyers... you grow the list, hurt your deliverability with low-engaging emails, and stall revenue at the same time.

The real problem is the lack of sales you get...

Say someone opts in to win a $2,000 chair and the winner is announced in 30 days...
[ul][li]Someone opts in hoping to win it... [li]They're not buying from you for 30 days, because they might get it for free. So why would they pay full price right now?[li]By the time it is 30 days later... the customer is cold and doesn't give a shit any more about the brand

You end up with a bigger list, worse deliverability, lower revenue per opt-in, and a 3-week stall on everyone who was actually going to buy...

INSTEAD...

The second someone opts in, hit them with an upsell...

=====

"We're expecting over 20,000 people to enter this giveaway. The odds of you winning are low... roughly 0.005%

Because you opted in, here's $250 off exclusive to you which expires in 3 days.

You're still be entered to win the giveaway... And if you do win? We refund you in full, ship the chair anyway, AND give you a $500 Amazon gift card."

=====

Look what just happened...

The giveaway hook stays and we get loads of opt-ins, but now they've got a real reason to buy NOW while they're warm.

Urgency on a tighter timeline than the giveaway, and zero risk of missing the prize since they're still entered.

Converts way better than letting them sit on the list for a month. And you still get everything that made the giveaway worth running... the list growth, the brand awareness, and the viral reach.

So whenever a client wants to run a giveaway, build this post-opt-in flip before it goes live!

Without it, you're leaving most of the revenue on the table and training the warmest subscribers to not buy.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
It's a weird thing to navigate through. Would need to know more about the situation to give a definitive answer. Do you have a contract in place with the brand you've been working with for over a year that explicitly states you can't work with competitors?

Relationships are everything in business, and that triumphs over money. If they find out, you not only lose the client you're actually close with but the relationship as well. And who knows, they could badmouth you as the cherry on top. You've been working with this client for over a year, and I assume you and whoever ur day-to-day contact is from that brand have a strong bond together, and maybe they've thrown you testimonials, are easygoing to work with, etc.

To play it safe, I personally wouldn't. There's such an abundance of everything out there that we want \(clients, cash flow, opportunities, relationships, etc.\). But curious to hear other thoughts.

Do not create multiple lists- segments is better for that. You set rules to carve up your list.

For example, you main list could be Subscribed.

posts.title: Should I have different discount codes for my different flows?
posts.content: For example, "Deal15" for my checkout abandon flow. "Shop15" for my cart abandon flow. "Discount15" for my browse abandon flow, etc. Or should I make all of my flows have the same discount code, like "Inbox15"?

user.name: Jack Cabrera
user.bio: Jack Cabrera

comments.content:
Gotta do different codes per flow, always.

I only say that because if every flow uses the same code, then u can't tell which one actually drove the conversion. It makes ur own data becomes useless. Meanwhile unique codes give you a free tracking layer independent from Klaviyo attribution.

It also helps me catch leaks too \(from a personal perspective at least\). Say I have a code named something simple like CHECKOUT15. Well, if CHECKOUT15 shows up in orders that never entered your checkout flow, someone shared it. Swap that one code without touching the others. If you want to eliminate leaks entirely, Klaviyo can generate unique dynamic codes per profile.

Honestly worth questioning if all of those flows actually need a discount fr. Browse abandonment is very low intent. So offering a code to someone who just looked at a product will train them to expect deals for visiting your site. I'd just use discounts for checkout and cart where intent is high. Use product recommendations or social proof for browse. Never give away margin where you don't need to.

posts.content:
I have an ecomm client who has been selling in Shopify for the past 3 years and contacts have been loading into a Klayvio account but they have never sent any follow up emails. Ever.

So we are going to implement a buyers sequence and want to start doing broadcasts but need to know what send rate we should start with AND what she we get them to do first?

Would love other ideas and suggestions. Want to make sure we nail this. Thank you!

user.name: Dolan Gadoury
user.bio: online marketer working with brands and experts to do damage online

comments.content:
Hey what's up [@Dolan Gadoury](obj://user/5bb9ecd6210c4309b119f0c66700120d)! I agree with you that a testimonial request as the first send is a smart instinct bc they can generate a shit ton of replies. But there's major groundwork you gotta cover first so that this all runs smoothly.

So 3 whole years of contacts with zero emails means a lot of that list is stale bro. Run the whole list through a platform like DeBounce to strip out invalid addresses before anything goes out. Hard bounces on a first send will tank your rep immediately unfortunately. Make sure SPF, DKIM, DMARC are set up properly too.

Then I would segment by purchase recency just like this:

Week 1: 30-day buyers only. Testimonial request can be your first send. If that segment is under 200, then that's actually ideal for warmup. If it's larger, then just batch it across a few days and you'll be straight.

Week 2: Expand to 60-90 day buyers. Have the content read along the lines of "How are you enjoying your purchase?" Still engagement-focused, and not selling yet.

Week 3: 6-month buyers with a re-introduction. This can be along the lines of "We've been quiet, that's changing."

Week 4+: 6-12 month buyers, similar re-introduction tone.

12+ month contacts: These people bought years ago and have never heard from you. So you gotta send a re-introduction and let natural unsubscribes clean the segment. Anyone who doesn't engage after 2-3 sends should get suppressed. Never wanna send promos straight to 2-3 year old contacts lol.

Keep in mind the testimonial ask only works for recent buyers tho. So someone who bought 2 years ago getting a review request as the first-ever email is gonna to feel kinda weird ngl.

Just build the flows alongside the warmup but turn them on gradually. Welcome and abandoned cart first, and then everything else as reputation builds. LMK ur thoughts!

posts.title: KLAVIYO PRODUCT SECTIONS 👀
posts.content:
Many times... especially for stores with a lot of products... using Klaviyo dynamic product sections is the move \(especially in flows\)!

Every high-SKU brand hits this problem... with many products, how do you know which ones to feature in our emails that will perform the best? We don't know and we're guessing

Also we have the problem of, say you are a fashion brand, we set up flows with graphic product sections in January... but by summer the products in the email are out of style and so they will be much lower converting.

Klaviyo dynamic product sections fix ALL of this...

Instead of you picking, Klaviyo picks per person, pulling in what they've viewed, added to cart, or is likely to buy.

The downside is that dynamic feeds give you way less design control... Less pretty and less on-brand. But they're often way more relevant.

One caveat... this is for high-SKU stores and brands and also ones whose catalog changes a lot. If you're a 3-product hero brand, don't bother, a clean designed section is better because you already know what everyone should see. The more products you have, the more this is relevant.

Test it on your flows or campaigns and let the numbers decide!

posts.title: Optimizing Around Key Churn Dates As A Subscription Brand
posts.content:
This is one of the most useful things you can look at for a subscription brand. It's a churn chart mapping exactly when people cancel in their first 90 days, and the spikes are not random. Every single one lines up with a moment YOU control.

Look at the main spikes people cancel their subscription...

Day 0: Day Order Placed
[ul][li]Reason For Cancellation: The person was just there for the deal and wanted to leave OR they instantly felt regret.[li]How To Overcome: Build a strong, heartfelt post-purchase thank you message. Set the expectation of what's coming, remind them why they bought, get them excited instead of leaving them alone with buyer's remorse.

Day 7-ish: Order Delivered
[ul][li]Reason For Cancellation: It's a reminder they subscribed, doubt makes them cancel. Or they try the product and didn't like it.[li]How To Overcome: Don't just use a bland "your order was delivered" email. This is prime real estate... customize it to teach them how to use the product, walk them through getting the most out of it, and reaffirm the benefits they signed up for. Consumption is what kills churn, so the delivery moment is where you can drive it.

Day 27: The Billing Reminder
[ul][li]Reason For Cancellation: This one's obvious as brands have send an email 3 days before someone is charged that they are about to charge them. but underworked. People see this and get scared and cancel... especially if the email doesn't have proper information.[li]How To Overcome: Reframe the reminder around value, remind them what they're getting and what's coming next, so the charge feels earned instead of surprising. Make it less focused on you are about to be charged. Add friction to the cancel option \(move the manage my subscription button to the very bottom of the mail\).

Day 30: Customer Is Charged For 2nd Order
[ul][li]Reason For Cancellation: The customer was just charged and they got a scary Shopify notification showing that they placed another order... they get scared and cancel.[li]How To Overcome: This is the most underrated spike on the whole chart, and it's the biggest. If you're on Shopify Plus, you can contact their support team and turn that default confirmation email OFF. Then rebuild it in Klaviyo and reframe the whole thing, reaffirm the benefits, make it feel warm instead of scary, remind them why they're here.

The big idea here is simple is that churn isn't random, it clusters around specific moments, and every one of those moments is a message you can optimize.

Make sure you have custom emails for first placed order, order delivered, billing reminder, and recurring charge notification.

posts.title: Simple Offer Mistake Most Brands Make...
posts.content:
Many brands ALREADY offer some sort of discount on their website at all times \(example below\)... which is fine...

But then they add ANOTHER discount in the pop-up form that is a WORSE sounding offer.

Let's look at this brand Chronic Australia:
[ul][li]They want to push people towards [this 3-pack](https://shopchronic.com.au/collections/bestselling-topicals/products/3x-hemp-magnesium-cream) \($139.90\) as the core offer over the single pack \($54.95\) [li]The advertise 15% off on the 3-pack... buy more save more...[li]But the 15% OFF on the 3-pack they give is equivalent to $25 OFF!!![li]$25 OFF is way more enticing than 15% OFF... so they should lead with that instead[li]Their pop-up form right now pushes $10 OFF[li]They already are giving $25 OFF on the 3-pack... why try to get people in by leading with a WORSE $10 off? 

We can frame this pop-up form way better...

To make this convert better, we need to frame the offer better.

We have two options...

1️⃣ Option 1: Get Rid of $10 OFF Completely
[ul][li]Save your margins by throwing away the extra discount you are giving away [li]Make the pop-up your $25 OFF offer \(You've Got $25 OFF\) and in the welcome flow give no extra discount and just drive people towards the 3-pack page.[li]This has another added benefit of disincentivizing people from taking the single pack with the original $10 OFF, because in this scenario you get NO discount on the single pack... but $25 OFF with the 3-pack

2️⃣ Option 2: Change Pop-Up + Welcome To $35 OFF The 3-Pack
[ul][li]$35 OFF is essentially what we are already giving away in the current setup... because it is $25 off the three-pack and the pop-up gives an extra $10 off... however the customer only perceives the value of $10 off [li]$35 OFF sounds way better than $10 off and will convert much better... so just lead with that! [li]Pop-up becomes "You've Got $35 OFF" and the welcome flow shows how the 3 pack is already $25 off and an extra discount gives an extra $10 off [li]I would further incentivize the 3 pack by not having the discount work on the single pack... of people want to buy the single pack they have to do it at full price!

Just like that, without giving any extra discount, we will increase our core offer's take rate AND get higher overall conversions because the offer is framed better!

Review your accounts and see where you can implement this!

🧠 10 Second Summary: You may be already giving a better discount on your site than what your pop-up leads with... add it all up, lead with the bigger number, and drive people to your core offer. Same margin, better framing, higher take rate towards the product you want people to buy.

posts.content:
Hey guys, been having an issue with some of our clients that the welcome flow starts out with good numbers, 50%+ open rate and 5-10% CTR, however, as the flow goes on the Open Rate goes down drastically.

For example, for one brand we have:
Email #1 - Open Rate 43.1%, CTR: 5.6%, Placed Order: 4.6%
Email #2 - Open Rate 36.2%, CTR: 0.7%, Placed Order: 0.5%
Email #3 \(Smart Sending ON\) - Open Rate 32.1%, CTR: 0.9%, Placed Order: 0.6%
Email #4 \(Smart Sending ON\) - Open Rate 29.9%, CTR: 0.8%, Placed Order: 0.4%

This same brand has 65%-70% Open rate in Campaigns.. Which is what's been confusing to me.

Would really appreciate your feedback on what I can do better to have better deliverability on flows, and fix this issue on welcome specifically, although I'm seeing it across all flows in this account.

Thank you so much!

user.name: Samuel Hanono
user.bio: Founder at Rettain: helping 7-9 figure brands scale profitably

comments.content:
Sup [@Samuel Hanono](obj://user/ad5db17b2841451681f64922347278b6) first thing that comes to mind is the content of the emails after Email #1. With an average of a 32.7% open rate for Emails #2-4, I don't think this is a deliverabillty problem. You are getting solid opens, just lack of engagement from your list. What are the remaining emails about? Social proof/reviews, FAQs, founder stories, etc? It's normal and expected to gradually have a drop off in open rates as the welcome flow progresses so don't worry about that.

You have a clear drop in CTR and place order rate tho. email #1 is getting people to actually click and buy, but emails #2-4 are all sitting around 0.7 - 0.9% CTR and 0.4 - 0.6% placed order rate. To me that says people are still opening the emails, they just arent finding enough reason to keep engaging or make a purchase.

I'd start by looking at the content, messaging, product selection, CTAs, and overall value each email is giving. Focus on educating and giving them a reason to buy rather than push the welcome discount/code. Throw in multiple CTAs throughout the email too. My guess is there's just not enough keeping people interested after they see the discount in Email #1. Id try to replicate the winner in email #1 too

My question is, any ideas on what a good pop-up strategy could be? They have a "welcome kit" so to speak and it costs $150. We're thinking about saying that if you sign up, you get the kit for 40% off.

Any thoughts? Id really welcome any thoughts on how to set this one up as well as any re-activation ideas for the 220 subs on the email list.

Thanks!

user.name: Vicente Hosie
user.bio: Growth Partner. He ayudado a más de 64 negocios con marketing y generado $3M para clientes.

comments.content:
Hey what's up man [@Vicente Hosie](obj://user/245dc0422e314695897bd992d1467c80). So imo, at $2,500-$4,500, the popup's only job is grabbing the email so ur welcome flow can build trust over weeks. Ain't nobody finna impulse-commit to a diamond ring from a popup 😂

The 40% off welcome kit has a positioning issue as a popup offer bc asking someone to buy something \(even if it's discounted\) is a purchase decision, not an opt-in. It's wayy too much too soon bro. For lab-grown diamonds, an educational lead magnet, a style quiz, or a free ring sizer mailed to them would all capture the email and start the relationship without asking for a credit card off the bat.

The welcome kit offer actually works better inside your welcome flow. So after 2-3 weeks of trust-building emails, saying "get your welcome kit for 40% off" feels earned. But on a popup before they know you it's just gonna be noise for them.

And that means the welcome flow needs 30+ days at this AOV.

It should center around education, mission, social proof, and then a purchase or consultation CTA. U don't need everything built before launching so I'd just start with what you have and add more emails as you go.

Also with 220 subscribers that means the list is small enough to where deliverability prob isn't a concern. You should send a "we're officially live" campaign and flow them into that same trust sequence. Btw 8 sales from 220 subs is a 3.6% at this price point, so there's more conversion sitting in that list.

I'd say list building is ur priority #1. Every subscriber is a potential $3K+ customer. LMK your thoughts!

posts.title: Email Flows Timing ⏱️
posts.content:
Nothing more important in your flows than TIMING!!!

This is one of those things where you spend two minutes changing a number and see crazy results...

Timing is one of the most underrated levers in all of email. The gap between your flow emails and how fast that first one fires has a massive impact on conversions... but most brands just leave the platform defaults in place and never touch them.

So here's a clean guide for how to time every core flow...
[ul][li]Welcome flow: First email fires immediately after someone opts in, the moment they're most interested. You can optionally drop a second or third email that same first day, around two hours apart, but in general run it one email per day, 24 hours apart.[li]Site abandoned: Two hours is the standard, you can test shorter or longer. 24 hours between emails.[li]Browse abandoned: 30 minutes to an hour.[li]Cart abandoned and checkout abandoned: Never go longer than 30 minutes. 15, 20, or 30 is the sweet spot. This is one of the easiest quick wins in the whole account. The one or two emails a day is great. [li]Post-purchase: Fire the first one immediately, then space the rest every couple of days.[li]Replenishment: Take the average time between purchases for your brand and send the reminder a few days before they're likely to run out.[li]Win-back: Set the first email at roughly 3x your average time between purchases. So if a supplement brand sees repeat purchases around day 30, your win-back starts around day 90.

But remember... TEST TEST TEST.

Every brand is different so you should test this. The great part is this: it literally takes a couple of minutes to set this up as a test and it can have massive results.

posts.title: MMS Marketing 💬
posts.content:
One thing that should be utilized more is including IMAGES in your SMS marketing \(images turn an sms into an mms, idk why the name switch lol\).

However, you need to do it strategically and be mindful of it...

MMS messages cost 3x more than regular SMS messages.

Even though they cost 3x more... they can sometimes still result in higher gross profit for the brand, so make sure to calculate it.

Example of the finances breaking down \(first screenshot\):
Revenue: Version B \(MMS\) produced 116% more revenue.
AOV: Increased from $64 to $86
Net Profit: Doubled from $309 to $658.
Even though MMS costs more per credit, we saw a net profit increase of $349 for an extra $24. We’ll run a confirmation test soon, but for now, visuals are winning.

You shouldn't use MMS messages every time, but you should use them strategically when an image will help push the sale forward.

Example use cases:
[ul][li]Including an educational infographic in the welcome series[li]Visually showing a free gift a customer is getting \(like in the example AB test below screenshot 2\) [li]Highlighting a new product[li]Doing something funny like a meme 

I want to use MMS more... yes, it is a bit more work to get designer involved... but you can easily just adapt a part of an email design you made and use it as your text image!

What other results have you guys seen?

PS -[ Here's a massive swipe file of SMS messages you should save ](https://www.attentive.com/texts-we-love)

This is an 8-figure brand with data and numbers pulled from [Hiro](https://www.hiroanalytics.com/) \(these trends are consistent across other brands I tested\)...

[ul][li]Image 1: Number of people who sign up to the email list and when they ended up converting.  [li]Image 2: Same as above, but removing day 0 since it is such a massive spike[li]Image 3: Shows of people who converted first purchase from email, where they bought from [li]Image 4: Distribution of flows and what product the most first time revenue

Here's how it is broken down by day:

Day 0 \(Same day as sign-up\):
[ul][li]19.1k bought outside of email[li]9.7k bought attributed from email

Day 1:

[ul][li]124 bought outside of email[li]194 bought attributed from email

[ul][li]32 bought outside of email[li]44 bought attributed from email

Day 60:
[ul][li]9 bought outside of email[li]10 bought attributed from email

Do with this info what you will...

posts.title: Meta ads are down and it's taking email revenue down with it. WTF!
posts.content:
So my skincare client is currently having issues with their Meta Ads account, which has caused a significant drop in our total revenue.

The last 3 months have been really good:

March 105k
April 130k
May 112k

This month, it's already the 25th of June, and we have not even made 40k.

I realized from this experience how much impact meta ads/paid traffic can have on our email campaign and flow attribution, especially when we are using Klaviyo.

My campaigns used to average around 1k-2k.

Right now, it's only making $500, sometimes less!

That being said, Email + SMS is currently attributing around 50% of total revenue.

Which leads me to believe that email is doing a good job.

If it wasn't, attribution would be much lower \(even with Klaviyo taking credit for EVERYTHING. LOL\)

Which brings me to my question \(finally\):

How to squeeze even more juice from my email list in situations where new leads aren't coming in as fast as they used to?

I'm thinking of getting people to restock, for which I already have a replenishment flow.

But is there anything I can do from the campaign side?

My client doesn't have a subscription program.

Do you think building a subscription program will help keep things afloat when meta ads/cold paid traffic is down?

Any other strategy suggestions you have seen work well with your clients in similar situations?

We currently send campaigns to 30-day engaged, high-potential purchasers and VIPs, totaling about 70k people.

But because of this situation, I'm thinking of broadening my reach and send to 60-day or probably 120-day too. What do you think?

P.S. This scenario has made it really awkward since it happened right after I told my client I'm increasing my monthly retainer 😅😅😅

Tagging the email Gods in this channel to grace us with their timeless wisdom:

[@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
Nah you're right here [@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703)! Email at 50% of revenue while everything dropped means email IS working imo. Campaign rev went down because fewer people are entering from Meta, not because email itself got worse. You'll know bc the 30-day engaged segment shrinks every week without fresh acquisition replacing it. So it wasn't email that broke here, the pipeline just did.

I believe 60-day is a reasonable short-term move for broadening tbh. 120-day is riskier bc those are deeply unengaged subscribers who don't interact can hurt deliverability for the 30-day segment that's actually performing. I'd personally go 60 first, watch engagement, and then consider 90. But ofc have different messaging for lapsed segments tho.

The best immediate play i see here is running a win-back campaign targeting customers who bought March-May but just haven't returned. Basically ppl with actual purchase history who are due for a repeat buy. That's a way higher value than blasting cold subscribers, and while u do that \(if you choose to\) make sure to audit your replenishment flow timing as well. If it doesn't match when customers actually run out, then ur missing the reorder window.

Also def start that subscription program! Subscription revenue recurs without Meta needing to re-acquire the customer every cycle, so tackling that directly solves the dependency you're feeling right now.

And then about ur retainer, try your best to flip the narrative tbh. If i was in your shoes I would tell my client that email being at 50% while paid is down is the legit proof retention is worth investing in. Lmk ur thoughts ik that was a lot of yapping 🤣

[@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703) Good news on that man! Expected Date of Next Order is actually the best trigger for multi-SKU brands imo. posts.title: Unique Retention Play
posts.content:
I found this brand that has a super cool mechanism for getting people to consume their product...

Everybody knows the biggest driver of churn is that people have too much product. This is usually because they don't take it every day or they forget or whatever the excuse may be...

But what if you could incentivize them to take the product every day and help them track it and hold them accountable?

That's what this brand does.

They built a custom tracker where people can log in. Every day, as long as you submit it on that day, you will keep a streak. If you keep the streak for 70 days, you get this incentive.

Now I don't think a lot of people actually will fill this out every day haha but I think it is a good educational mechanism for really proving to people like hey you need to take this product every day.

For me personally when I received this, I was like, "I'm not even gonna participate cause I know I'm going to forget on some days..."

And so if I operated this, I would have different tiers:
[ul][li]If you make it happen for 50% of days, you get something small like this random free gift in your next subscription.[li]If you do it for 75% of days, you get this offer.[li]If you do 90%, you get this offer.[li]If you do 100%, you get a full refund on everything you've paid. Something crazy like that

Not sure exactly how they built this but I'm going to find out.

Let me know what you guys think!

Link to tracker: [https://challenge.drinkhyro.com.au/](https://challenge.drinkhyro.com.au/)

posts.title: Welcome flow structure
posts.content:
I've just setup a new welcome flow for a client, and I've experimenting with the structure.

In my mind it makes sense to add a conditional split after each email that says "placed order at least once since starting this flow" and the no branch would proceed to the next email and the yes branch would come to an end. Like would you want to keep sending an email with a welcome offer to someone that's already placed an order?

Let me know what you guys think and/or what structure has worked best for you.

user.name: Brandon Teyf
user.bio: Founder of Got Mail Media, specializing in email and sms marketing for health & wellness and luxury boutique brands.

comments.content: [@Brandon Teyf](obj://user/585440273f434171be9a7d9cb3bb131c) Instead have a profile trigger and not a conditional split every time an email is sent in the Welcome Flow. Make it "Placed order zero times since starting this flow". Once they opt in they get put through the sequence of your Welcome Flow and at any point if they purchase they are taken out of the flow completely. Don't want to send a reminder to "Use your 10% off code" if they just purchased a day a go with it. The profile trigger protects you from that. Technically your idea with a conditional split can still work, I just think this is an easier way to simplify your flow entirely.

posts.title: AGENCY MASTERMIND CALL RECORDING JUNE 23RD
posts.content:
Epic agency call today led by [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)

We covered:
[ul][li]Team structure for scaling. The four core roles every email agency needs — owner, account manager, designer, and Klaviyo tech — and what each one should actually be doing.

[ul][li]Account manager vs copywriter. Why merging the two roles reduces friction, keeps communication clean, and produces better output at an early-stage agency.

[ul][li]Workflow and project management. The campaign calendar process, email production workflow, and how to manage 50+ emails in flight across multiple clients without things slipping.

[ul][li]Where to find great team members. Personal brand, Upwork, LinkedIn ads, referrals, and when to use a recruiter — and why the best AMs often prefer a small agency over a big one.

[ul][li]Live Q&A. Hiring for premium fashion brands, design agencies vs in-house designers, what makes a great account manager, and how to handle client pushback without losing the relationship.

posts.title: SMS SEGMENTATION MOST PEOPLE F*CK UP
posts.content:
SMS SEGMENTATION MOST PEOPLE F*CK UP @channel

This is one of the most common SMS mistakes I see and it leaves a lot of cash on the table.

Most people build their SMS "engaged" segment off one single condition: "clicked SMS in the last 90 days". And on the surface it makes sense, those are your clickers, so those are your engaged people...

But that leaves a TON of high value leads.

Someone who just subscribed to SMS last week and is a SUPER warm lead but hasn't had the chance to click. Someone who's been on your site browsing all month. Someone who has placed an order before and clearly likes the brand.

None of those people clicked an SMS in the window, so your segment skips right over them, and these are some of your highest-value people to be texting.

So instead of one narrow condition, you want to go wide and stack a few with OR logic.

Here's a good starting point:
[ul][li]Can receive text message marketing[li]Subscribed to SMS in the last 90 days[li]OR clicked SMS in the last 180 days[li]OR active on site in the last 60 days[li]OR placed an order in the past 365 days

Use something like this as your base list then blast your WHOLE LIST once~ish per month for big events like sales and new products.

Play with the time windows to fit your brand. 90, 180, 60, 365 is a solid default, but a smaller list might go wider on the days while a massive list can afford to tighten up.

Go wide with SMS and you stop leaving high-value people sitting on the table every send!

Flow filters in Klaviyo are what you need.

The "Added to Cart zero times in the last hour" is a filter not a wait. After the 40 mins are up Klayvio is checking to see if this customer has added to cart in the last hour or not.

The only filters needed are to ensure that the checkout process hasnt started and that the customer hasnt placed an order \(both of which u have\).

posts.title: Post-Purchase Messaging
posts.content:
For consumable brands, consumption is the entire game 👀

This is the most important thing to understand about any consumable product...

Your number one job in post-purchase isn't upsells or cross-sells, it's getting the customer to actually USE the damn product every single day.

Because if they don't consume it, nothing else works. They won't see results, so they've got no reason to reorder, and if they're subscribed they're now piling up product they're not using, which is the fastest way to a cancel. No consumption means no results means churn.

So your post-purchase messaging needs to push CONSUMPTION harder than anything else. Look at how Gains does it. "One scoop, once a day, no matter what." They're hammering daily use, showing you how to make it a habit by stacking it with your morning coffee, and setting the expectation that the results compound over months.

Very key as well, you actually want to tell people they won't really feel much for 60 to 90 days. It sounds like you're talking them out of it, but you're doing two things. You're setting honest expectations so they don't quit at week two thinking it's not working, and you're buying yourself a 90-day runway. Because if you can get someone to use a product daily for 90 days, it's now baked into their routine and they are much more likely to stick with it.

So whenever you're writing post-purchase for a consumable, run it against this checklist:
[ul][li]Am I pushing them to USE the product as much as possible?[li]Am I giving them actual tips on how to consume it?[li]Am I setting the expectation that real results take 60-90+ days?

Nail consumption and the retention takes care of itself... Everything downstream, the reorders, the subscription, the LTV, all of it depends on the product actually getting used!!!

Not a sexy tactic, but extremely important!

posts.title: Live and Learn...
posts.content:
About a month ago, I posted about my client's email revenue suddenly going down the drain \(you can read about it here: [https://www.skool.com/email-marketerz/revenue-suddenly-going-down-the-drain-help?p=fb2e3714](https://www.skool.com/email-marketerz/revenue-suddenly-going-down-the-drain-help?p=fb2e3714)\).

And I couldn't figure out what was going on.

Deliverability was great, paid ads were firing alright.

But emails weren't converting. It was only attributing10-12% of total revenue.

After breaking my head trying to figure out new angles, etc., etc...

I finally realized something.

It started on the day when I suppressed the people in the suppression segment.

So I created a segment that contained the profiles I suppressed on that particular date, unsuppressed them, and then included the unsuppressed profiles in my campaign sends.

And now it seems like we're back on track. Email currently accounts for 37% of total revenue.

This was weird since I followed the suppressed segment instructions [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) shared in his course.

Based on this experience, I think we should also consider the list size before suppressing.

The list size of this client was around 6k-7k subs.

And I suppressed a huge chunk of it \(around 2k subs\).

I could be wrong, though, but I would love to hear some input from the email mavericks here about how or why suppressing profiles could have had a huge negative impact on revenue.

I have attached the definition I used to create the Suppressed segment.

CC [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)

Right now I do monthly retainers, but I've run into a challenge where clients are happy to pay for foundational flow setup at the start, then once those are completed, they start questioning the ongoing retainer price because "the flows are already done."

Looking back, I think this is something I should have clarified better during onboarding.

How do you package your services?
• Do you separate campaign management and flow management pricing?
• Do you have one retainer that covers both?
• Do you charge based on a set number of emails per month that includes both campaigns and flow work?
• Do you move clients into a lower maintenance retainer once flows are built?

Would love to hear what's working for you and how you've handled those pricing conversations.

Trying to improve my packaging and avoid getting stuck in the "but the flows are already done" discussion 😂

Thank you in advance!!!

posts.title: CLIENT UPDATES
posts.content:
Hey everyone! Quick question for those managing email marketing clients.

Aside from the standard monthly report, what other reports or updates are you sending to clients regularly?

I find myself sending weekly performance updates, but honestly, it feels a bit random and not very streamlined. I'd love to build a more structured reporting process.

Do you have a specific reporting cadence, template, or framework that works well for you? Any resources, examples, or best practices you'd recommend?

Thank you!

PS: Sharing a photo I took 😆

user.name: Marielet Laudit
user.bio: Klaviyo Email Marketer

comments.content:
Hi [@Marielet Laudit](obj://user/5ef883ed6a9f48e7b44c4d87cca18cbb) ! It prob feels random to you bc it's just a structure problem, not a frequency problem. Weekly is the right cadence, and I follow these rules below:

Weekly \(15-20 min\): You could simply go over campaign performance \(like sends, opens, clicks, revenue\), flow snapshot if anything changed, what was built this week, what's planned next week, and any flags a all. Always include comparisons too because they tell a story that raw numbers don't.

Monthly \(the deeper dive\): Here, you can go over total email revenue and % of store revenue. This can mean campaign and flow performance summaries, list growth and health deliverability, and A/B test results, among other topics to note. And most importantly: strategic recommendations for next month. This is the report that justifies your retainer.

U gotta make sure to be intentional about attribution settings and transparent about what the revenue number represents. Klaviyo's defaults can inflate significantly, so whatever settings you use, just be chill and upfront abt it, because a client who discovers the numbers don't hold up loses trust fast.

Also ensure that every report should end with a clear "what's next" after it.

posts.title: Grow Your Email List From Instagram
posts.content:
With Manychat / Klaviyo, new followers who follow you Instagram can now get a discount, hand over their email, land in your Klaviyo welcome flow, and get pushed to your site!

Here's how to set it up:
[ol:1][li]Get a ManyChat account[li]Connect your Instagram to ManyChat[li]In ManyChat → Settings → Integrations → Klaviyo, paste a Klaviyo public and private API keys \(generate in Klaviyo → Settings → API Keys → create private key, access to profiles and lists\).[li]In Manychat go to Automation → New Automation → "Say hi to new followers."[li]Set the trigger delay \(30 seconds is a safe default — immediate feels spammy\).[li]Switch to the Flow Builder: set the flow Live, then Stop — this unlocks the builder \(ManyChat quirk\).[li]Message 1: Welcome + offer. "Hey, welcome to \[Brand\]. As thanks, here's 10% off your first order. Want it?" + a Yes button.[li]Message 2 \(on Yes\): "Great — drop your email and we'll send your code." Add a Data Collection prompt set to capture email.[li]Action \(on reply\): Add Klaviyo action → Upload contact to list → map the email field → select the list tied to your welcome flow.[li]Success message: Confirm the discount + a "Browse site" button linking to your store.[li]Preview the flow, then set it Live.

One thing worth flagging: the whole funnel hinges on that list being correctly wired to your welcome flow's list trigger... test with your own email to make sure you get entered properly.

posts.title: Sneaky Way To Get More Clicks 🫵
posts.content:
Your footer is the most underrated highest-ROI section of your entire email.

\[The two on the left in the example are my favorite by far... they have all the points I listed below\]

Here's why the footer matters more than people think...

It's the only part of the email that stays the same across every send, so when you optimize it once it pays you back on every campaign and every flow you send from then on.

It's also one of the most-clicked sections in any email. The customers who didn't connect with the products you featured will scroll to the bottom looking for another way in. Or if you don't do any selling in an email and it is brand focused... your footer will pick up intent and clicks off of that.

And if all they find down there is legal text and an unsubscribe link, you just lost a warm customer who was already opened and already scrolling.

So let's give them somewhere to go.

Structure:
[ul][li]CATEGORY BUTTONS: Just a simple grid of "Shop Skincare / Shop Body / Shop Hair" or whatever the brand's main categories are. Someone reads an educational email, doesn't want that specific product, but scrolls down and realizes they actually do need a new X, and now you've got a click and a conversion you never would've gotten otherwise. Every footer gets category buttons, no exceptions.[li]Unique Selling Points / Brand Blurbs: This is your risk reversal and core selling points, stuff like "Free shipping on orders over $50," "90-day money-back guarantee," or even just the brand slogan.[li]Social proof: The footer is a great place to anchor some credibility right before the customer leaves the email. You can rotate through review stars and count like "★★★★★ 10,000+ reviews," press logos, a customer photo grid pulled from UGC, or trust badges like "Made in USA" or "60-Day Guarantee." Doesn't have to be heavy, one row is plenty.[li]\[Optional\] Social CTA: Something like "Tag us @brandname and we'll feature you on our story" or "Follow us on Instagram for new drops and behind the scenes." It builds the brand's social presence at zero cost, and the customers who actually engage tend to become your highest-LTV cohort anyway.

Keep it light so you're adding a few clean rows, not building a second email down there.

But get this dialed in once and it works for you on every single send going forward!

Extremely important to get right!

👉 The second screenshot shows an example of the footer links \(766 clicks\) pulling in more clicks than the core email \(722 clicks\).

posts.title: Send This Before Your Next Sale/Drop
posts.content:
The teaser email that hypes your drop AND boosts deliverability 👀

This is a deliverability boosting teaser you send a few days before a big sale or product drop...

It's a simple "something's coming, get ready" email to build hype BUT with added benefits of deliverability boosting / engagement.

You tell people to do four things to "get first dibs"...
[ul][li]Move this email to your primary inbox[li]Star it[li]Reply with an emoji so we know you're interested[li]Click the link below

Every one of those is a top-tier engagement signal to Gmail. Replies, stars, moving you to primary, clicks... it will also make us show in main inbox for that user going forward.

So a few days before you blast your whole list with the sale, you've just told the algorithm "these people love us." and your deliverability goes up right when it matters most.

\(You don't actually have to give anyone early access or even track who replied... since we will show up in main inbox if they engage they do have best chance of being first\)

Send it 2-5 days before the big drop or sale.

posts.title: Updating Pop-Ups w/ Sales
posts.content:
Say you're running a 40% off Fourth of July sale... Your site's pushing it... but your pop-up form still says "10% off your first order."

Now you've got a problem.

A new visitor sees 40% off everywhere, then your pop-up offers them 10%. That's conflict and confusion AND you're capping them at a worse offer than the one they could just grab on site anyway.

So when a sale goes live, the pop-up should go with it.

Change the pop-up wording to match the sale "Get 40% off, 4th of July Exclusive."

Then update the welcome flow the same way so the emails reinforce the same offer instead of the old evergreen 10% \(no need for design updates, just change the copy\)

No crazy redesign needed. You're swapping copy, not rebuilding anything. You can knock this out in 10-15 minutes.

You can schedule pop-ups and flows in Klaviyo easily so you can even do this ahead of time.

Easy increase in email leads and purchases!

posts.title: Subscriber Retention Giveaway
posts.content:
Stupid simple subscription retention play that doubles as marketing 👀

A monthly active product subscriber giveaway.
[ul][li]Every month, a few active subscribers win free product or some sort of gift[li]Stay subscribed, you're automatically entered[li]Brez does it. Super simple. 1-3 subscribers every month get an extra 16 pack pf product in their next order. 

You're giving people a reason to NOT cancel every month... and a reason for non-subscribers to finally start. All wrapped in something that feels like a gift instead of a desperate "please don't leave" email.

Here's how I'd run it...
[ol:1][li]Pick a day, say the 1st of every month, and announce the winners. [li]Send a campaign every month showing who won and exactly what they got \(ideally show images of past winners, if you can ask them to send photos\). Tell active subscribers to stay subscribed so they're in next month's draw. Tell everyone else to subscribe to get included.[li]Then plug this benefit and past winners it into every subscriber touchpoint you have. Billing reminders especially right when someone's deciding whether this charge is worth it, you remind them they're entered to win. And show real past winners. Names, faces, what they got. People need to SEE it to believe it's real and picture themselves winning.[li]\[BONUS\] Tie entries to how long they've been subscribed. 4 months subscribed = 4 entries. 6 months = 6. The longer you stay, the better your odds. And if you cancel, your streak resets to zero. Now canceling isn't just "I'll pause this month." It's "I'm throwing away the 8-month streak I've been building." You've turned the cancel button into a loss.

Fun way to add extra bonus to subscribers.

In general:

[ul][li]For brands with bigger catalogs, the email dopamine hit will be more around getting customers to view the catalog rather than educational or social/review emails. [ul][li]the product feed is email html, which means it's a bit finnicky if you are using Figma to design your emails and Dark mode- make sure you test the preview in Litmus \(the Klaviyo email preview in real inboxes\).

posts.title: Customer retention via email marketing - NO SUSCRIPTION MODEL
posts.content:
Hey everyone, looking for some advice on customer retention via email marketing.

Here's where my head is at:

Post-purchase flow: I want to make it longer and more extensive than the standard 2-3 emails.
Refill flow: build out a more detailed sequence to bring people back when it's time to reorder.
Incentive: I'm thinking about offering a meaningful discount to drive repeat purchases, somewhere around 20%, possibly delivered as store credit rather than a straight discount.

My main questions:
1. Is a ~20% store credit offer a good idea for the brand, or does that eat too much into margin / train customers to wait for deals?
2. What retention strategies or tips have worked best for you with email specifically?

Would really appreciate any insights. Thanks in advance!

user.name: Luca Nari
user.bio: Brand Owner

comments.content:
I got you [@Luca Nari](obj://user/1f91415663ec4a8d89429e6bbd87b5d4)

So what I'd do first is extend the post-purchase flow wayyy past 2-3 emails. For a non-subscription consumable, this is your most important retention lever. Would prob around 5-7 emails over 30-45 days and you could just talk about usage tips, results timeline, social proof, cross-sell for complementary products, and then a replenishment nudge as they're running low. The biggest predictor of a repeat purchase is whether they had a great first experience and the flow's job is making that happen.

For replenishment specifically, ur gonna want to match the timing to the actual product consumption rate. So let's say like if the product lasts 30 days and your email arrives at day 45, that prob means they've already reordered elsewhere.

I also do feel like store credit over percentage discount is the right call here tbh.But 20% across the board is too aggressive imo. You should tier it bc active repeat buyers just need a well-timed reminder, not a discount. People approaching the end of their replenishment window get a small nudge. Lapsed customers who haven't bought in 2x the normal window get the real incentive and that's where I see the 20% belongs. Wouldn't give away margin on people who would've bought anyway.

Rly all u gotta do is build enough value through education, cross-sells, and content that most repeat purchases happen without needing any incentive at all.

user.name: Aven Tedros
user.bio:

posts.title: 4 Step Campaign Calendar Creation Process
posts.content:
DO NOT just use AI to build your campaign calendars. You will get just shit ideas, nothing new, in basic shit.

The ideas come first... from real data. Then AI comes last.

Here's the order we actually follow, every single month...

1. Past winners
[ul][li]Start here ALWAYS.[li]Pull your best-performing campaign angles from the past 12-24 months and reuse them![li]Customers need to be reminded more than they need to be taught... people forget, and they're seeing hundreds of brands a day.[li]So whatever your winners are, reuse them. Light copy/design refresh if you want, but if an email rips, it goes back in the calendar.[li]Use a couple of these every month in your calendar.

2. Winning ad + landing page angles
[ul][li]Go ask your ads team what's getting the most spend right now.[li]Or you can literally view any brand's Meta ads on [Meta Ads Library](https://www.facebook.com/ads/library)[li]If an angle is working on Meta with real dollars behind it, it's proven and we can make an email out of it[li]Same with landing pages... if you see success there, bring it to email[li]Another couple sends can come from this in every month in your calendar

3. Competitor + brand swipes
[ul][li]Now... we steal![li]Follow brands you admire on a tool like [Milled](https://milled.com/) and watch what they send. Sign up to email lists and see what others are doing.[li]Use Pinterest, Instagram, Tik Tok, WHATEVER to get inspo.[li]A lot of the best ideas are already being used! Just reuse them yourself and skip the hard part of ideation

4. AI ideation... LAST
[ul][li]Notice we haven't touched AI yet.[li]By now you've got a stack of real ideas from winners, ads, and swipes.[li]NOW you bring in AI... not to invent your calendar, but to round it out and place the dates. Fill the gaps, balance your content pillars, lock the schedule.

Quick example of the whole thing for a creatine brand...
[ul][li]Resend last quarter's 3 best non-discount emails with a design and copy refresh \(past winners\)[li]Build 2 campaigns off the "too tired to train" angle and the "creatine with no bloat" angles crushing on Meta \(ad\)[li]Swipe 2 random other brand emails of "your body is a temple, treat it like it" and "leaked marketing intern email accidentally releasing a discount" and send to your list \(swipe\)[li]Hand all that to a properly trained AI and say "give me options on a ton of different email ideas to round out a full month at every-other-day, even split across pillars of educational, social proof, community, direct product pitches, and sales"

You've got a data-backed calendar in an hour instead of guessing!

Do the work first before handing it to AI

user.name: Jan Uroda
user.bio: Looking for 7+ figure founders who are genuinely interested in serving the world to make more impact.

comments.content:
Biggest thing is flows and making sure you get flows live, because those are the highest engaging emails and that'll slowly warm up your account.

And then for campaigns, I'd start sending to a list of just 2,000 to 5,000 people and make them the most engaged people from ConvertKit. Download the most engaged people and upload that list to Klaviyo and only send to them for about a week. Use Klaviyo's gradual send time feature when you're scheduling the campaign so you don't just blast the email all at once.

Then slowly start adding more people. You should ramp up pretty fast, as long as you have above 50% opens. We have been able to warm up accounts with over a million profiles in just four weeks 💪

posts.title: What are people's thoughts on sending an existing list through a flow?
posts.content: Working freelance with a small ecom brand that is just starting email. They have an existing list of emails that they would like to send through our welcome flow. A lot of these emails are friends and family and people already familiar with her. Have never done this before, so curious as to what best practices would be. ty!

user.name: Olivia Wegner
user.bio: ecom + email marketing + paid ads

comments.content:
I'd say it depends on the size of this list and how engaged it is. If you dump them into your welcome flow and the engagement is low, then that's not good for your deliverability. People who go through welcome flow kinda expect these emails because they've signed up recently.

A few years ago, I had a client who wanted to do the same thing. He was really pushing this idea. Didn't work out well.

If the welcome flow is long, I would send these emails as campaigns, and then after 1-2 emails, create an engaged segment from this list \(based on these Welcome sends\) and send the rest to them.

I'm curious what others would do, though.

replies.content: [@Robert Flaga](obj://user/9a2462a02eea49c4b9b9a5ec53fa483f) Thanks for the insight! This is really helpful. The welcome flow is a bit long, so I think I'll send as regular campaigns to those who are still engaged after our re-engagement campaign. To your point, I would rather gradually warm and build a list organically than dump them cold into a welcome flow.

user.name: Olivia Wegner
user.bio: ecom + email marketing + paid ads

comments.content:
Yoo what's up [@Olivia Wegner](obj://user/de68333ddea64b3a9623b03db618e96f) ! So I personally wouldn't run them through the standard welcome flow tbh. That's built for strangers who just opted in, so anybody who already knows the brand getting a "hey, nice to meet you" sequence is going to feel hella weird imo.

Firs thing is to make sure these people actually agreed to receive marketing emails. Personal contacts collected informally is fs gonna be different from people who opted in through a form.

Would also clean the list and run it through a validation tool like DeBounce to strip out dead addresses. Then instead of the welcome flow, u could send a single campaign that acknowledges who they are. Have it read something like: "You've been part of this from the beginning, we're launching our email program, here's what to expect, and here's a thank you offer for being an early supporter." The tone's gotta be different here because the relationship is completely different.

If the list is larger \(like several hundred+\), then I'd prob stagger the send over a few days rather than all at once.

And after that initial send, fold them into your regular campaign audience. They skip the welcome flow entirely and join the normal cadence. Lmk ur thoughts!

posts.title: DMARC Enforcement Check
posts.content: Is it necessary to adjust the DMARC policy or will it have a negligible impact on outgoing emails?

user.name: Curtis Wright
user.bio: ecom since 2018

comments.content:
Yeah, you need to set it on the domain.

Google and Yahoo will block you if you dont; major email providers now require DMARC. If you don't have it set up correctly, even your real emails will start getting dumped straight into your customers' spam folders.

Just go to your domain register and add a TXT file

[ul][li]Type: TXT[li]Host / Name: _dmarc       \(Make sure to include the underscore!\)[li]Value / Text: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=[mailto:your-email@yourdomain.com](mailto:your-email@yourdomain.com)

Note: Replace [your-email@yourdomain.com](mailto:your-email@yourdomain.com) with the actual email address where you want to receive reports from Gmail, yahoo etc.

It's rare, but you will know someone is sending spam using your domain because unfamiliar servers and random IP addresses will appear in your DMARC reports \(emails not from Klaviyo\).

after about 2-3 weeks you can update the DMARC file but I don't think there are many scammers sending emails from ecomm brands tbh.

posts.title: Client Retention Maxxing 💯
posts.content:
Max posted this on X:

[Churn has been higher this year. It's structural. Brands are leaving around the 4-6 month mark after we finish the bulk of their flow builds. This is the biggest thing we need to solve and a big reason we're repositioning as a retention partner. Prevent the 4-6 month churn. ](https://x.com/maxwellcopy/status/2063396833645203535)

And I know that from personal experience too. After that 4- to 6-month mark the incremental value of your work starts to decrease and clients may think, "I can do campaigns myself and all the other stuff deliverability, signup forms, flows is good enough. Don't have to pay an agency for all that."

So please let's break down what being a retention partner actually entails and all the things you can do to keep clients as long as possible.

[ul][li]Doing deep dives into analytics beyond Klaviyo, so getting something like Hiro Analytics, and doing geeky stuff like cohort CLV analysis.[li]Being part of their strategy not just executing. That also requires a good relationship with the decision maker. [li]Constantly bringing in new ideas. [li]As an agency you never like to do this but when clients open the discussion of them wanting to leave, reducing your retainer price while at the same time reducing the service you deliver as well. 

I don't know. I'm not super happy with my list. Maybe you guys can add some more points on what we can do to keep our clients long-term beyond the basics we are all doing anyways.

comments.content: Also I don't really like the term "retention partner" because the philosophy of email marketing that we practice around here is also very much about optimizing acquisition. Hey, you guys should partner with this agency that we work with. Hey, do you need any support with anywhere else in the business? I'm happy to set you up with some referrals in whatever thing you need."

That's really what we're going for. Something that we've thought of is just charging more for the first three to four months and then dropping it down after, so the client feels like, "Okay, it is more work, but now this is like the lower price." Where some brands are like, "Yo, I get all the value, I get a ton of value in the first three months, and then it's fewer returns later on, but I'm paying the same price." AB testing feature to maximize results..

Klaviyo lets you test on a small slice of your list first, then auto-push the winner to everyone...

So essentially you're letting a sample tell you what works, then sending the proven winner to the majority of the list automatically.

Here's the setup in the screenshot...

We send the campaign to just 25% of the list as the test.
[ul][li]12.5% gets variation A[li]12.5% gets variation B. [li]Klaviyo waits 4 hours, looks at the results, then sends the winning variation to the remaining 75% automatically.

Perfect for subject line tests.

One thing that matters more than the feature itself...

Set your winning metric to PLACED ORDER RATE in most cases.

I don't give a fuck about opens, and I don't give a fuck about clicks. A subject line can win on opens and lose you money. All I care about is placed orders and revenue.

Try it out.

Another note: the bigger your list is, the more it makes sense to do this. If you have a small list, there's going to be a lot more variability in results. I would only do this regularly if you have an engaged list of at least 100,000.

posts.title: Testing free size exchange vs GWP in abandoned flows - anyone done this?
posts.content:
Hi everyone - first time posting, so bear with me!

I head up marketing for a premium DTC outerwear brand. We sell duck down jackets, raincoats and apparel - fully e-commerce, no brick and mortar. Our AOV sits around $150 USD.
Because we're online only, sizing is a genuine friction point for us. We have a detailed sizing guide and it works well, but the majority of our exchanges are still size-related. Currently customers pay a small fee to exchange.

We're sitting with a fairly high checkout abandonment rate and are trying to decide between two incentives to test in our abandoned cart and checkout flows:
[ol:1][li]Free size exchange on first order - removes the risk of getting the wrong size[li]Gift with purchase - adds perceived value to close the sale
Before committing to either, I built a one-question exit intent survey on our checkout page to try validate the actual reason people are abandoning - price vs sizing vs something else. but the submissions are quite low as most customers are on mobile.

Has anyone tested free size exchange as a conversion or retention tool? And has anyone used exit surveys at checkout to inform their abandoned flow strategy? Would love to hear what's worked \(or hasn't\) before we go all in on one direction. Or am i thinking about this the wrong way completely?

user.name: Kassandra Sass
user.bio: I am a passionate digital marketer working for a great fashion brand!

comments.content:
Awesome question. It's a great one for your first post. Keep them coming!!

I'm attaching here a survey email that people will actually respond to. If you send people to a Google Form, that's a lot of friction. I recommend always doing surveys as multiple choice, where all people have to do is click a button.

Super easy to do this. Just send each button to a different landing page or just a different link on the website, and then inside of Klaviyo you can look at the clicks and how many people clicked each one, as long as they are different links. That's the simplest way to do it. You can get feedback that way and send that as a campaign towards non-buyers.

I have not actually tested this, but I know brands who offer free size exchange just as an evergreen thing. Anybody can always do size exchanges for free. They just pay for shipping. That would be a nice thing to be able to throw on all your abandonment emails, just like, "Hey, we do free size exchanges." I would recommend that.

To your question about exit surveys, the most we do is the example attached.

Feel free to send your website. If you want, you can do it in my DMs, and I can take a look and see what needs to be optimized.

Typically, offers such as free shipping will work the best for abandonments. In order for the free gift to work, it actually has to be a gift people give a fuck about. That's the hard part about it. Typically, we just see discounts work the best.

posts.title: How do you deal with "never ending sale" clients?
posts.content:
One of my clients recently became heavy on promotions. Some months it's 3 weeks of promos, other times it's the whole month. Up until this point, we've been dealing with it like this \(example screenshot attached\):
[ul][li]Open promo and end promo with an email.[li]During promos, send regular content campaigns with promo topbar / banners

My concern is: when there are multiple short promos next to each other, it's easy to end up with calendars packed with "sale starts today, sale ends tonight" emails. That's where the "problem" appears. End of the month comes, we analyse everything and it turns out we've been mostly talking about promos.

Sure, we include regular content as well, product edu, us vs them, testimonials etc. BUT for some reason all I see as a customer is: promo, promo, products, promo, etc.

I'm wondering if any of you guys have similar cases, and if so - how do you deal with that?

Maybe I'll find some new approaches I haven't considered before.

posts.title: Klaviyo Warmup
posts.content:
Hi guys, hope everbody is winning💪🏼!

I’ve got a problem… One of my client’s Shopify store got suspended, so everything moved to a new domain. The old domain + email address are no longer accessible, so we’re on a fresh sending domain that was only registered yesterday → full warmup required in Klaviyo.

Problem: it’s World Cup month, his absolute peak \(~$800K/month, 100K+ list, 60%+ open rate and 3-4% clickrate\). A brand-new domain forces me into weeks of slow ramping right when he needs full volume this month…

I can still use the same Klaviyo account, but need a new dmarc etc so that’s the annoying part..

Has anyone tackled this differently? Is there a way to speed this up without burning the domain, or do I really have to go through the full warmup? 😅

user.name: Fabian Toet
user.bio: Fabian - Email Marketeer

comments.content:
What's up [@Fabian Toet](obj://user/d1a089c4e1264a248b6e4d5c71b41c09)! So ima just be real with you bro there ain't no way to way to skip warmup on a domain registered yesterday. Pretty sure Klaviyo domains under 30 days old need standard warming, plus any warmup services that fake engagement will 100% cook you. ISPs catch on and the damage becomes worse.

Gotta accept that you'll lose some peak season email volume. But here's how I'd minimize it:

So if you're on shared IPs \(which i think most Klaviyo accounts are\), then the IP already has a reputation. You only need to warm the domain, not the IP, which is a much faster path than a fully cold start.

I'd also prob ask Klaviyo support if you could temporarily send from their shared sending domain while your branded domain ages past 30 days. The shared domain has established reputation so you might get higher volumes immediately. Now, the emails may come from a generic domain here, but with 800 racks at stake it might be worth the hit imo.

For branded domain warmup I would just start with 7-day clickers only in small batches and watch opens and spam complaints. If opens stay above 20% and complaints near zero, then slowly increase daily. Go to 30-day engaged, then 60, then 90 over the following weeks. Turn on welcome and abandoned cart flows first, but keep everything else in draft until the domain has traction.

Make sure to lean hard on every non-email channel during ur warmup bc you may as well. SMS, social, retargeting, WhatsApp, or anything similar is not affected by domain reputation.

Also bro why was the Shopify store suspended? If it was policy violations or complaints or stuff liek that, then that root cause could follow you to the new domain regardless of warmup.

Went through everything i could in your data man [@Theo James](obj://user/aae70eb889404394bd01dbc257d7481f) and I think you have a content AND deliverability problem on ur hands, so fixing just one won't break the cycle.

Your click rates range from 0.24% to 1.06%. Your "Heatwave Edit" hit 1.06% and "Payday" to clickers hit 0.91, which are both 2-3x higher than your other sends. If this were purely deliverability, then all the campaigns would perform similarly. But the fact that certain angles and segments produce meaningfully better results tells you content and targeting matter here too, not just inbox placement.

The 71 deliverability score pops out a bit imo. And post-MPP, your 40-50% open rates might look healthy but you gotta realize that Apple generates phantom opens even on emails landing in spam. Those opens could be masking the fact that a chunk of your list isn't actually seeing these emails.

To actually fix these, there are certain things you'll need to dive into.

For the content issue I'd need to see the actual emails to give specific feedback, but at 0.42% average click rate something in the design, angle, or CTA structure is underperforming. Try and reverse-engineer what made Heatwave Edit and Payday work better than the rest. Are the CTAs bigger, or is the angle more compelling? Just replicate whatever those two did differently.

Then for deliverability, drop ur campaigns per week to 3 temporarily. Every low-engagement send compounds the negative signal to ISPs. Also bro, you should segment on clicks not opens. Your "Payday" send to clickers already outperformed. Open-based segments are unreliable post-MPP and likely include people who never actually see your emails.

Ur actual issue is that the low clicks u get tell ISPs the emails aren't wanted, which means deliverability drops and fewer people see them, so then clicks drop further. You gotta break it by tightening audience to clickers, reducing frequency, and improving content simultaneously.

posts.title: The Elite Subscription Journey Checklist 💊
posts.content:
Optimized Frontend Offer For Subscription
[ul][li]Good and strong % OFF[li]Free gifts that go with the product to help with consumption \(mixer, scoop, cup, free guide, course, etc\)

Optimized PDP Page For Subscription Take Rate
[ul][li]Subscription auto-checkedValue of savings on subscription very clear[li]Show free gifts in buy box AND in the image gallery

Shopify Confirmation Emails moved to Klaviyo \(Shopify Plus only\)
[ul][li]Custom and split by one-time purchase or subscription

Post-Purchase Onboarding Education
[ul][li]Emails leading up to delivery on education[li]Sell that you need to use product for months to see results[li]Educate on increasing consumption and tips to use every day[li]At least 4-5 emails here. [li]Ideally 3ish leading up to deliver and other 2-3ish after delivery[li]Can time across post purchase trigger and delivered product

\[Optional\] Quizzes / Courses
[ul][li]Create a fun educational course or quiz on Typeform in first month for customers to learn and quiz themself. Can ask questions as well and upload profile properties into Klaviyo[li]Check-in typeform at first rebill… ask if they have felt benefits and get commitment that they will stick with product.

Packaging / Unboxing Experience
[ul][li]Apple level unboxing experience… people should WANT to take a picture and post on their Insta story
[ul][li]Educational package slips on timeline of results, consumption tips, etc

\[Optional\] Delivered Handwritten Cart From Founder
[ul][li]Great way to contributed to experience especially with influencer led brand[li]Postpilot or Paper Run can execute this[li]Send near delivery or 1 week milestone thanking, congratulating, and educating customer

Optimized Billing Reminders
[ul][li]Educate on benefits, social proof, make exciting, allow delay subscription, manage subscription button low in email[li]\[Optional\] Zaymo for Billing Reminders: great tool to allow people to edit subscription within emails

Free Gifts Along The Way
[ul][li]Orders 2, 4, 6 are key points in journey, come up with nice gifts to include that are low costs.[li]Nice bonuses such as samples of cross-sells, branded gifts that make sense, etc

Minimal, Meaningful Campaigns
[ul][li]If we send too much, we run risk of increased cancellations. [li]Subscribers don't buy too much outside of their subscription so it is minimal upside to send to them.1-2 meaningful subscriber newsletters per month is perfect... insider information, soft cross-sells, founder notes, etc[li]Exclude from all other campaigns.When running sales… give subscriber specific sells such as discount on one-time add ons.

Product Development
[ul][li]People will unsubscribe when they are bored... don't let them get bored! Come out with new flavors and new products and allow subscribers to easily swap
