posts.title: Easy way to hit higher email volume without more work 👀
posts.content:
Was auditing a massive brand recently... and got confused.

Their agency has the brand on a 20 emails per month plan... meaning they make 20 new email campaigns every month to send.

But I looked at their Klaviyo and they were sending an email every day, sometimes two a day. 30-40 sends a month 🤯

I'm sitting there like, what the fuck is going on here? That's a LOT of creative to be producing and the agency is only making 20 emails/mo??

Then I see it... resends of past emails.

But not the same-day resends you're used to seeing... \(this isn't sending an email at 11am and resending that same email at 6pm later that day to non-openers\).

They're pulling 10-15 winning campaigns/mo from 2-4 MONTHS ago, making zero changes, and dropping them back into the calendar as fresh sends.

That's how they hit 30-40 campaigns a month without producing 30-40 new emails.

Beautiful.

Whether you run a brand or manage one, this is an easy lever to pull. Want more volume but don't want to pay for \(or produce\) a pile of new creative? Clone a past winner from months ago and just send it.

Make it a recurring thing.

Stupidly simple and very effective.

Couple things to keep in mind so it actually works:
[ul][li]Pull from your WINNERS, not random old sends. The whole point is it already proved it converts.[li]Space it out enough that it reads as new... months back, not weeks.[li]Light touch refresh if you want... new subject line and preview text is plenty.

And no, your list will not notice.

Be honest, if you got an email months ago and it landed in your inbox again, would you catch it? You're a brand owner or email marketer yourself and even YOU wouldn't. The customer list won't remember and they won't give a fuck.

Mine the archive. 🔁

Hey [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/21f3182f7b7446e098d30584d504095e),

user.name: Clément Brice
user.bio: Built different.

comments.content:
Yooo what's good [@Clément Brice](obj://user/9e12f419c8354cbe99ef92f66320917d) a bit to unpack here but will dump my thoughts below:

So a healthy mix of inbound + outbound has worked for me in terms of getting leads. Research a brand's email setup, find specific gaps, and reach out with something concrete. Not "hey I do email marketing" but "hey, I actually signed up to your email list, looked at your welcome flow, and noticed X. that could be leaving Y amount on the table". That specificity is what gets responses bc it proves you weren't doing random mass outreach bs.

Biggest thing that made it work was niching down hard. Ik that's prob an unpopular take in this community, especially when the core of email strategy industry to industry is pretty much the same, but for me in my case, every case study and example I share speaks directly to the brands I'm reaching out to. It'll make lowering your prospect's wall easier and whatever outreach you send will hit harder and land better imo.

Also, I use AI tools daily and they actually make email marketers more valuable, not less. AI can write decent drafts, but it can't get into the actual weeds of retention & lifecycle fulfillment to where it's telling you that your billing reminder is triggering churn, or that your attribution is inflated 4x from phantom opens, or that your replenishment flow fires after customers already reordered, or that a $6k AOV welcome flow needs a completely different structure than a $50 one. Don't fear it, just stay on top of it and use it to make u better.

posts.title: Sale Follow Up Email
posts.content: SULT ran a sale this weekend, and this is the follow up email which I think is a very nice way to drive subscription. Frames the subscription offer as very valuable as it's 26% off forever and the 20% was only available for 3 days. Also really like their upcoming subscription benefits section.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
I fw it [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)! I feel like using post-sale FOMO to pivot to subscription is something most brands be missing tbh. "The sale gave you 20% for 3 days, subscription gives you 26% forever" makes the subscription feel like the better deal than the one people missed. Timing is perfect because the loss is fresh, and then just stacking benefits at deliveries 2, 4, and 6 are a nice churn prevention touch too.

But lowkey, I feel like the email doesn't actually bridge sale buyers to subscription. Someone who just bought at 20% is now seeing 26% and might think why weren't they told of this before. I'd add a line like "already bought this weekend? Subscribe and your next order is 26% off automatically". That would prob catch those people and make subscription the natural next step.

There also isn't much urgency on the subscription itself imo. The sale had a midnight deadline but the subscription is just always there. That's the value prop they're tryna lead with, but it means there's no reason to act today. A soft nudge of some sort would prob move ppl on the fence without pressuring them into an quick commitment.

This is def good enough to systematize tho. Would just try to find a way to make this repeatable post-sale play after every promotional event.

posts.title: Creating Offers
posts.content:
Your offer is everything... but that doesn't mean a bigger discount. @channel

Offer = PERCEIVED value... not necessarily more $$ off.

So when a brand tells me "we don't discount, ever" I don't panic, I get curious.

First question every time: what are you ALREADY giving away that you're not bragging about?

Because most brands bundle a ton of free shit into the product... then bury it halfway down a product page nobody scrolls to.

Take this premium chair brand Anthros for example who refused to discount.

But look at what comes with every single chair:
Free 2-day shipping
60-day risk-free trial
12-year warranty
Free posture consult with a licensed therapist \($200 value\)
Guidebook, video series, a free month of corrective exercise, owners community
Plus it's $250 cheaper than their custom build

That's a STACKED offer.

We can add nothing extra discount wise but just advertise that offer on the frontend more to gather emails and increase conversions.

Now the pop-up isn't "10% off." It's "Free 2-day shipping + $200 in free gifts"...

Same product and margin but way higher perceived value.

This is the muscle you need to be be building...

Before you ever reach for a discount, ask:
What are we already giving away I can frame as a bonus?
How do we package it better?

Reframing costs nothing. Pull that lever first. :repeat:

posts.title: Perceived Value

Sometimes you can make an offer rip without changing it's value at all, just its perceived value. We have a high ticket client that offers $700 as a welcome offer, and then most people use an influencer code to get another $200-$400 off.

For memorial day we ran $1000 store credit and it absolutely RIPPED. Despite the fact that most people save this much anyway, the perception was changed. posts.title: Coming up with offers
posts.content:
Hi everyone 👋🏻 Hope you're doing well and crushing it.

Just wanted to ask a quick question:

How do you guys come up with offers for your clients?

Offers you can test in pop-ups, win back, campaigns, or promo seasons.

Do you look at specific metrics or datas to come up with them?

user.name: Elton Korpuzi
user.bio: Just an email marketer who does BJJ and gym

comments.content:
First place to look is what the client is already offering. Ask if they give any free gifts or anything already when somebody buys. Oftentimes brands do; they just don't advertise this. Are they giving away any booklets, little bags, accessories, etc.? That can be baked into an offer.

I usually get my offer ideas from stealing from other brands, lol. I'm just looking at brands every single day, and I follow brands' emails very closely. If I see an offer I like, I'll steal it.

All offers come down to percent off, dollar off, bundles, and free gifts. Every offer is a variation of that.

It just comes down to testing all of these in different situations and building intuition on what you think you should start out with for a brand in their unique scenario.

The easiest to start off with is always dollar off and percent off. If it's a high AOV brand, dollar off typically performs better.

Free gifts are typically nice value adds to help with conversion rates.

BOGOs and bundles typically work best for past buyers.

That's generally a good rule of thumb to start with.

posts.title: A/B testing decision
posts.content:
Hello everyone, I hope you are doing well!

I have a question about an A/B test I have been running for about 12 days now \(Dutch market\).
I have been testing the welcome offer: standard 10% OFF vs Mystery discount.

We tested the offer in the popup form. People who saw the 10% off popup form already saw the discount code in the success step of the popup. Plus, they received the welcome email with the 10% off.

People who saw the mystery discount popup received the welcome email with the Mystery discount code that they had to fill in in the checkout in order to see the discount amount \(also 10%\).

Now I'd like to have some advice in choosing the winner here:
As you see in the metrics of the popup form its clearly visible that the 10% off is winning , and it gets way more orders \(probably because the code is in the form\)

However, when you take a look at the metrics of the welcome email the difference is massive and the mystery discount is winning significantly.

What would you advice me to do here in determining the winner of this A/B test?

comments.content: my advice is to only test one variable at a time. If you want to test 10% versus mystery discount, cool, but I would not introduce another variable to the same test.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content: Exactly as Matthias said, you need to make sure everything is exactly the same, besides one thing. You can't have a different offer and then also the discount codes entered in different places and judge results. I'd restart it and make sure they're both the same in how you deliver the discount.

posts.title: New client, help pls. Higher-ticket DTC brand
posts.content:
What's up y'all,

About to take on a client that sells premium protective cases for firearms and cameras.

$40M+ brand, 500-600k email list, already has core flows in place. They just parted ways with an agency and are bringing email in-house. I want to walk in with a clear strategic framework of what generally works for a brand like this before I even have access to the account.

Open rates are solid \(~52%\) but click rates are around 0.8% and apparently have been dropping. Email-attributed revenue has also been dropping.

My main issue is that I have experience mainly in replenishment products. The average time between purchases is around 55 days for those who do repurchase, but a lot of customers just buy once. They do have supplementary products that could be upsold but it's largely untapped.

A couple of specific questions:
[ol:1][li]Should I segment by product category since their buyer personas are pretty distinct? Firearms buyers vs camera buyers. Or should I stick to one large engaged segment and just let the content do the work? Haven't dealt with a catalog this wide before.[li]What's the best strategy to increase LTV for someone who bought a $150 case and probably won't need another one for a year or two? How do you keep them warm and in the ecosystem without burning them out?[li]What do high-converting flows emphasize with a brand like this vs. a typical impulse-buy product? [li]Any big brand's emails I should take inspiration from?

Any experience with similar brands or product categories is MUCH appreciated. Thanks in advance.

posts.title: How I make Claude x Klaviyo MCP read full email copy
posts.content:
Hey guys,

I was watching yesterday's call recording and there was some talk about Claude's MCP reading SLs and PTs only + how it can't read full email copy, break down what works, where it works, why it works there \(Max's new MX Claude skill will be handy to combine with here, I think\), etc.

I'm quickly gonna break down what I'm doing, and then please feel free to do the same or let me know where I can do it better!

So maybe I'm late to the party and some of you guys are already aware, but Claude's MCP can read the alternative text you put in for the images.

Luckily I've added alt. text as a best practise, but if you plan to utilize this, then maybe it's worth adding alt text to some of your flows at least, and reaping those deep Claude 4.8-breakdown benefits later💯

So I've just done that and asked Claude to break down why certain angles and offers work post-purchase, pre-purchase, etc, and just playing around with it, because it always flags if it has any counter-ideas based on; you guessed it, reading all the other flow copy and data across the Klaviyo account.

I think it's amazing, it does what I need, and I'm super stoked to connect it to the MX skill \(hopefully it has some info on offer-creation too\).

Just make skills per brand, and allow Claude to update those files itself \(perhaps you'll need to download the desktop app\), so it reads Klaviyo's full emails and data together -> adds it right to a doc so you can make it a library instead of always checking Klaviyo \(and if your chat compresses or anything happens, it's all in your iCloud/downloads\).

Tell the 'Klaviyo-checking' skill to make sure it's connected to the right account, let it know when you've updated flows and it updates the docs for you, and tell it that data changes so it must still go into Klaviyo to see the updated data.

🙏Hopefully you didn't read allat and you knew it already, but maybe someone didn't know!

posts.title: Klayvio vs Northbeam attribution issue
posts.content:
My client is switching to Northbeam and also wants to start tracking email with it.

My concern is the attribution differences might significantly affect my bonus comp based on hitting % revenue benchmarks. [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/21f3182f7b7446e098d30584d504095e) what are you doing for the most accurate software/fair model for email attribution with clients?

Right now I'm using the default 5 day open/click in Klayvio with 7 day SMS click, based on checkout started. This is how he was tracking email/SMS revenue with the previous agency.

I don't want to get screwed over.

user.name: Florian Ruhstaller
user.bio: Email list manager with big dreams

comments.content:
We don't really use any other software besides Klayvio, and we just do whatever the attribution settings are when we come to the account. Probably the most accurate for immediate sales and direct sales is one-day opens, one-day clicks, but five-day opens and five-day clicks is the industry standard. It's easier to benchmark results to that.

To your question, yes, it will have an impact, and you need to renegotiate your bonus terms. This is why we never do bonus terms. There's too much back and forth, and somebody's always upset, and it's just a pain and a hassle. I've never had to deal with it, but in my opinion you have to renegotiate the terms. Be like, yeah, well, the attribution we agreed on this deal based on these attribution settings, so if we're changing that, we need to change these terms so I can still get kind of what I've been getting.

posts.title: How to export Figma designs to Klaviyo?
posts.content:
Hey [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/21f3182f7b7446e098d30584d504095e) [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d),

Thanks in advance, Clément

user.name: Clément Brice
user.bio: Built different.

comments.content:
Wsg gang [@Clément Brice](obj://user/9e12f419c8354cbe99ef92f66320917d) gonna hop in here bc this is easy but there's currently no native Figma-to-Klaviyo export that exists.

So below are three ways to handle it:

[ol:1][li]Slice and rebuild. Just export images from Figma and rebuild them in Klaviyo's drag-and-drop editor using those images alongside native text blocks, buttons, and product blocks.

2. Emailify plugin. It's a Figma plugin that exports email HTML with Klaviyo-specific formatting built in. Icl tho this only works if you design using Emailify's own components inside Figma. Can't convert an existing regular Figma design retroactively. Great if you're starting fresh.

3. Hand-code it. A dev codes the HTML from the Figma file as reference and imports into Klaviyo.

Whichever route you take just make sure u avoid slicing the entire design into image-only sections. All-image emails get flagged by spam filters, break when images are blocked, and screen readers can't read them. You always wanna mix live text, native buttons, and images.

posts.title: Pop-Up Offer Testing
posts.content: Hey guys. Going to be running 3 offer tests for a client in the popup. $, %, and free gift. My original thought was to create one popup and a/b test each variation with a micro commit & teaser and see how it goes. Then I was thinking if I play more of the long game where I would only have 1 popup running with one offer for example the $ off where I a/b test a micro commit vs no micro commit. Run that for 30 days, choose winner, and create another form with the % off and do the same thing. If that makes any sense. The goal was just to provide enough data for one specific offer to see which one works better. Am I overcomplicating it? What would you guys recommend?

user.name: Brandon Teyf
user.bio: Founder of Got Mail Media, specializing in email and sms marketing for health & wellness and luxury boutique brands.

comments.content: I'd say you're overcomplicating it. Only test one thing at a time. You can't test an offer and form style at the same time. Just test one thing. An offer is going to be higher leverage, so choose whether you're doing micro commit or no micro commit. Typically micro commit will perform better, so I just start with that and do an A/B test of the three different offers on a micro commit form. After you get the winner, then you can test form style.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
One of my clients do courses and events, up to $7000 per. It's usually a matter of getting booked calls like Max said, but I'd also say that the brand and credibility is super important too and your emails will depend on that. Meaning, they won't be able to do all the heavy lifting themselves and need to be supported by content.

Do they have a strong organic presence? And do they have lots of proof / testimonials? This is what my client has \(personal brand\) - so there's not a doubt about the quality of the product anymore, it's just a question of using consistent emails to get that final push to book a call. Sometimes the lifecycle can be multiple years and you have to wait for the timing to be right. A lot of people tell us that they got an email at the perfect time etc. when in reality they've been getting emails for years.

Also, side note. I think email could be super valuable for their existing customers to cross-sell and get referrals. Maybe extras they can add-on or maintenance. But if the customer is $40,000 deep, it's super important to reinforce the purchase and create a community of those owners. Kind of like how expensive mattresses are a one-time for life purchase but consistent emails can get people talking and referrals do the selling for you.

Just my 2cents hope this gives you some ideas and sick that they reached out!

posts.title: Increase Opens / Engagement Trick
posts.content:
Changing your sender name to increase opens and engagement!

One thing I see this brand do that I don't really see any other brand out there do... changing sender name based on the email.

Your sender name is your first subject line and the first thing people see when they get a notification. Why not use that space to your advantage?

Ideas / Examples:
[ol:1][li]Well Copy SALE - for when you do sales [li]Well Copy REWARDS - for when you give people credit or gifts[li]Well Copy EARLY ACCESS - for early access on sales or restocks[li]Well Copy NEW - for announcements or new products [li]Max | Well Copy - for messages from a specific person [li]Well Copy Customer Service - for flow emails like abandonments to say there was an issue with their order[li]Your Well Copy Stylist - personal sort of vibe... using "your" to get attention. If you sell clothing this could then be an email about recommended products.

Easy way to stand out and get attention ‼️

posts.content:
First month with this brand. Two tests in.

Everyone overcomplicates pop-ups... multi-step quizzes, spin-to-win, three fields and a phone number.

We did the opposite.

Micro-commit. One ask. Aggressive timing. Built in klaviyo.

We also didn't invent a new offer and didn't suffer any margins. The offer was already on the site, already converting. We just put it in front of people with a bit of "exclusive" framing.

Results on the form: 37% pop-up cvr
Store-wide CVR moved: 3% –> ~4%

The pop-up isn't a side quest guyss, we are seeing similar results for a few other brands, and it's helping soo much with the overall store performance.

I try to use it as much as I can in every work flow I have to save time and make better decisions.

I personally have an email agent, copy agent and AB agent that does a lot of the hard lifting for me.
I then take that copy and have claude co work put it into notion for me where I can edit it and review it.

I do one last manual review, because rule #1 is don't trust AI and it gets sent out.

posts.title: How Do You Build Brand Loyalty?
posts.content: We're running a collab with a larger brand, and it's bringing in a wave of new customers, all coming in through a free product redemption as part of a giveaway. No purchase intent, no prior brand affinity. How do you structure the post-purchase experience to actually build loyalty with this audience?

user.name: Zeina Hassan
user.bio: Copywriter and Brand Strategist

comments.content:
Hi what's up [@Zeina Hassan](obj://user/7617efcabe704980ac4fb7703d331968)! So this audience is actually completely different from a normal customer, as they didn't choose your brand, they just chose a free giveaway. There's zero purchase intent behind that. The only conversion lever you have is the product itself.

What'd I'd personally do is build a trust ladder tbh. They know you exist, then they try the product, they realize it's good, and then they choose to buy.

Day 0-1: A welcome message, but more like "here's what you got through our collab with \[partner brand\] and why we're excited for you to try it." You could lean into the partner name bc that's the trust they already have. I'd abuse that straight away lol.

Next for Day 3-4: Nudge them to actually use it. All I'd do here is give clear, digestible usage tips if the product needs education, or just a reminder to open the box. Hella important step, prob the one step you can't afford to drop the ball on.

Day 7-10: Simply just social proof. That could mean UGC, reviews, and testimonials. This reframes it from "something I got for free" to "something people pay for and love." You can add a soft CTA here for people who are already sold here too.

Day 14-18 should be the brand story. Like the mission, values, what makes you different, all that jazz. If someone's hypothetically two weeks in, and if they've tried it and liked it, then they're primed to care imo.

Day 21-25: Now here's the actual purchase incentive. Wouldn't overthink this, would juts have it read along the lines of "Here's X% off your first order." It's gonna resonate completely differently after weeks of product experience than a discount on Day 1. Also don't rush the ask either because discounting a free product audience too early devalues the brand.

I'm also tagging every profile with a source property so I could track this cohort's conversion separately from organic customers. And if you captured phone numbers, SMS can be powerful for that "actually try it" nudge. Lmk how this goes!

posts.title: CAMPAIGN REVENUE DROPPING
posts.content:
Hey guys, just wanted to get some thoughts on what I could potentially be doing wrong here.
I manage email + SMS for a 7-figure/month word-of-affirmation clothing brand, and email currently drives around 45–50% of total revenue.
Because of the size of the brand, we typically send daily campaigns and our revenue split is roughly 30:70 between campaigns and flows. Last month we ran into a bunch of backend issues with both our Meta and Shopify accounts, which forced us to scale down pretty aggressively. Ever since then, campaign performance has dropped off quite heavily.
What’s confusing is that our core engagement metrics opens, clicks, unsubscribes have stayed relatively consistent despite the revenue drop.
Some people have suggested it could be customer fatigue from similar offers/creative angles, while others have mentioned that since opens are still healthy, sending to a broader/full list again might help.
Would love to hear if anyone’s experienced something similar or has advice on what you’d test next. Is this more likely an offer/creative issue, deliverability/list segmentation issue, or just a matter of refreshing angles and messaging?

Would love to hear some of your thoughts! thank you

posts.title: High Performing Email To Steal
posts.content:
One of my favorite emails for quick cash / putting in your site abandonment

[ol:1][li]Switch your sender name to "Rewards at XYZBRAND"[li]Say somebody has store credit of a specific dollar amount \(important to add decimals to make it look official and automated... such as $25.00 instead of $25"[li]Give them a discount code for a $ off offer[li]Frame it as "store credit" instead of $XX OFF

The psychology of having store credit in your account hits wayyyy harder than $ OFF... because if you have money in your account you feel like you are losing $25 if you don't lose it... and this triggers loss aversion in humans. We hate losing shit.

Try it out ASAP. Easy cash.

So if it's possible, [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) can we have some sort of chart of the main flows, along with the benchmark they should meet and exceed to be considered good? And what to do if certain benchmarks are not met?

Just the main flows that you teach in the course?

I know how to create flows, but if you tell me to optimize it, or even if I SHOULD optimize it, I don't even know where to start. Thanks.

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
Unfortunately, it is literally impossible to have benchmarks because brands are so different. I have some brands that I'm stoked with a 3% converting welcome flow, while some were at 10%, and I think it should be better.

And there are just way too many nuances. For example, an email welcome flow for a brand that only does email and not SMS is going to have a way higher attributed revenue because people need to buy from that email. However, if you have an SMS welcome flow as well as an email welcome flow, your email welcome flow is going to be way too low compared to just having an email welcome flow.

Things like this make attribution benchmarks so difficult, and so it's your job to just make sure you're following all the best practices to get your brand's specific benchmark numbers first and then iterate and test from there to improve it. Every brand is going to have different benchmarks based on their traffic, the decision cycles, how long it takes to decide you want that product, all that sort of stuff. There's a reason why I don't have a lot of benchmarks posted anywhere.

posts.title: Father's Day Opt-Out Email
posts.content:
Father's Day is coming up, so now is the time if you want to start sending Father's Day opt-out emails to do that.

Essentially, all you do is send an email saying, "Hey, if you want to opt out of Father's Day emails, click here," and then you exclude the people who click from your Father's Day campaigns.

The easiest way, in my opinion, to execute this is to send a plain text email with only one link, and you have that be the opt-out link. You just send those people to the home page of your website, and then you create a segment of anybody who clicked that campaign.

That's going to be your exclusion segment. Anybody who clicked that campaign, exclude that segment from all your Father's Day emails.

A lot of people appreciate the message, and it can be some bonus points, both to the list and with clients.

posts.content: What's your process to clean the account so the client can save money? I also don't want to delete contacts that could be recovered for additional revenue.

user.name: Florian Ruhstaller
user.bio: Email list manager with big dreams

comments.content:
Yooo [@Florian Ruhstaller](obj://user/25feaa3355334940a0919731e28915d7) you actually wanna suppress, not delete. Suppressed profiles stop counting toward Klaviyo billing and stop receiving emails but their data stays intact. So if they ever spin back, all their history is preserved. Only delete hard bounces and invalid emails bc those are never coming back.

Before suppressing anyone make sure to give them a last shot. Build a sunset flow targeting 90-120 day unengaged profiles, about 2-3 emails, and frame the whole thing along the lines of "we miss you, here's one last chance." Stuff liek that recovers 3-10%. Anyone who doesn't engage gets suppressed. Also suppress profiles who never engaged at all and never opened or clicked once.

Good to make this a system too, not a one-time cleanup imo.

posts.title: POP-UP FORM MASTERY
posts.content:
Locking in your pop-up forms to maximize list growth... one of the biggest levers in email marketing.

Here's some common mistakes and a QA list to go through before setting pop-ups live.

COMMON MISTAKES CHECKLIST
[ul][li]❌ Setting delay over 6 seconds[li]❌ Asking for email + SMS on the same step[li]❌ Adding "join our community" or "get exclusive updates" copy[li]❌ Quiz question with 5+ answer options[li]❌ Small modal instead of full-page[li]❌ Setting a 10% off offer and never testing alternatives[li]❌ X button in top right with no alternative close method tested[li]❌ Treating the pop-up as "done" once it's live

QA CHECKLIST: BEFORE A POP-UP GOES LIVE
[ol:1][li]Delay is set between 2–6 seconds[li]Full-page confirmed on mobile AND desktop[li]One input per step, no multi-field steps[li]Offer is the visually dominant element[li]All unnecessary copy has been removed[li]Quiz question \(if used\) has 2–4 simple options max[li]Close mechanism has been intentionally chosen and noted[li]Form has AB tests set up[li]Offer has a testing roadmap, not just one static offer[li]SMS step is included after email step

👉 If you want to generate the best results... use [Alia](https://www.aliapopups.com/) for pop-up forms. It absolutely rips every time and beats all other forms. Free trial as well so you can see the results before deciding if you want to move forward :\)

^ great reply from Max - Sales attribution is the main source, good sales means good marketing.

Imo if you are justifying email marketing \(particularly with Klaviyo\) I would position it as:

[ul][li]There are many sales funnels, and email marketing is part of a store's marketing[li]The sales funnel is short for some brands \(one product stores- click ad, buy\), and different for others \(fashion- browse, furniture- considered, long purchase\)[li]Open rates are inflated on Apple devices and so they are unreliable[li]The easiest ways to measure this is through attribution windows and email clicks \(selling the click\) - and clicks can be compared with clicks on platforms like Meta, Tiktok and Google.

SO... say for example you are selling to a supplement brand with Cost per Click
Let's ignore \(CPM- Cost per Mille and CPA- Cost per Action\)

Advertisers typically pay between $1.30 and $2.50 per click for supplement ads on Facebook in the US- so let's say $2 per click for simplicity.

If an email you send you gets 500 clicks, you generated $1,000 worth of comparable value to Meta for this email.

BUT Klaviyo contacts are warmer- they are further down the sales funnel.
[ul][li]They have expressed interest by entering their email address or have purchased already[li]There is a higher change that  the clicks are grom your VIP segment which generates 80% of your sales[li]They are already cookie'd from the email so you can track all their website actions to view what they're interested and helps you target them more effectively[li]They technically performed two clicks- the email open and the click onto the website[li]They automatiaclly trigger abandoned cart emails, trigger upsell emails, get re-enabled for weekly campaigns from Klaviyo etc.[li]They are definitely your target audience, not some random browsers on facebook 

So the click is worth more- how much more is hard to say, but you can add a figure like +20% - +50% for the value.

So this email generated ~$1,200 in value for you and also raised awareness for your brand.

posts.title: Flow for pending payments?
posts.content:
My peptide client usually sends payment link via email and once they complete payment then only order will be sent.

He is doing this because last time his payment processor blocked him. I dont know the details. But this is what he is wants to do now for extra precaution.

As expected, many people are ordering but not completing the order. Probably email landing in spam, or I dont know what.

So he told me to create a flow to remind people to pay, otherwise order will be cancelled in 24 hours \(legit since payment link expires in 24 hours\)

At the check out we also tell them thay they will receive a secure payment link in their email to continue payment.

My question is, is there a way to set up this flow in Klaviyo? I have already created 3 emails. First email will go out once they complete the check out. The other 2 is reminding them 12 hours later, and when they have only 6 hours left before payment link expires.

Is there a way to create this flow in Klaviyo? If so, how?

If not, how?

Cc: [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5) [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6)

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
What's up [@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703) ! So yeah this can be built in Klaviyo, but my question is how does Klaviyo know when someone's actually paid?

You're gonna need a conditional split before Email 2 and 3 that checks payment status, otherwise everyone gets all three emails including people who already paid. The easiest way imo is a custom event or profile property that updates when payment completes, which can be either via webhook from the payment processor to Klaviyo, or a Zapier/Make automation that watches for payment confirmation. I wouldn't rely on Shopify's standard Placed Order event tbh since your checkout is non-standard with the delayed payment, so it might not fire how you'd expect it to.

Ur structure and timing is solid tho. But before building the full flow, if you see Email 1 is hitting spam, two more emails going to spam won't fix anything. I'd just check SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication.

The payment link itself might also be the trigger bc I've seen third-party processor links get flagged by spam filters before. And given that peptides are a restricted category, you'll prob face tighter filtering than a normal brand. You should consider a separate sending domain for these transactional payment emails to protect your marketing domain.

Might also be worth it to consider SMS for this flow tbh. If spam is ur main issue, SMS avoids it entirely, and ur messages should get seen right away. Just make sure it clearly identifies the brand and references the specific order so it doesn't read like a scam text or smth 😂. But lmk!

posts.title: Countdown Time on Abandon Checkout/Cart?
posts.content:
Hey guys, recently watched a video about a US based ecommerce brand adding a countdown timer to their checkout page and claimed it added another 90k to his store. I can assume the urgency factor is very persuasive.

I was wondering if the same element can be applied to the abandon checkout/cart emails? If so, which email in the flow sequence would it be? Also would this work for the other abandons?

Very curios about this since I have added this element to the second to last email in the welcome flow and it converts pretty well.

Has anyone tried something like this?

user.name: Brandon Teyf
user.bio: Founder of Got Mail Media, specializing in email and sms marketing for health & wellness and luxury boutique brands.

comments.content:
Yo yooo [@Brandon Teyf](obj://user/585440273f434171be9a7d9cb3bb131c) since it's already converting in your welcome flow the same principle will apply to abandonment emails, it just needs the right placement fr.

I personally wouldn't put it in Email 1. The first abandoned cart/checkout email should be a simple reminder with no discount or timer. If you lead with urgency on Email 1, you'll just train customers to abandon on purpose to trigger the deal.

Email 2 \(around 24 hours after abandonment\) is the sweet spot.

Bc atp the reminder didn't convert, so now you escalate. Timer counts down to a cart expiration, discount deadline, or free shipping window. If you have an Email 3 at 48-72 hours, that's your final push with the strongest urgency.

This all fits best on checkout and cart abandonment where intent is high. Browse and site abandonment are weaker bc a ticking clock for someone who just glanced at a product feels aggressive for that level of intent imo.

The deadline has to be real though too bro. If the customer ignores the timer and the discount still works 3 days later, you've taught them your urgency is fake. Gotta use unique codes with actual expirations.

Also for the setup, Klaviyo doesn't have a native countdown timer, so you'll need third-party tools like MailTimers, Sendtric, or CountdownMail and embed the HTML into a Klaviyo HTML block. For flows specifically, use a constant timer \(starts counting when opened\) rather than a fixed-date timer, since everyone enters at different times. Also worth lyk that timers can display incorrectly in Apple Mail since it pre-loads content, so always test across clients. Lmk ur thoughts!

Founder of Magtania, specializing in retention & lifecycle marketing for the pet care industry.

Believe you can achieve it, and you're halfway there.

replies.content:
[@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) yeah this makes a lot of sense. Right now I have the abandon cart/checkout flows split between purchased 0 times and purchased at least once over all time. The emails are the same except the split with purchased 0 times has the welcome discount.

Would you keep the split and have 2 discounts? One is welcome the other is the specific abandon email that will expire.

user.name: Brandon Teyf
user.bio: Founder of Got Mail Media, specializing in email and sms marketing for health & wellness and luxury boutique brands.

replies.content:
[@Brandon Teyf](obj://user/585440273f434171be9a7d9cb3bb131c) I'd keep the split tbh, but don't stack two discounts.

The first-time buyers already have the welcome discount here. So I wouldn't add another one on top fr. Instead, you can use the abandonment email to remind them the welcome offer exists and put the countdown timer on that one specifically. Could have it read along the lines of: "You left something in your cart — your welcome offer expires in 24 hours."

It's basically just urgency around something they already have, so there's no extra margin given away. If 15% off wasn't enough, another discount wouldn't fix that so we can't have them finesse us lol. It's prob more likely trust or timing.

But for this to work the welcome discount needs to actually expire. If it's a static code that works forever, the countdown is fake and customers will figure that out. I'd use a unique code with a real expiration.

And for returning customers \(since they trust the brand already\), most returning customer abandonment is timing or distraction, not price. You should have a simple reminder as Email 1, with no discount. If you escalate in Email 2 or 3, a small incentive can work but keep it smaller than the welcome discount and make it the exception.

Also make sure your welcome flow and abandonment flow aren't firing simultaneously for the same person, so use flow filters to prevent that overlap.

Ik ts sounds like a lot but the problem is that every discount trains behavior. So if people learn abandoning triggers a deal, they'll start doing it on purpose to finesse the system 🤣 so we gotta take preventative measures.

posts.title: Quick highlight - New Drop Strategy + A/B Test
posts.content:
Hey everyone! 👋

Merlijn here, head of email marketing at Scalehuse. Just joined the community and wanted to introduce myself. Really excited to be here, ask questions, share what I'm learning, and grow alongside all of you.

Quick context on what I do.

We run two belt brands, one for men and one for women \(Bella Belts on the women's side\). Email used to live with an agency, but as of now it's fully in house and on my plate \(+ my amazing designer!\). Lots to figure out, lots to test, and a lot of fun so far.

Wanted to share something we just ran that worked really well, in case it sparks ideas for anyone else.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
⚙️ The setup

Earlier this year we launched a new collection to an early access list and it TOOK OFF ✈️!

We then opened it up AGAIN, now to the full list and the thing sold out.

About a month and a half later, we restocked, revamped the website, and officially launched the new collection to everyone. Another big email announcement, another big wave of traffic.

For the main launch we tried something different on the creative side. Instead of our normal headers, we built the email around a GIF showcasing the belts across different outfits, an Instagram story inside the inbox. The thinking: break the reader out of inbox autopilot and hit them with a layout that doesn't feel like every other email.

That email pulled in $13,791.88 in revenue at a 48.64% open rate on the BIG LIST send.

👀 Here's where it got interesting.

What do you actually send as a follow up to catch the traffic you didn't get the first time?

The play we landed on:
Day 1. New collection launch at full margin, leaning on the sale already running on site.
Day 2. Exclude everyone who purchased and send a founder style "oops, we totally forgot to celebrate" message. \(A discount code + giveaway as celebration\)

The angle is honest. In all the hecticness of the relaunch, we forgot to actually celebrate the new collection, the new website, all of it. So we're celebrating now, and here's a little present, a nice discount.

That follow up outperformed the original launch email.

Traffic we would have completely missed showed up because we gave them extra value, and a completely different angle.

A couple of things on this:

We don't overuse this. The "oops" angle only lands when it feels real. The moment it becomes formulaic, the trick is dead.

Variations like "oops we forgot to add the right link" or "oops we forgot to email" right after a campaign also work surprisingly well. People open out of pure curiosity, and that opens the door to a second touch at almost zero extra cost.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

📝 Bonus test \(textual styling on Bella\)

On the women's brand we A/B tested this follow up.

Variation A was a textual email with a bit of Bella flair, light styling that feels on brand for women.
Variation B was the plain "friend just typed this to you" version.

Variation A pulled $9,017.92 \(113 orders\). $80 AOV
Variation B pulled $6,164.26 \(88 orders\). $70 AOV

Big uplift on revenue from the styled version.

The weird part: click rate was basically identical between them \(0.96% vs 0.96%\). Same volume of people clicking, but the styled version converted noticeably better once they landed on site.

I want to run this a few more times to see if it holds up structurally, or whether the brand flair is doing something pre click that we're not picking up in the metrics.

If anyone has tested styled vs plain textual on a feminine brand, I'd love to hear what you saw.
\(I'll be trying some A/B's on our Male brand soon\)

Anyway, that's me. Excited to be here and looking forward to learning from this group and sharing my bits. 👋

posts.title: Sign Up Rate Dropping Suddenly
posts.content: Hey there guys, do you have any idea what might be causing this? I did launch an A/B test then but it was just a simple: pop up appears after 3 seconds vs 8 seconds. Would that cause this big of a drop?

comments.content:
Hey Chris, the conversion rate did drop significantly, although the last 2 days seem to have stabilized a bit.

That said, what stands out the most isn't the conversion rate itself, it's the massive drop in pop-up views. You went from ~550-700 views/day \(May 8-10\) to ~100-200 views/day \(May 12-14\). That's a 70-80% traffic drop.

An A/B test changing the delay from 3s to 8s wouldn't cause that. At worst, the 8s variant would have slightly fewer views because some users bounce before the trigger fires, but never this magnitude.

The conversion rate drop is likely a consequence of the traffic drop, not the cause. When top-of-funnel volume collapses like this, you usually lose the most qualified traffic first \(paid campaigns\), leaving a residual mix with weaker intent, which crushes conversion rate.

Worth checking:
- Did any ad campaigns get paused, rejected, or hit budget cap around May 10-11?
- Any tracking/site issue in that window?
- Did a specific traffic source \(paid, referral, partnership\) go dark?

I'd start by pulling traffic by source/channel for those dates before blaming the A/B test.

For some reason, the email revenue of one of my clients in the peptide space is going down the drain, and I have no idea why.

Does this have anything to do with the meta ads?

Did it change the attribution since he started running meta ads?

Are the Meta ads gobbling up the attribution that should've gone to Klaviyo?

Am I outlandish in suspecting that my client may have purposely screwed up something so I don't get as much commission?

Another thing: we ran a 48-hr \(+24-hr extension\) Earth Day BOGO promo flash sale that ended on the 22nd of April.

I understand that revenue goes down after promos. But I don't think it should take this long for it to get back up, right?

So meta and klaviyo don't share an attribution model so there won't be any 'attribution stealing' happening, and tbh it's usually the opposite way around where klaviyo over attributes.

In general, Meta ad traffic is going to be colder than organic. This means that the new customers coming onto the email list from your pop-up will be a bit colder and therefore cause a drop in email revenue.

Coming back of the sale could also be a contributing factor. You're right, it shouldn't take that long to bounce back but if the list isn't growing super quick \(which I presume it isn't at that revenue level\) it could take longer.

How long have you been running email for this brand? Then because the brand isn't huge, the list isn't growing full of new customer that quickly. Then add in to this that the new traffic is colder and lower intent.

I think it's very possible that you're not doing anything wrong here man and you might just need to ride it out.

Also I doubt your client is trying to sabotage you. If attribution setting are still default then I don't think there's anything he could do.

posts.title: How To Make Emails Convert More
posts.content:
One singular statistic you find on the internet can transform how your emails/copy converts.

Stop making general statements. Start finding statistics, numbers, studies, and proof.

“The more facts you tell, the more you sell.” — David Ogilvy \(goat\)
“Platitudes and generalities roll off the human understanding.” - Claude Hopkins \(goat\)

“Supports recovery” is weaker than: “Reduced soreness by 32% in a clinical study.”

Numbers feel real while generalities feel like marketing that don't mean anything.

AI makes this insanely easy now.

Ask it to find these numbers for you with a simple prompt of “What numbers would strengthen this copy?”

One strong statistic or proof point can completely change an email.

posts.title: Text Based Emails Masterclass
posts.content:
Text-based emails look like they're coming from a real person… no graphics, no designed layouts, just plain text in the inbox like a message from a friend.

They convert extremely well when used as a pattern interrupt within your regular graphic-heavy calendar, but writing them is a different skill than writing copy for designed emails.

👇The Three Formats

1️⃣ Short Form SMS-Style \(Under 30 Words\)
Super short. Super direct. Literally a couple of sentences and a link. These work because they feel effortless and urgent — like someone grabbed their phone and shot you a quick message.

Example:
"Hey — we just restocked \[product\] but last time it sold out in 48 hours.

Grab yours before it's gone: \[link\]

Max
Founder of XYZ"

That's the whole email. Just the point. These are great for restocks, flash sales, and time-sensitive announcements where brevity IS the urgency.

2️⃣ Medium-Form \(Most Common\)
This is your workhorse text-based format. It has a simple structure:

[ul][li]Intro — A short, personal opening. Set the tone like you're writing to someone you know. [li]Body — The main message. This is where you pull in a story, share a specific insight, or make your case. Keep it tight, every sentence earns its spot. [li]CTA — One clear call to action at the end. Don't scatter buttons throughout like a graphic email. One ask. [li]PS — Always include a PS section. More on this below.

This format works well for founder messages, personal recommendations, story-driven product pitches, and educational content that feels more intimate than a designed email would.

3️⃣ Long-Form \(Classic Direct Response\)
The most under-appreciated. This is where real copywriting craft shows up. Long-form text emails use classic direct response principles... you're telling a story, building tension, and writing each line so it pulls the reader into the next one. The goal is that once someone starts reading, they can't stop.

This format works for deeper brand storytelling, high-AOV product sells where you need to build the case, emotional narratives, and any email where the story itself is the selling mechanism. It's the hardest format to write well, but when it hits, it outperforms everything.

👇 Formatting Rules \(All Three Formats\)

Even though these are "plain text" emails, formatting still matters:
[ul][li]Bold your main points. The reader's eye needs anchors, even in text-only emails. [li]Use line breaks a lot. Short paragraphs. One to two sentences, then a break. White space is what makes text emails feel easy to read instead of overwhelming. [li]Use bullet points when listing anything. Don't bury three items in a run-on sentence when bullets make them scannable. [li]No large copy blocks. The same rule from graphic emails applies here — if you have more than 2–3 lines without a break, split it up.

👉 The PS Section
Include a PS in every \(or at least most\) text-based email. PS sections are statistically the most-read part of any email. People scroll to the bottom, see "PS," and read it even if they skimmed or skipped the body. Use this to your advantage. Your PS should contain your call to action restated, a final hook, or a piece of urgency. It's your second chance to convert someone who didn't engage with the main body.

👉 CTAs
Don't overload text-based emails with multiple calls to action. One CTA at the end of the body, and one in the PS. That's it. Text-based emails convert because they feel personal and simple. Stacking CTAs throughout the email breaks that illusion and makes it feel like a sales pitch wearing a costume.

👉Magic Button
An easy way to increase your click rates is by using a magic button in your footer. Often times, this absolutely crushes because the intrigue just gets people, but you just link this to some random page on the website or the home page.

replies.content:
[@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) I brain dumped the concept and rough storyline into claude using wispr flow and then it wrote me this mega specific and long prompt which I gave to NB with some reference images.

Prompt:

Create an 11-panel comic strip in the classic Tintin / Hergé "ligne claire"
style, faithful to the panel layout style of Tintin albums like "Tintin in
Tibet". Clean, confident black linework. Flat colour fills with no
gradients or shading. Hand-lettered speech bubbles with rounded edges.
Cream/off-white panel backgrounds. Muted period palette: dusty reds, soft
blues, ochre, mustard yellow, sage green. No neon. No modern digital
effects.

PANEL LAYOUT — VARIED WIDTHS WITHIN ROWS \(this is critical\):
Like authentic Tintin pages, panels within each row should have DIFFERENT
widths to create visual rhythm. Wider panels for establishing shots and
emotional beats, narrower panels for reaction shots and dialogue. Thin
black borders between panels. Narrow white gutters.

ROW 1 \(the cartel — three panels\):
- Panel 1: WIDE \(roughly 45% of row width\) — establishing the boardroom
- Panel 2: MEDIUM \(roughly 30%\) — close on the villain's grin
- Panel 3: NARROW \(roughly 25%\) — reaction shot of laughter

ROW 2 \(the betrayal — three panels\):
- Panel 4: MEDIUM \(roughly 35%\) — shop counter scene
- Panel 5: NARROW \(roughly 25%\) — extreme close-up of the tape
- Panel 6: WIDE \(roughly 40%\) — dynamic motorway action shot

ROW 3 \(the engineers save the day — three panels\):
- Panel 7: WIDE \(roughly 45%\) — busy workshop establishing shot
- Panel 8: NARROW \(roughly 25%\) — heroic adapter reveal
- Panel 9: MEDIUM \(roughly 30%\) — the click moment in the garage

ROW 4 \(anatomy and ending — two panels\):
- Panel 10: MEDIUM-LARGE \(roughly 40%\) — the infographic
- Panel 11: EXTRA WIDE \(roughly 60%\) — cinematic sunset ride

CHARACTERS \(keep consistent across all panels\):
- THE RIDER: Mid-50s man, salt-and-pepper hair, neat beard, weathered but
kind face. Wears an adventure-style motorcycle jacket in navy blue.
- THE EXECUTIVES: Three sinister suited men in their 60s. Dark pinstripe
suits, slicked hair, cigars. Villainous but cartoonish — not menacing.
- THE ENGINEERS: Three friendly British workshop types in their 30s-40s.
Rolled sleeves, aprons, one in a flat cap. Tea mugs everywhere.
- THE SALESMAN: Balding, apologetic, wearing a shop apron.

PANEL 1 \(WIDE\): Mahogany boardroom, full establishing shot. Three
executives around a long table. Outdated intercom units and helmets
scattered on the table. Executive #1 slams his fist down, red-faced.
Speech bubble: "Gentlemen! Our intercoms sound like a tin can in a
thunderstorm. What do we do?!"

PANEL 2 \(MEDIUM\): Tighter shot on Executive #2. He grins wickedly, holding
up a motorcycle helmet with a deep proprietary recess carved into the side.
Speech bubble: "Simple! We design our helmets so ONLY our terrible
intercoms fit! They'll have no choice!"

PANEL 3 \(NARROW\): Tight reaction shot. Three executives erupt in cackling
laughter. Cigar smoke curling. Brandy glasses raised. Caption box at
bottom: "And so the great helmet conspiracy was born..."

PANEL 4 \(MEDIUM\): Motorcycle shop interior. The Rider at the counter
holding a pristine motorcycle helmet in one hand and a Cardo intercom in
the other. The Salesman behind the counter shrugs apologetically. Speech
bubble from Rider: "But I already own a Cardo..." Speech bubble from
Salesman: "Then I'm afraid you'll be needing the tape, sir."

PANEL 5 \(NARROW\): Extreme close-up. A grubby grey square of 3M sticky pad
being slowly pressed onto the side of the gleaming helmet by gloved hands.
A single tear visible in the corner of the Rider's eye at the edge of
frame. Whispered speech bubble: "...there must be another way."

PANEL 6 \(WIDE\): Dynamic action shot. Motorway scene at 80mph. The Rider
on his motorbike, mid-ride. His intercom is mid-flight, ejecting from the
side of his helmet and bouncing down the tarmac behind him with motion
lines. Shocked speech bubble from Rider: "MY £300 CARDO!!!" Caption box:
"The tape had failed him. As it had failed thousands before."

PANEL 7 \(WIDE\): A cosy, slightly cluttered British workshop. Full
establishing shot. Three Engineers hunched over a workbench covered in CAD
drawings, prototypes, and a motorcycle helmet. Empty tea mugs everywhere.
A small 3D printer humming in the corner. Engineer #1 speech bubble:
"Lads. What if... the intercom just... clipped on? Properly?" Engineer #2:
"Like the helmet was made for it?" Engineer #3, stroking his chin: "By
Jove. They'll never let us get away with it."

PANEL 8 \(NARROW\): Tight heroic pose. Engineer #1 holds aloft a small,
perfectly-formed black plastic adapter \(about the size of a matchbox,
slightly curved, with mounting tabs\). Light streams down from above as if
from the heavens, with radiating background lines. Speech bubble: "Behold!
No tape. No glue. No bodgery. Just engineering!"

PANEL 9 \(MEDIUM\): The Rider in his home garage. He clips the small black
adapter into the helmet's existing comm recess. His Cardo intercom snaps
onto it — sitting flush, factory-fit. He stares at it wide-eyed. Sound
effect in bold lettering: "CLICK." Speech bubble: "It looks like Shoei
made it themselves..."

PANEL 10 \(MEDIUM-LARGE\): A technical-style infographic panel inside the
comic universe. The black PA12 nylon adapter floats in the centre of the
panel in 3/4 perspective view against a cross-hatched sky background.
Four hand-drawn arrows fan out to four hand-lettered labels in classic
comic-book script:
- Top-left: "PA12 NYLON — Aerospace grade. Tough as a Yorkshire winter."
- Top-right: "CLICKS IN — No tape. No glue. No regret."
- Bottom-left: "ZERO WOBBLE — Tested past 130mph. Still where you left it."
- Bottom-right: "FACTORY FIT — Like the helmet maker built it themselves.
\(They didn't.\)"
Caption at bottom of panel: "One piece of plastic. The size of a matchbox.
The end of a thousand small irritations."

PANEL 11 \(EXTRA WIDE\): Wide cinematic shot. Coastal road at golden hour.
A small pack of three motorcyclists riding into a glorious orange and
pink sunset, seen from behind. The Rider in the lead, two mates flanking
him. Their Cardo intercoms sit flush and proud on every helmet — no tape,
no flapping wires. A pelican glides overhead. A lighthouse on a distant
cliff. Long shadows stretching toward the viewer. Warm, nostalgic mood.
Speech bubble from lead rider: "Right lads. Pub?" Reply: "After you."
Third reply: "I can actually HEAR you for once." Caption box at bottom
in classic Tintin script: "And so they rode on — gear secure, helmets
unmarred, intercoms exactly where they belonged. The end. \(...or rather,
the beginning.\)"

STYLE NOTES:
- All speech bubbles white with thin black borders, hand-lettered text
- Caption boxes in pale yellow/cream with black borders, like classic
Tintin albums
- Sound effects in bold chunky comic lettering
- Panel widths VARY within each row — never make all panels in a row the
same width. This is essential for authentic Tintin feel.
- All panels in the same row share the SAME HEIGHT
- Row heights can vary slightly between rows
- Keep all character designs consistent across panels — same faces, same
outfits, same proportions
- The adapter itself should look the same in every panel it appears in
\(panels 8, 9, 10\): small, black, matchbox-sized, slightly curved with
visible mounting tabs
- Final image dimensions: tall portrait orientation, optimised for email

posts.title: Friday May 8th Call Recording
posts.content:
BANGER CALL ON FRIDAY GOOD SHIT EVERYONE WHO PULLED UP AND ASKED QUESTIONS

Uploaded into classroom the recording and summary \(formatting below is bad... check classroom for better layout\)

[Call Recording >> ](https://fathom.video/share/V7aWybgxbc2RuNxZ1GuFy5yeVevjW_zv)
Summary Below 👇

Opening & Wins \(0:00–4:30\)
Max opened by reading member wins: Matthias hit 0% churn in 2026, someone booked their first call from the Klaviyo Directory, a member restocked after months stuck in customs and immediately did 50K, and a Mother's Day campaign pulled 10K in two days. Max's win: Kim Kardashian's beverage brand booked a sales call with Well Copy — rare enough that he's personally taking it.
He reminded people to send campaign copy for review and teased that the existing GPT tool is outdated and he's planning to build a custom Claude skill file to replace it.
Magic Buttons in Footers \(4:30–6:45\)
Max showed how Breeze, Hormozi, and his own newsletter use clickable footer elements \(mystery buttons, memes, linked images\) to inflate click rates. The principle: never show content inline if you can force a click to reveal it. Hormozi shifted from embedding memes to linking them. Max does the same with his "email inspiration of the day" — forces the click instead of displaying the design. Recommended adding a small "magic button" under the founder's sign-off in any text-based email. Links to homepage or wherever — the point is the click.
Campaign Philosophy — Full Framework \(6:45–28:00\)
This was the bulk of the call. Max walked through the campaign philosophy he's been codifying internally for his team:
Email's real job isn't generating direct sales — it's staying top of mind so when the customer is ready to buy, your brand is first. Proof: switching Klaviyo attribution from 5-day open/click to 1-day click drops email revenue from ~40-50% down to ~8%. That gap is invisible warming work — someone gets a great educational email, doesn't buy, but converts off an ad three days later because the email pre-sold them.
Frequency is the #1 lever. More sends almost always equals more revenue. Max is running a multi-brand scatterplot study correlating campaigns sent per week against click rate, RPR, and unsub rate. Early findings: click rate dips slightly with more sends, unsub rate barely moves \(one brand actually had higher unsubs at 3x/week than at higher frequency\), and revenue trends up. He'd rather send one general email to 100K engaged subscribers than a hyper-targeted email to 5K. Audited a brand that day making exactly this mistake — segmenting down to 5K sends on a 50K engaged list. Segmentation is kept extremely simple. A blank email with just a logo and a shop-now button sent 4x/week would make money.
75/25 graphic to text-based mix. Text-based emails convert better on a percentage basis but work best as a pattern interrupt. Higher unsub rates if overused. Can mix in semi-designed text emails with a founder headshot. 25% of sends should be plain-text style from a real person.
Specificity is the #1 copy principle. The angle behind the email matters more than anything else. One email, one micro-topic. "How magnesium improves your REM sleep" beats "5 benefits of our greens powder." If a customer can't summarize the email in one sentence after a 3-second skim, the email failed. Max called out the classic bad example: "How our product supports your overall health" with six bullet points — customer reads all six, retains zero.
Five content pillars, kept in roughly even rotation:
[ul][li]Educational — micro-topic deep dives \(ingredient breakdowns, how-to, FAQs, product science, use cases\)[li]Social proof — testimonials, reviews, customer photos, before/afters, influencer mentions, awards, milestones[li]Community/brand — founder stories, brand mission, behind-the-scenes, team intros, text-based founder emails[li]Product/collection highlights — single product features, new arrivals, restocks, seasonal collections, gift guides \(restocks especially rip — the implication that it sold out does the selling\)[li]Sales — discount-driven sends with creative framing
Discounts — use them, but twist the framing. The 2026 customer is numb to standard percentage-off. Reframe as store credit \(even small odd amounts like $13.42\), mystery discounts, first-100-people flash sales, order lotteries \("we'll randomly refund 3 orders in 24 hours"\), UUP late-night sales \(send at 9-10 PM, live for 3 hours, morning email says "you snooze you lose" with a smaller code\). The store credit email that looks like an automated "credit applied to your account" notification rips every single time. Big mistake: running the same % off rotation monthly and wondering why conversion drops. The offer isn't the problem — the predictability is.
Non-discount emails should do one of three things: educate the customer, bring them closer to the brand, or build trust through social proof. One job per email.
Repeat Your Winners \(28:00–34:00\)
Major emphasis. Max is frustrated that his own team \(and himself\) will send a banger email, celebrate, then never send anything like it again. The mandate:
[ul][li]Resend winning emails at least monthly \(bi-weekly is fine too\)[li]Put them into flows — welcome, abandonment, everywhere relevant[li]Redesign if you want, but keep the same angle[li]People won't notice resends — they're zombies scrolling their inbox
Two examples: a long-form testimonial email that ripped every time it was resent and eventually got added to welcome and abandonment flows. A "our creatine isn't cheap" objection-handling email that became a monthly staple. Charlie from the community sent the store credit email 10 times in two weeks and had his brand's biggest month ever.
Principle: people need to be reminded more than they need to be taught. Customers see hundreds of brands a day — they forget your message. Drill it in.
Recurring Themes \(34:00–35:30\)
Recurring email themes work when not forced. Bi-weekly to monthly cadence — weekly is too much and fatigues the audience. Examples:
[ul][li]Build of the Month \(German car accessories brand — customers submit car photos, winner gets a gift card\)[li]Staff Picks \(rotating team member each month\)[li]Ask a Urologist \(health brand with a professional on staff — issue 20+, strong engagement\)[li]Slow Sip Sundays \(Breeze — Sunday wind-down email\)
Calendar Building Checklist \(35:30–36:00\)
Minimum 3 sends/week for any brand. Balance the five pillars. Pull from your winners list. Layer in timely content. Mix graphic and text-based formats. Max noted that once you follow all of this, the problem isn't finding enough to send — it's fitting everything in.
Custom Claude Tool \(36:00–36:30\)
The existing GPT for campaign strategy is outdated. Max committed to building a Claude skill file to replace it, likely the best path forward since the internal tool isn't public. Shared the Gamma presentation with call attendees only.
Q&A — Referral Emails, Non-Opener Resends, Resend Timing \(36:30–39:00\)
Referral emails: Max has never had good success with "give $25, get $25" mechanics. Brands like it, but he's never made it work.
Resending to non-openers: Fully supports it. Some brands resend every campaign to non-openers the next day with a different subject line. He walked through building the Klaviyo segment \(received email ≥1 time + opened 0 times, filtered by specific campaign message\). His honest preference: just resend to everybody.
Resend timing for winners \(Aven's question\): Monthly minimum for the same angle. Bi-weekly is fine. Single-SKU brands can go even harder — Mars Men essentially sends the same angle every time. Customers are seeing hundreds of brands daily; they forget your core message fast.
Q&A — Gifting Brands \(42:19–48:30\)
Mapa's question: What changes for a gifting brand \(wildflower gin, honey, tea\) in terms of flows, frequency, and strategy?
Max's answer: Not much changes structurally. Same playbook, same frequency, same flows. What changes is copy and angles — everything frames around gifting occasions. Showed the "Instead of Flowers" brand as an example \(meals as gifts — testimonial email about gifting new parents since all presents go to the baby\). Gifting brands are seasonal and mostly one-time-purchase, so optimize for first-purchase profitability rather than banking on LTV. Higher frequency still drives more revenue even for gifting brands. The counterintuitive data: repeat purchases happen much sooner than expected — people find a brand they like and buy a few times quickly before the novelty fades.
Max floated a tangent idea: wildflower delivery subscription service \(flowers die, recurring delivery is a natural fit\).
Q&A — Dropshipping & Retention / LTV Rant \(48:52–56:00\)
Jeremy's question: Tips for retention on a dropshipping brand with a bad product? They sent ~30 emails/month for a year with minimal results.
Max's answer: "You can't polish a turd." No email strategy fixes a bad product. The #1 driver of retention is product quality — everything else is incremental. Switching Klaviyo attribution from 5-day to 1-day click proves most email "revenue" is really just brand warming. For consumption brands, #1 reason people come back is taste.
This launched a broader retention/LTV rant:
[ul][li]Email flows and cross-sell sequences can get 10% incremental improvements[li]The big jumps in repeat purchase rates come from new product launches, new flavors, and collabs[li]Fashion brands are dead without constant new releases — that's the only LTV driver[li]Dr. Squatch runs a new collab practically every week to drive repeat purchases on a product \(soap\) that people rarely run out of[li]Grooms does quarterly limited-edition flavors that spike repeat purchase rates \(referenced the My First Million podcast episode\)[li]Max spent two weeks on a deep audit for a beverage brand trying to get churn under 18% — concluded the real unlock would be dropping new flavors, which would likely drive a 50%+ increase in repeat purchase rate[li]The more he's in retention, the more he sees: acquisition is driven by offers, retention is driven by product
Q&A — Retargeting Ad Spend & Post-Purchase Timing \(56:08–1:01:30\)
Biel's question: A supplement/subscription brand is spending almost nothing on retargeting ads \(<5% of budget\) and pushing email to do all the retention work. How much retargeting is normal?
Max's answer: ~10% of ad spend on retargeting is standard. Many supplement brands \(especially subscription-first\) don't retarget at all. The biggest lever is still product quality — for supplement brands, repeat purchase rate is the clearest signal of product-market fit.
For one-time purchasers converting to repeat buyers: the sweet spot is days 20-30 post-purchase for cross-sells and upsells in email flows. Max showed a cohort analysis: days 15-21 post-purchase had 14.2% of conversions, days 22-28 had 17.1% — both higher than days 29-35. Most brands don't start replenishment reminders until day 30-40, which is too late based on actual data.
Q&A — Pop-Up Optimization \(1:01:30–1:05:00\)
Biel's follow-up: Pop-up opt-in rate dropped from 14-16% to 9-10% for a Spanish brand. What to test beyond images?
Max's answer: Offers are the biggest lever \(percent off, dollar off, different amounts, gifts, bundles\). After that, form style — Plinko, spin-to-win, micro-commit questions, different quiz questions. Max cited a recent test where simply changing the quiz question on a pop-up got 25% higher opt-ins. Had to cut the answer short due to running late to his next call.

I'm running an analysis on my Klaviyo campaign data for \[BRAND NAME\],
a \[BRIEF BRAND DESCRIPTION\].

I've uploaded two files:
1. Klaviyo campaign export \(CSV\) with columns including Campaign Name,
Subject, List, Send Time, Send Weekday, Total Recipients, Unique
Placed Order, Placed Order Rate, Revenue, Open Rate, Click Rate,
Unsubscribes, Bounces, etc.
2. Shopify monthly conversion rate export \(CSV\) with Month, Sessions,
and Conversion rate.

Please produce an .xlsx analysis with the following structure and
methodology — this is a refined approach we've iterated on, please
follow it precisely:

## METHODOLOGY

**Primary metric: RPR vs \[45\]-day rolling baseline**
- RPR = Revenue ÷ Total Recipients
- For each marketing campaign, compute the weighted-average RPR
\(total revenue ÷ total recipients\) of all marketing campaigns sent
in the prior \[45\] days
- The campaign's adjusted score = its RPR ÷ that baseline. >1.0 means
above baseline.
- Require minimum 3 prior campaigns for a baseline; otherwise leave blank
- This controls for list-growth dilution and brand evolution over time

**Secondary metric: Conv-Adjusted \(reference only, not primary\)**
- Compute monthly conversion index = month's CR ÷ overall average CR
- Conv-Adjusted = \(RPR vs baseline\) ÷ conv index
- IMPORTANT: Site-wide CR is a noisy proxy for email-subscriber behaviour
\(traffic-mix changes affect it\). Use only as a sanity-check column,
NOT as the headline ranking. Be honest about its limitations.

**Reliability flag**
- Add a column showing how many prior campaigns built each baseline
- High = 8+, Med = 5–7, Low = 3–4, "—" = insufficient
- Colour-code \(green/yellow/red\) and exclude Low-reliability campaigns
from "top 5" highlights

**Categorisation**
- I'll provide categories. If I don't, propose 4–6 based on scanning
campaign names/subjects and ask me to confirm before proceeding.
- My current categories: \[LIST CATEGORIES HERE, e.g. "Product Launch,
Educational Promotional \(reviews/FAQs/us-vs-them\), Educational Brand
Led \(community/rides/updates\), Holidays, Sales"\]
- Compute within-category averages and "vs Category Avg" per campaign

**Operational sends**
- Flag and EXCLUDE from rankings any campaigns with <500 recipients
\(these are typically pre-order/shipping updates, not marketing\)

## DELIVERABLE: .xlsx with these tabs in this order

1. **Summary** — headline metrics, top 5 / bottom 5 by adjusted RPR
\(reliability-filtered\), category performance table with verdicts
\("Strong over-performer" >1.5x, "Above baseline" >1.1x, "Roughly
average" >0.9x, "Below baseline" >0.7x, else "Significant
under-performer"\), and 6–8 key insights as bullet points with
specific numbers from the data

2. **Adjusted Ranking** — every marketing campaign ranked high to low
by "vs 45d Baseline". Columns: Rank, Campaign, Subject, Category,
List, Date, Recipients, Revenue, Raw RPR, vs 45d Baseline,
Reliability, Baseline n, Conv Index, Conv-Adjusted \(ref\), vs Cat
Avg, Open Rate, Click Rate. Colour scales on the metric columns.
Highlight top 5 \(green\) and bottom 5 \(red\) — reliability-filtered.

3. **By Category** — table of category averages with conditional
formatting, plus a "best campaign in each category" and "worst
campaign in each category" section below.

4. **True Winners** — campaigns that beat BOTH their 45-day baseline
AND their category average. Sorted descending. Below that, a
"True Losers" section \(below both\).

5. **Methodology** — definitions of every column and the rationale
for each adjustment. Be explicit about caveats: conv-index
limitations, small-sample categories, observational vs causal data.

## FORMATTING

- Arial font throughout
- Headers: white text on dark blue \(#1F4E78\), wrap text, centred
- Section headers: white text on coloured fill \(green for positive
sections, red for negative, blue for neutral, orange for insights\)
- Currency: £#,##0.00 / £0.000 for RPR
- Ratios: 0.00x format
- Percentages: 0.0% or 0.00%
- Freeze panes on ranking tabs
- Colour scales \(red → yellow → green\) on all ratio/RPR columns

## TONE FOR THE WRITTEN INSIGHTS

- Lead with the data, not flattery
- Cite specific campaign names and adjusted scores
- Be willing to push back on assumptions if the data contradicts them
- Flag caveats honestly \(small samples, low-reliability scores,
observational limits\)
- Avoid generic conclusions — every insight should reference an
actual campaign or category number

After generating the file, give me a chat summary covering: the
category ranking, top 3 surprising findings, and any caveats I
should know about. Don't over-claim — observational data isn't
causal evidence.

posts.title: Quick Win For Welcome Flow
posts.content:
If someone opts into your email list and they don't buy within the first 30 days, the odds that they ever buy are really really low...

And so in my mind if that's the point of no return, we might as well send them our best offer we can do or our heaviest hitter... and guess what that is: our store credit email!

A quick win and tactic you can do is this: after the last email in the welcome flow, set a time delay of anywhere from 14 to 28 days and send the store credit email.

If somebody buys before receiving that, for example, they buy from a campaign, then they won't receive that last email because they exit the flow because of the filters. We have this store credit email in place just in case somebody doesn't buy during that period, because they're likely never going to buy. Might as well hit them with our best email.

Implement this!
