posts.title: Pop up timing
posts.content:
Hey guys,

For our brand, we've always wanted to delay our pop up timing, to make sure we would not give discount to customers that would've bought anyways. That's why we put the timer on 90 seconds \(based on average website session which was about 75-80 seconds\)

However, we've also been excluding product and even collection pages, which made us realize that since it's almost only showing on the home page anyway, we can lower to pop up timing.

Running a 90 vs 60 second test, where we see the 60 second timing capturing double as much sign ups. Which made me realize how much we've left on the table there...

After the weekend, we will start running 60 vs 30 seconds, to see the results from that.

Two questions here:

1 - What would you recommend as timing for a home page pop up in this case?

2 - What % of website sessions would be healthy to capture in the sign up form?

Thanks in advance!

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
10-20% would be really healthy!

have you tried scroll percentage triggers? Seen great results + makes sure people view details before giving them an offer. \(like scrolling 30% of the page\)

Or even showing the pop-up after people see 3 or more pages for example - this makes sure they explore buying options and gives them a chance to buy without the offer.

Still not sure why you wouldn't want as many people to see the form. I do get margins but it gives you the chance to capture their data and get them in your organic funnel to send them more content and have them come back more.

You're sacrificing people that would've bought anyways and giving them a discount to making sure the offer appears at the right time and convincing way more people that maybe needed just a small incentive / nudge.

user.name: Catalin Tebu
user.bio: artaddict

replies.content: [@Catalin Tebu](obj://user/6cedadf2eb0b4a76845f18725af49eb9) Thanks a lot!! Makes sense 🤝

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
I think you're harming yourself more than you're saving yourself. There's a reason the fastest growing brands have pop-ups that fire only a few seconds after page load. You're still showing discounts to people who would have bought anyways.

Think about it: does anybody buy within 90 seconds on a website? No. Yes, your average site session may be that, but what's the average site session of someone who purchases? Probably longer.

I think you're still showing the discounts to people who would have bought anyways, but you're missing all the leads who potentially could have bought if you got their email and you were able to retarget them and all that sort of stuff. I would follow the regular system or do an A/B test on conversion rate, which you can see with Alia, and do what all the other brands do.

posts.title: Intro - My Journey
posts.content:
What's up everyone!

Pumped to be a part of this community. Wanted to share a little bit about my email marketing journey.

Started learning email marketing on my own in early 2024 with the goal of learning a skill to get a job. Job market was f'ed \(still is\) so I knew I needed something to stand out. I studied marketing in college so it felt like a fit.

Used UpWork to get my first few clients. Really small retainers $300-500 per month. But the goal was to get hands on experience. Throughout the summer of 2024 I tried a few different strategies to get clients, like cold email, upwork, DM's, etc.

Realized my leg up was leveraging in-person connections, sending real personalized cold emails, and targeting local businesses to get more clients.

I was literally working at a grilled cheese restaurant while doing all of this.

Early 2025 I landed a job at a big national agency. I felt like an imposter, but came to realize I knew the fundamentals to be successful. I worked on accounts like Cuisinart, Nutrafol, Dermalogica, Cmfrt, and more. It's an insane feeling to hit send on a campaign that's going out to 2m+ people at a time.

The entire time working for this company I was juggling the same handful of clients I got in 2024, and even a few more that were added throughout early 2025. I started charging more for my services, from $1500 --> $2000 --> $3500 --> all the way to $5000+

Last week I left this agency after 1.5 years. It was a great experience and something I'm happy to have done. Going all-in on my agency \([insendra.com](http://insendra.com)\) now. Still nervous, but excited about the opportunity.

If anyone wants to chat about what it's like at a national agency, lmk, I might be able to answer a few questions. It might be more similar to your business than you think!

Anyway, glad to be here and connect. WE RIDE!

posts.title: Deciding on campaign winners vs losers
posts.content:
Something I'm keen to get more in depth on for my clients is deciding which campaigns are winners or losers, other than the obvious ones.

For example one of my clients is scaling rapidly in last 3-5 months so it's hard to compare the success of campaigns now to ones a couple months a go as the list is constantly growing, the sites conversion rate is changing, new products are getting added.

I'm struggling to come to clear conclusions on which campaigns are the best when I consider all the external factors. One way I thought of doing it is comparing revenue per recipient \(RPR\) of the campaign against to the average over the surrounding 30 days. Reckon that's reliable?

Keen to hear your guys thoughts on this!

Also if i used Hiro would it work all this stuff out for me lol?

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
yeah RPR is good and then also my take is that things change right. The list is constantly growing. That means the people you send to today are not the same people that you've been sending to five months ago. The seasons change, they have new products, like you mentioned, so I always question the long-term validity of winning factors. That means that constantly testing is more the way to go imo.
And yeah I like to get my hands on Hiro as well. I have to convince a client to get this.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

replies.content: [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) I feel like comparing to the 30 day baseline on RPR helps with this bias though. So you rank the campaigns on how much better they performed than the 30d baseline which then lets you see clear winners in a more fair way. This way you are no longer comparing RPR but instead RPR against I got claude to rank my clients all time campaigns like this and the results were pretty interesting and probably pretty valid IMO.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

replies.content:
[@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5) "This way you are no longer comparing RPR but instead RPR against I got claude to \(...\)" 🤔🤔
Against 30-day baseline you mean probably?
And I see how that makes sense and I believe clients also want this, right. They want you to tell them, "Yeah we AB tested and we got the result that this sending time works great for your brand and now we're going to do that."
My point is that things change, right? The best sending time is different in the summer than in the winter and all that so yeah, gotta keep testing.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
I think, low-key, you might be overcomplicating it.
[ul][li]Look at placed order rate.[li]Look at revenue per recipient.[li]Look at new customer placed order rate.[li]Look at returning customer placed order rate if you want to go more in depth.

Honestly, just go based on the placed order rate and then trust your gut as well. No need to get too granular with it. If something performs better or above expectation

The clearest thing to look at is revenue compared to recent campaigns. For example, if today the brand gets an average of $5,000 per campaign but you had one that generated $12,000, then that's a good metric. If in the past you were only getting $1,000 per campaign but one of them got $4,000, then that campaign is a good metric and one to go off of. I'd say that's probably the clearest: local revenue maxes.

If one month we really want to focus on getting repeat purchases then you get insights on what generates repeat customer revenue. For this example it was new product releases.

posts.title: Promote Post Purchase Upsells in Emails
posts.content:
Hey guys,
This is something I'm about to test as I do upsells for some of my clinets, but I think it could be a cool angle as you are assuming the sale.

Bascially you could look at post purchase upsells and if there you have "the best offers" with highest discounts, you could promote it as a special upgrades after orded.

We have the biggest sale of the year with this niche brand, and we want to get people to purchase, and pay attention to post-purcahse upsells as well so we are setting them up for that.

user.name: Jan Uroda
user.bio: Looking for 7+ figure founders who are genuinely interested in serving the world to make more impact.

comments.content:
Ngl i think whether this works out or not comes down to how you frame it.

Because if teasing the post-purchase upsell introduces a separate decision, then ur splitting attention when you need simplicity. The customer starts thinking if they should buy less now and wait for the upgrade, especially if you reveal what the upsell actually is. I'd imagine that'd nuke initial AOV lol.

BUT if you frame the upsell as added value of purchasing, it can actually improve the main conversion. It's basically the same psychology as a gift-with-purchase. The customer feels like they're actually getting more by buying now, not being asked to make a second decision. You gotta keep it vague enough that they can't game it tho, and frame it as a bonus not a separate offer.

If you do end up going for it, just make sure to keep the teaser super subtle. Prob like a P.S. line or a secondary callout, not the main selling point of the email. The primary CTA still needs to be "buy now" without any qualifiers too.

You might already be hip to this as well, but email fits into post-purchase upsells most naturally though order confirmations and shipping confirmation emails. Always gonna be a very natural fit. But lmk your thoughts [@Jan Uroda](obj://user/1fccd4458e464a529c54b980fb705f17) !

posts.title: EMAIL AGENCY COFFEE HOUR CALL RECORDING
posts.content:
Shoutout to you guys for pulling up yesterday for the weekly email marketing coffee hour!

Call recordings are up to date, if you want to access past ones follow the screenshots I have attached!

Here's yesterday's summary and recording \(a bit weird formatting so I suggest going into the Classroom to read\)

[Call Recording >>](https://fathom.video/share/pWtyyhxgMHN4rZn9V9U5NUsRi8xTxK9_)
Full summary below 👇
Main Topic: Well Copy’s Client Reporting System
Tristan walked through the reporting framework you shared with the group, and everyone viewed it as one of the strongest agency systems they’d seen. The biggest takeaway was that your reporting system is not just about analytics — it’s designed to constantly reinforce client confidence, reduce buyer’s remorse, improve retention, and keep clients emotionally connected to the agency.
The framework was broken into four layers:
1. Daily Reporting \(Slack Communication\)
Your team sends updates in Slack every business day to keep clients in the loop in real time. The purpose is less about “formal reporting” and more about maintaining visibility and reinforcing activity.
Examples discussed:
[ul][li]Approval requests[li]Tool/access requests[li]Upcoming campaigns[li]Product launch updates[li]Operational changes[li]Deliverability concerns[li]Quick wins from campaigns[li]Any time-sensitive issues
The group repeatedly emphasized that this level of communication helps avoid the common agency problem where clients feel forgotten after signing. It creates the perception — and reality — that the agency is deeply embedded in the account daily.
There was also discussion around:
[ul][li]Not forcing daily updates unnecessarily[li]Focusing on meaningful communication instead of filler[li]Messaging heavily during the first two onboarding weeks to reduce buyer’s remorse and build trust fast
Several members specifically referenced your onboarding communication cadence as something they wanted to implement immediately.
2. Weekly Reporting
Every Tuesday, your team sends a structured weekly recap summarizing:
[ul][li]Total store revenue[li]Email-attributed revenue[li]Best-performing campaigns[li]A/B test results[li]Wins and lessons learned[li]Upcoming campaign plans[li]Needed approvals for the next week
The group liked that your weekly reporting is not just “numbers,” but also strategic interpretation.
Important elements they highlighted:
[ul][li]Showing top-performing campaigns proves the agency is paying attention to creative performance rather than blindly sending emails[li]Explaining why something worked builds authority[li]Including Klaviyo screenshots increases trust and prevents clients from needing to dig through the platform themselves
There was also discussion about whether reporting should be AI-generated or manually written. The consensus was:
[ul][li]AI may help with formatting and summarization[li]But strategic insights and “quick wins” likely still need human interpretation because AI can misidentify what actually matters
One member shared a system using:
[ul][li]Airtable forms[li]Slack automations[li]AI integrations[li]Klaviyo connections
…to semi-automate daily and weekly reporting workflows.
3. Monthly Reporting
The group spent a lot of time discussing your monthly reporting process using Hiro analytics.
Your monthly reports include:
[ul][li]Month-over-month growth[li]Year-over-year growth[li]Campaign performance[li]Flow performance[li]SMS breakdowns[li]List growth[li]Deliverability[li]Sign-up form metrics
The reports are delivered as detailed PDFs with charts and visualizations.
A major point of discussion:Many agency owners admitted they currently do very ad hoc reporting and saw your system as much more sophisticated and scalable.
However, some questioned whether clients actually read large reports.
The conclusion from the group was:
[ul][li]Even if clients don’t fully read them, the existence of detailed reporting increases trust and perceived professionalism[li]The Slack summary is the quick-read version[li]The PDF exists as validation and proof for clients who want deeper analysis
The idea was that reporting is partly operational and partly psychological.
4. Quarterly Strategic Reviews
Quarterly reporting was framed as the “zoomed out” strategic layer.
Instead of focusing on short-term metrics, the quarterly review analyzes:
[ul][li]Long-term trends[li]Campaign vs flow contribution[li]Email vs SMS performance[li]Deliverability patterns[li]Strategic pivots[li]Bigger-picture account direction
The group liked that this creates a rhythm where:
[ul][li]Daily = tactical[li]Weekly = operational[li]Monthly = analytical[li]Quarterly = strategic
Several attendees said they wanted to adopt this exact structure.
Discussion Around Client Communication & Pushback
A major theme throughout the call was balancing expertise with client management.
The group discussed:
[ul][li]How much pushback to give when clients request bad revisions[li]Whether to let clients override strategy[li]How to establish authority early
The general consensus:
[ul][li]Give professional pushback once[li]Explain why the recommendation matters[li]If the client insists, execute their version[li]Keep receipts with performance data[li]Use results later to reinforce authority
One attendee emphasized that clients hire agencies to be experts, so consistent micromanagement is usually a sign of poor fit.
Another strong point:Setting expectations early during onboarding is critical.
One member explained that they explicitly tell clients:
[ul][li]“We will always tell you the truth”[li]“We won’t just say what you want to hear”[li]“We’ll test disagreements whenever possible”
This creates stronger long-term trust and gives the agency more strategic freedom later.
Retainers, Pricing & Contracts Discussion
The second half of the call shifted heavily into pricing models, retainers, setup fees, contracts, and risk management.
Pricing Ranges Shared
Attendees shared retainers ranging from:
[ul][li]~$1.5k/month[li]~$2k/month[li]~$4.5k/month[li]Up to aspirations of $10k+/month retainers
Aven specifically mentioned:
[ul][li]$3k/month is now his minimum[li]Older legacy clients are lower-priced[li]He recently signed a $4.5k/month client
The group agreed:
[ul][li]Pricing confidence increases with experience/results[li]Simpler pricing models reduce sales friction[li]Higher retainers often work better than low retainers + complex setup fees
Setup Fee Discussion
There was significant interest when Tristan mentioned that Well Copy has moved away from setup fees.
The group discussed:
[ul][li]Setup fees help protect agencies if clients churn early[li]But they can add friction in sales[li]More mature agencies with better retention can often eliminate them safely
Jan specifically pointed out:
[ul][li]Setup fees are very important early-stage because flow builds are front-loaded labor[li]Without setup fees, early churn can make accounts unprofitable
Contract Lengths & Churn
The group debated:
[ul][li]Month-to-month[li]60-day commitments[li]90-day commitments[li]6-month contracts[li]Annual agreements
Consensus:
[ul][li]60–90 days is usually the minimum needed to properly test email marketing[li]Long contracts can create sales friction[li]Reputation and relationship quality matter more than legal enforcement in many cases
There was discussion about:
[ul][li]Chargebacks[li]Clients disputing payments despite results[li]The importance of choosing the right clients
Jan emphasized that bad-fit clients create major stress and operational headaches even when revenue is attractive.
Retention & “Endorphin” Strategy
One of the strongest ideas came from Mapa regarding client retention psychology.
Her framework:Create multiple “big wins” during the first 90 days to flood clients with positive reinforcement.
Examples:
[ul][li]Fast optimization wins[li]Clarity/customer research wins[li]High-performing launch campaigns

posts.title: 4th rejection for Toll-Free verification (US Market).
posts.content:
Hi everyone! I’m really hoping someone here has cracked this code. I’ve been trying to set up Klaviyo SMS for the US market \(apparel niche, t-shirts\), but I just received my 4th rejection from the carriers: "Your toll-free number verification was rejected."
We are running on Shopline, and our main goal is to collect phone numbers via a pop-up.
Here is what we’ve already checked and implemented:
[ul][li]Site status: The store is live, products are in stock, and the checkout is fully functional.[li]Legal: Privacy Policy and Terms of Service are in place. We’ve added the mandatory SMS consent language and the "Message and data rates may apply" disclaimer.[li]Submission: We provided clear screenshots of the pop-up including all the necessary legal fine print.
I’m feeling pretty stuck. Are there any "tiny details" the carriers are being extra picky about lately? Is there something specific to the Shopline checkout flow that might be triggering this? Also, is it now a hard requirement to show the Double Opt-in flow in the application?
I’d be incredibly grateful for any advice or success stories from those who have managed to get through this recently. I really don't want to jump to a different platform, but I'm running out of ideas.
Thanks in advance!

user.bio: Hi

comments.content:
Damn, that sucks. Sorry you're experiencing that.

I have never really dealt with this, so maybe someone else has and maybe they can help. It seems like you're doing everything that you should, but there's just one thing that's off. I would hit up Klaviyo Support, and they will give you an answer. If you haven't already, Klaviyo Support is super helpful.

user.name: Max Sturtevant
user.bio: Owner of Well Copy - $200M Generated Through Email

comments.content:
ChatGPT gave me this:

Most likely, this is not a SHOPLINE issue. The carriers have become extremely strict over the last 6–12 months with toll-free verification \(TFN\), especially for ecommerce brands collecting SMS via pop-ups.
A few things I’ve seen trigger repeated rejections in Klaviyo specifically:
[ol:1][li]Consent language is not explicit enoughThe biggest one. Carriers want VERY clear wording that says the user is agreeing to receive:
[ul][li]marketing/promotional text messages[li]recurring automated messages[li]from your brand name specifically
Good example:
“By entering your phone number and submitting this form, you agree to receive recurring automated promotional and personalized marketing text messages \(e.g. cart reminders\) from BRAND NAME at the cell number used when signing up. Consent is not a condition of purchase. Msg & data rates may apply. Msg frequency varies. Reply HELP for help and STOP to cancel.”
A surprising number of brands get rejected because their language is too vague like:
[ul][li]“sign up for updates”[li]“get texts”[li]“SMS alerts”
[ol:2][li]Missing TCPA disclosures near the CTA buttonThe legal copy must usually be:
[ul][li]directly under the phone field/button[li]visible without scrolling[li]not hidden in tiny unreadable text[li]linked to Privacy Policy + Terms
If the carrier reviewer has to “hunt” for the disclosure, rejection risk goes way up.
[ol:3][li]Pre-checked consent boxesHuge rejection trigger now. If you use a checkbox:
[ul][li]it MUST be unchecked by default[li]user must take affirmative action
[ol:4][li]Double opt-in is not technically required, BUT…It massively improves approval odds right now.
A lot of brands getting approved lately are:
[ul][li]collecting number in pop-up[li]then sending confirmation keyword or confirmation text before marketing starts
Carriers are extremely sensitive about spam complaints currently.
[ol:5][li]Your website may look “too new” or “too thin”This is another big hidden one.
If your store:
[ul][li]has low traffic[li]limited products[li]generic product images[li]minimal branding[li]thin About Us page[li]no social presence[li]no reviews
…the carrier may flag it as high-risk regardless of compliance.
Apparel/t-shirt stores are unfortunately one of the highest-risk verticals for spam/scam behavior.
[ol:6][li]Your opt-in screenshots may not be enoughFor TFN verification, I’ve seen approvals improve when brands submit:
[ul][li]pop-up screenshot[li]landing page screenshot[li]checkout screenshot[li]privacy policy screenshot[li]SMS welcome flow screenshot[li]abandoned cart SMS screenshot
Basically proving the full ecosystem exists.
[ol:7][li]Your privacy policy may not explicitly mention SMS sharing/useMake sure your privacy policy explicitly states:
[ul][li]phone numbers are collected for SMS marketing[li]consent data may be stored[li]opt-out instructions exist[li]data isn’t sold/shared improperly
[ol:8][li]Carrier mismatch between use case and messagingA VERY common rejection:You submit:
[ul][li]“promotional marketing”
But your flows include:
[ul][li]abandoned cart[li]browse abandonment[li]customer support style messages
Sometimes carriers want the use cases spelled out more explicitly.
For ecommerce brands, I usually recommend describing:
[ul][li]promotional campaigns[li]cart reminders[li]post-purchase messages[li]customer care/support notifications \(if applicable\)
[ol:9][li]Toll-free verification is simply brutal right nowNot joking — many legitimate brands are getting rejected 2–5 times before approval.
Especially:
[ul][li]apparel[li]supplements[li]dropshipping-style stores[li]new domains[li]aggressive discount pop-ups
That’s become pretty normal.
My recommendation:
[ul][li]Enable double opt-in[li]Strengthen consent copy[li]Ensure checkbox is unchecked[li]Add very explicit TCPA language[li]Submit MORE screenshots than they ask for[li]Make the brand/site feel as “real” and established as possible[li]Mention exact message types in the application
And honestly, if it still fails after another round, I would strongly consider switching from TFN to:
[ul][li]10DLC registration[li]or dedicated short code later at scale
A lot of ecommerce brands are having smoother deliverability and approval there now than TFN.

posts.title: Email Flow Frequency
posts.content:
I'm seeing a lot more brands being a lot more aggressive with how often they send when somebody signs up to the email list. For example, Mars Men are sending at least three emails a day for the first few days when somebody signs up, as well as multiple SMS.

The reason brands are doing this is for two reasons:
[ol:1][li]When somebody clicks an ad and opts into your email list, that's the warmest they're ever going to be. Every hour, every day, they get colder and colder and farther away from the time they were on your website.[li]If a customer clicks one of your ads, it now knows that you are in the market for whatever you sell. For example if I sell protein powder and a customer clicks on one of our ads, Meta knows now that person is shopping for that. It's going to show all of our competitors. If somebody doesn't buy from me, they're seeing all of my other competitors. If I don't hit them with frequency, they might just go buy from a competitor.

I've become a lot more open to this idea and I want us to do it a lot more. A/B test having lots of frequency on the front to see if we can get more people because we might be able to convert extra people by hitting them with frequency rather than letting them get cold or go buy from a competitor.

It makes the most sense for any brand where you don't get a lot of repeat purchases because all you care about is getting that first purchase. For brands that want to get repeat purchases and they need the customer to actively make a choice to come back, you don't want to annoy them and hurt your potential to get them back by over-sending. For brands where all they give a shit about is getting that first purchase, then I'm okay with this sort of frequency. Subscription brands and high AOV brands I think are the best use case.

posts.title: Don't Sleep On Klaviyo Product Sections
posts.content:
Here is a brand for which, for some reason, the Klaviyo product blocks work better than our product blocks that we design in Figma. Instead of us designing in Figma, we just drag in Klaviyo's dynamic product feed when we're building the email.

Couple reasons that this could work better:
[ul][li]Deliverability: it gets delivered better.[li]Since it's a dynamic product section and we choose the feed that shows items the person has left behind before, as well as best sellers, that makes it work \(more relevant products\)[li]It could be that customers just prefer it.

You can see the difference in click rates, and it's been consistent every single time that it works better, so we have made the switch completely for this brand. It's not the same for every brand, but this is one thing you should definitely test.

posts.title: IF you haven't set this up, do it NOW.
posts.content:
Just dropping a bit of a value bomb here.

Not all of your email subscribers are sms subscribers.

Changing that can help you boost your revenue.

Check out the screenshot of my SMS-only pop-up form.

In the month of April, it had 36.28% submission rate and made $8k revenue

The pop-up form is pretty similar to the usual email & sms pop-up form.

For this SMS-only pop-up form, I'm offering a 10% discount in exchange for their number.

If you want to apply this, make sure to set it to "show to email only subscribers" in the Target & Behavior option.

AND make sure to tick mark "Don't show multiple forms at the same time" in the form settings.

If not, you risk showing both pop-up forms during the same visit.

Which could lead you to giving the discount in the original email & sms pop-up form AND the sms-only pop-up form.

posts.title: Best practices for email/SMS sequence pop ups?
posts.content:
Should you do separate pop ups for email/SMS or keep them in continuous steps?

Curious if anyone has tested this and seen better results.

user.name: Florian Ruhstaller
user.bio: Email list manager with big dreams

comments.content:
Hey [@Florian Ruhstaller](obj://user/25feaa3355334940a0919731e28915d7) they need to be in the same pop-up form but separate steps. Ask for email first, then once they submit, ask for SMS to activate the discount. This usually does pretty well. I think [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) has a post or a video here somewhere that shows how it looks like.

I also have an SMS-only pop-up that's triggered ONLY when an email-only subscriber visits the site. For them, I offer an extra 10% off SMS subscriptions.

I also make sure only one pop-up gets displayed per visit. Otherwise, once they subscribe to email, the SMS-only pop-up will appear on the same visit. Which means, you end up giving them 2 discount coupons.

Hope this makes sense.

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

replies.content: [@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703) I use Omnisend and their pop up only allows for 2 steps before the success form, on Klaviyo can you have a micro commit -> Email form -> SMS form -> success form?

replies.content: [@Macen Emmons](obj://user/9a16c196ce334c4aa76484be2ee12a58) Yes.

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content: Have them in the same form but separate steps: you ask for email first, and then, once they submit email, you ask for SMS. The reason is that if you ask for email and SMS on the same step, it looks like a lot of work for the customer, and so they're much less likely to opt-in. Maybe you get 5% opt-in rates on that. However, if you split it out and you do email, then SMS, somebody sees email and they will opt in at 10, and then you hit them with SMS, and then maybe 5% will enter SMS. In both scenarios you get 5% of phone numbers, but in the second scenario at least you get double the email addresses as well.

posts.title: OFFERS ARE EVERYTHING

This goes beyond email...

This is an interesting story of a brand that needed to turn down their demand because they were having shortages of inventory including the whole industry as a whole \(baby feed product\).

Their competitors shut down, but they stayed live… and parent needed the formula for their babies so there was a ton of demand for her store.

Seems like a good thing but they were running out of inventory.

SO they needed to slow down growth….

To slow down growth they turned off ads, but still demand was the same.

So then they turned off their email campaigns.

But still demand kept coming and was the same.

Then they turned off all their email flows but still demand kept going and it was the same.

The last thing they did was they turned off their acquisition offer their trial bundle discount offer and then IMMEDIATELY demand an orders cut in half.

Offer is everything and is the ultimate driver of demand and conversions.

Offer is everything guys!!

posts.title: Creating an Email Retention Offer
posts.content:
Hi guys,

Previously, I was an email copywriter who'd charged $100/email.

I'd write an email in a GDoc and submit it to the client, and that's it.

However, I have now transitioned to a full email retention specialist, where I take over a DTC brand's email marketing engine and rebuild it into a cash-printing machine.

However, I'm at a loss on how to create an offer for this service.

Should I charge them separately for integration and setting up Klaviyo \(a one-time charge\), and then charge a different rate for a monthly retainer in which I optimize pop-up forms, flows, and campaigns?

If so, what's the current rate for such service \(you don't have to tell me your exact rates if you're not comfortable, I am just asking for a ballpark figure\).

If not, how would you structure your offer?

And how would you make your offer attractive?

CC [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
I have literally always just done a flat retainer. I manage all of your email and SMS marketing. Here's my cost, and then I just do everything.

Now we split it by number of emails: 12 emails, 16, 20, 24. Anything above that is custom, and it's just a monthly charge that goes up based on the number of emails. We choose what we do with those emails, and we do everything. I don't recommend anybody charges anything less than $3,000 a month for managing an account fully. That gives you enough to be able to reinvest over time, and that's a fair market rate you

I would just explain that the benefit of working with you is that you manage absolutely everything about the email channel so that the brand doesn't have to worry about it. That's the offer. You don't need to have some crazy sort of setup. I just do that.

I don't think, in my experience, I've ever tried to make an offer "attractive" for me. I've just kept my offer the same: "Hey, I'll manage all your email marketing." What makes that offer attractive is all the value that I give in my content. People see my content, and they're like, "Holy shit, this guy's smart as fuck." It makes my regular offer more attractive than a faceless guy who doesn't post any content who says, "Hey, let me manage your email marketing." Who do you think the brand is going to pick? Me, with all the value I put out, they just click on my socials and they learn some shit, or the guy who's faceless? They're always going to choose me.

I do charge a set up fee to cover flows in the first month, but after that I'll do anything the client needs as long as they are paying me. user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
Agree with the other guys in here!

So I wouldn't split setup and retainer into separate charges, as that overcomplicates the offer and gives the prospect two things to say no to. The Klaviyo setup, flow builds, and popup work just happen in months 1-2 as part of your onboarding. One monthly retainer covers everything imo.

Email retention for D2C brands generally runs $2,500-$5,000/month depending on brand size and scope. My floor is $3k tbh. And don't price based on what you used to charge per email because you're selling revenue infrastructure, which needs its respect.

Also I actually use a 90-day money-back guarantee. Sounds risky but it almost never gets triggered if you're good, and it makes the client's decision way easier because you're carrying the risk. Make sure to set a minimum contract length too \(I do 6 months\) so you have real runway to build the system and prove results.

You may already know this too, but never discuss pricing over email or DMs. Always just push to a discovery call. You can communicate value and handle objections live in ways you can't over text.

posts.title: LTV
posts.content:
Hey everyone,

Right now our 90-day LTV and lifetime LTV are only about 10% apart. So everything is very front-loaded, and retention after that window is pretty minimal.

We recently sent a campaign for a product we normally don’t promote \(without discount\), and it actually crushed. Made us realize we’ve probably been under-communicating with our existing list.

So the plan now is to:
[ul][li]New product / color launches: shift from only targeting 60–120 day engaged subscribers to all-time buyers \(based on relevant products\)[li]Start testing more SMS around new colors / new product launches

Curious to hear what’s worked for you guys to extend LTV beyond that initial window. Any tips or ideas would be super appreciated!

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
The biggest drivers of LTV and getting repeat purchases are new products, new flavors, and newness. People want new; they like new, so the more you release new stuff, usually the better your retention is. That applies to fashion and for CPG brands. Notice how Gruun's has a new limited edition flavor every two months because people like new and they like the fun of it.

Other than that, it's just to continue to make better content in your campaigns and better strategy. There's really no secret beyond that, and then offer testing. Test the fuck out of your win back offers, and don't just throw up a regular 10% off. Find out what product paths people typically go down after buying one product. What's the next one? What are some offers we could build? Just like how you have acquisition offers, you need to have win back offers that are good as well. I'm curious what you're running there.

1 - making sure customers are aware of the new launches \(bigger segments + SMS launches + possibly 2 emails about the launch, not just 1\)

posts.title: Flow tagging error
posts.content:
Hey guys, I've just dug into a clients' flows and basically, they set up a profile property update to tag anyone who enters a flow so that we could add them to a segment for campaign exclusion. However, I've noticed that some of the flows didn't have that set up correctly, in that some of the end branches didn't update the tags to remove the inflow status. Meaning we have a pool of customers in limbo right now, stuck with the in-flow tag. If I were to just delete this entire segment, though, that would mean that customers who actually are in flows would start getting campaigns.

What's the best solution here? Would it be to just export this segment and then just manually delete anyone who still has the in flow tag over 35 days ago \(which matches the length of our post purchase flow where the error was happening\) or something?

user.name: Michael Gorodi
user.bio: A copywriter based out of Koh Samui, Thailand - just living the island life and enjoying being a student of the craft.

comments.content:
Couple of options:
[ol:1][li]You could create a segment of anybody who got the flow entered tag added to them 10 days ago or longer, because that would be people who didn't get their thing removed \(assuming your flow is 10 days long\), and then you could export that or just remove the profile property for all those people and then continue as usual.[li]Alternatively, what I would do is I would just delete everybody with that tag. Yes, you'll have a couple people who are in limbo right now, but for a couple weeks they receive a couple extra emails. I don't think that's a big deal.[li]What I would do is I would set up a segment of anybody who has received a flow email in the past 48 hours and exclude that from your campaigns over the next couple weeks, because then if somebody's received a flow email in the past 48 hours, then they're excluded from a campaign. That's essentially doing the same function as your tagging issue. That's what I would recommend.

posts.title: Exclusion Segments
posts.content:
I'm working with a one product, one time purchase brand right now and not sure whether to exclude past purchasers from the campaigns.

For context, they have a very very strong brand and very very good product \(reviews are insane\). We've built a solid community around the product/brand and even created a bit of a fictional character around the brand \(sounds naff but trust me it works\).

They are working hard at developing cross-sells to increase LTV but in the meantime I'm split whether I keep emailing the purchasers when they have nothing to buy. I feel like the emails could make the customers feel even happier about their purchase and continue to tie them closer to the brand. But on the other side, maybe we end up pissing people off and increase un-subs.

Maybe the solution is only email the past-purchasers with brand led content and exclude them from pure selling 🤷‍♂️

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
Keep emailing purchasers so you will be on top of mind. Should be value-based and soft sell. Email marketers tend to overestimate our lists' attention span. 😅

If its a repeat purchase item then you can do pure selling occasionally around when they would normally restock. Or do pure selling once a week.

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
Yeah, I would go with just less frequency for those people. Past buyers, maybe instead of receiving emails three times per week, they receive emails once per week or once every other week. You could also set up a long-term post-purchase flow and just exclude them from campaigns always. Just have that long-term post-purchase flow guide the whole journey for people who buy.

You can also do a study. You can do a quick analysis of people who have bought, people who have unsubscribed over the past six months. How many of them were past buyers, and you can see if it is that impactful and if you are getting a ton of unsubscribes from people who have bought in the past. I'd just say send them a little bit less email.

posts.title: Retention metrics: Consumable Subscription brands
posts.content:
Hey guys! I am working a lot more recently with subscription brands and am wondering what you guys use as retention benchmarks. How much % of subscribers should still be subscribed after first renewal, 60 days, 90 days etc.

Would love to hear what others have seen for brands!

[@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) I thought i heard you say once that having 70% still active after the 4th order is a good benchmark but i'm not sure.

user.name: Rinze Nauta
user.bio: 21y/old Marketeer helping companies with their marketing

comments.content:
Hey [@Rinze Nauta](obj://user/55587d5f076d4db3a7816c88710bddf4)! I personally think that's achievable for a top-performing consumable brand but keep in mind that ain't average lol. Most usually land closer to 57-65% at that stage, but it's a good target to aim for tho.

The biggest churn events are always between order 1 and order 2 \(universally speaking here\) and that's roughly 25-35% cancel before their second order ships. This is where billing reminders, skip & delay options, and post-first-order education do the most leg lifting for you. After that initial drop you should see churn stabilize. From what I've known and seen, most healthy consumable subscription run below 4% monthly churn. By month 6, expect 50-65% of a cohort still active.

Make sure ur tracking your own cohort curves too man. Group subscribers by start month and track what percentage are still active at 30, 60, 90, 180 days. That shows what to fix and where the drop-off is.

posts.title: Using Odd Send Times
posts.content:
We tested a regular send time \(9:00 AM PST\) vs. an "odd" send time \(9:42 AM PST\) to avoid the top-of-the-hour inbox clutter.

The Result: The odd timing was the clear winner. We saw an increase in Open Rate \(74.54% vs 72.53%\) and a significant jump in Click Rate \(1.04% vs 0.63%\).

Every brand sends at a flat hour, like 9 a.m. PST. The result is that the customer gets like five emails at once, and then your email gets buried among the others. If you use a random time, then you can stand out.

posts.content:
Max posted the following on X \([https://x.com/maxwellcopy/status/2047814143797772470](https://x.com/maxwellcopy/status/2047814143797772470)\)

It is now possible to have AI running your whole email channel. We're here.

Many agencies are going to get fucked.

Having true taste, elite strategies, and deep analytics is the only thing that agencies will allow agencies to survive.

The ones with access to mass amounts of data and results will win. Taking learnings from other accounts and applying to all accounts as the differentiator. Data and strategies is the only competitive advantage.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
Wanted to discuess this in here since we have many agency owners.

First of all do you guys agree?

Maybe I am a bit behind but I have not seen something that gives you strategy, flows, campaigns, popups, everything with ongoing A/B-test, deliverability, reporting and consulting all in one.

AI helps with every aspect of that but connecting it all into one I have not seen.

And that is what the brand would need, right?

And even if that existed they would still need someone to tell them if the output is good.

Will agencies be able to charge less because clients understand the work can be largely done by AI? For sure.

So that will take revenue out of the agency market and leave it with the brand owner which means I agree with the main point of Max‘s post. Just think it will be more of a slow decline.

And as an individual agency you can protect yourself by staying on top of the game, as always.

What do you guys think? Have clients asked you to pass on efficiency savings enabled by AI?

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
Essentially, AI can do all functions now; however, it is very broken, and you have to use all sorts of different tools, and there's not one central thing, an easy thing. We have a lot of time here, and still nobody wants just an AI running the whole channel. You need human oversight; you need somebody to oversee everything.

Instead, I think that copywriters, designers, and creative executors are going to get put out. I don't think that all of them are going to go, because for specific brands they don't want AI, and for specific brands AI is just not going to be able to get it right, so you need a human to jump in.

Instead, the route we're going is something like you have an account manager running absolutely everything with their AI agents that we've created and trained. They have an AI agent for strategy, copy, design, and that agent is doing everything. The account managers are just overseeing it, and if a client is upset or they don't like the direction or the AI is messing up, then we'll bring in our copywriters and designers.

That's sort of the route that I see, but still strategy, client communication, and reporting are going to be run by one head. I think that copywriters and designers are going to slowly fall out, and there's going to be less of them. They're not going to disappear, because there are still businesses out there that use facts machines. It's not like old technology; it's funny that humans are considered old technology now, but it's not like old technology doesn't exist. You're still going to have humans; you're going to have brands that don't adopt AI still be successful.

As far as what is the outlook for agencies, I don't think too much changes. I still think that brands want somebody with experience overseeing everything. I think that the execution agencies will slowly get replaced, but still it's a lot for brands to learn how to use all these tools and whatnot until there's a super easy tool that does everything for you all in one place, which Klaviyo needs to come out with.

In short, agencies will never go away; however, how the execution happens needs to adjust, and the strategy that you do needs to adjust. You need to start becoming a retention team and really start to understand actual e-com strategy and numbers, not just living inside a Klaviyo.

posts.title: Single SKU struggles
posts.content:
Hey guys, for one of my clients, I've really been having a hard time bumping up the attributed revenue.

Can't get it higher than 5-8%.

With my previous email clients, it felt easy, like you'd hit 20% just by having core flows + 3x campaigns a week.

Is this somewhat inevitable, given I don't have anything to cross-sell or upsell them with other than more of the same? + longer buying cycles?

Our main acquisition comes from a buy-one-get-one-free offer that covers a 60-day supply. They already go through a bunch of upsells, so many customers end up with a six-month supply or more.

Core flows could definitely be stronger. They’re still kind of underperforming, but even then, 5% seems extremely low. I’m having a hard time figuring out what I can do here.

user.name: Michael Gorodi
user.bio: A copywriter based out of Koh Samui, Thailand - just living the island life and enjoying being a student of the craft.

comments.content:
What are the attribution settings? Is it not five-day opens, five-day clicks, and it's actually way lower? That could be why. Is it a product that doesnt get repeat purchases? That could be why. Here's some past info I've written on this.

I’m breaking down the 3 most common problems I see with stores that are stuck with email revenue between 10%-30%.
But before we get into that, you must ensure you have the fundamentals down:
[ol:1][li]Strong site traffic with a 10%+ opt-in rate popup[li]All your core flows built out with at least 3 emails in each[li]3-4 email campaigns going out per week.
That's the basic formula every ecom store should follow.
If you're not doing those three things, go do them. Seriously, stop reading this and go do them. There's no secret hack that bypasses the fundamentals.
But if you ARE doing all that and you're still stuck at 20-25% revenue from email, something else is broken.
Here's the 3 problems that hold most stores back:
Problem #1: Your Email List Is Too Small
This is the most common reason I see, especially with newer stores that are scaling hard.
Here's the thing: your list takes time to build.
You're not going to launch a store, set up your flows, and immediately see 40% of revenue coming from email.
That's not how it works.
Email works because you're building an owned audience over time.
Every subscriber you capture is someone you can monetize over and over again without paying for another click.
The key metric to watch: your popup form submit rate.
If your pop-up is converting at 10% or higher, your list growth should naturally scale with your traffic.
More visitors = more subscribers = more email revenue.
If you're below 10%, you're leaking potential subscribers every single day. And that gap compounds over time.
A store doing 100K visitors per month with a 5% popup conversion rate adds 5,000 subscribers per month.
That same store with a 12% popup conversion rate adds 12,000 subscribers per month.
After a year, that's the difference between 60,000 and 144,000 subscribers.
Same traffic. Wildly different email revenue.
Do you think the 144k subscriber list is more likely to hvae 40% of their store revenue coming from email? The answer is yes.
How to diagnose your popup:
Pull up your popup analytics and look at two numbers: your view rate and your submit rate.
View rate seems low compared to your site traffic? Your popup might be triggering too late or not firing on mobile. Test earlier timing \(5-8 seconds or 25% scroll\) and make sure it's actually showing on all devices.
View rate fine but submit rate under 10%? Your offer isn't compelling enough or your popup design is killing conversions. Test a stronger offer \(mystery discount, free gift, dollar amount off instead of percentage\). Simplify the design. Reduce form fields to just email.
Already at 10%+? You're good. Keep scaling traffic and your list will grow proportionally. The 40% email revenue will come as your list compounds over time.
If you're a newer store and email is "only" driving 18% of revenue but your popup is dialed and your list is growing steadily - relax. You're on the right track. The compounding just needs time to work.
Problem #2: Your Conversion Sucks When People Join The List
You've got a popup with a solid opt-in rate. People are joining your list. But then... nothing. They don't buy. None of your flows or campaigns are converting and you’re left wondering what the hell is going on?
Usually it's one of two things: your offer or your buying process.
Potential Issue #1: The offer isn't strong enough.
"10% off your first order" has become too common nowadays. But many customers are getting bored and tired of this offer.
It can work for some stores… but not all.
Maybe your product is already priced high and 10% feels like nothing. Maybe your audience is discount-fatigued. Maybe 10% just isn't exciting enough to create urgency.
Test different offer structures:
[ul][li]Mystery discount \("Reveal your discount" - could be 10%, could be 25%\)[li]Free gift with purchase \(often outperforms percentage discounts\)[li]Dollar amount off \($15 off feels more tangible than 15% off on a $100 product\)[li]Free shipping threshold \(works great for lower AOV brands\)
Always test new offers and don't just assume your offer is the best just because everyone else does it.
Potential Issue #2: The buying process is confusing.
I see this a lot with brands that have complicated products, quiz funnels, or checkout processes that add friction.
Particularly in the CPG space.
Someone joins your list, gets the welcome email, clicks through... and then they're hit with a 15-question quiz before they can even see a product page. Or the checkout has 47 upsells. Or the product options are so confusing they bounce.
Stop losing traffic due to complicated offers and buying processes!
If your flows have solid open rates and click rates but garbage conversion rates, you’ve found where the problem lies.
Simplify your product pages. Use clear value props, easy checkout setups, and don't make people work to give you money.
Problem #3: People Aren’t Coming Back
If your flows are dialed, your campaigns are consistent, your list is big enough, and you're still not hitting 40%... people might just not want to buy from you again.
Email is a retention channel. It's designed to bring people back.
But it can only bring back people who actually want to come back.
If you're selling a consumable product and people aren't reordering, that's usually cause your product sucks. They tried it, they didn't love it, they moved on. No amount of email optimization fixes that.
Now, there are exceptions.
If you sell something with a naturally low repeat purchase rate \(I.E. furniture, mattresses, etc.\) you're not going to see the same email revenue percentage as a brand selling protein powder or skincare… That's just the nature of the product.
Email crushes it for brands with normal to high natural retention. Consumables, refillables, clothing, products people use up and need to replace.
If you sell something people buy once every five years, email is still valuable for that one purchase, but it may not drive 40% of your total revenue \(you should still shoot for 30% minimum\).
Be honest about what category you're in.
If you're a CPG brand and people aren't coming back, the hard truth is your product might not be good enough. Or your product line is too narrow and people don't have a reason to return.
Sometimes the fix isn't email. It's expanding your product suite so there's actually something for customers to come back and buy.
Final Thoughts
40% of store revenue is the baseline we hit for nearly every client we work with.
If you're not there, run through this:
First, check the fundamentals. Make sure…
[ul][li]Your popup converting at 10%+[li]All your core flows live with at least 3 emails each[li]You’re sending 3-4 campaigns per week
If you’re not doing any of those, fix that first.
Second, check your list trajectory. Is your email revenue percentage trending up over time? If yes, you might just need patience. If it's flat or declining, something's broken. Try testing a different popup form.
Third, check your flow conversion. Good open rates and click rates but low conversion? The problem is likely your site, your offer, or your buying process.
Fourth, check your repeat purchase rate. If first-time buyers aren't becoming second-time buyers, email can't fix that. You've got a product problem.
The path to 40% is the same every time.
[ol:1][li]Grow your list[li]Build the flows[li]Send campaigns[li]Make sure your offer converts and your product brings people back.
If something in that chain is broken, figure out which link it is and fix it.

posts.title: Mother's Day Opt-Out Email
posts.content:
You may see a lot of brands do this email right here, the Mother's Day opt-out email. It's mostly just for branding and goodwill. A few years ago, it seemed like it was the most virtuous email ever. It's a bit overplayed lol but a lot of brands are doing it this year.

Essentially, all you do is send an email saying, "Hey, if you want to opt out of Mother's Day emails, click here," and then you exclude the people who click from your Mother's Day campaigns. The easiest way, in my opinion, to execute this is to send a plain text email with only one link, and you have that be the opt-out link. You just send those people to the home page of your website, and then you create a segment of anybody who clicked that campaign.

That's going to be your exclusion segment. Anybody who clicked that campaign, exclude that segment from all your Mother's Day emails.

posts.title: Billing Reminder Emails For Subscription Brands
posts.content:
cannot stress enough how important this is. Nailing this billing reminder email is super important and we've been able to decrease cancellations by up to 33% for brands by updating and optimizing this email.

Essentially when you are about to charge somebody when they're on subscription, you legally should send an email to them roughly three days before they're about to get re-billed. Now most brands just tell people, "Hey you're about to get charged. Manage my subscription" button right there and then people cancel. Instead you should optimize this email and add a bit of friction before the customer can cancel.

Make it beautifully designed and remind them of all the benefits of subscription and of all the benefits of your product. Push people to delay their order instead of cancel because a lot of people cancel because they have too much so give them the option to delay and then finally, at the bottom of the email, do give them the option to manage their subscription where they may cancel.

Here are a few examples of how you can change the framing of this billing reminder email, which is usually a machine that loses you revenue, into something that can limit that and actually contribute to the customer experience.

posts.title: Excluding Apple Privacy Opens 💀
posts.content:
Guys I excluded this for one brand now and the attributed revenue DROPPED.
For example for March the attributed revenue including privacy opens was 80k € now excluding privacy opens it is 55k €. That is about one third of the attributed revenue GONE.

I was expecting some revenue decrease yes, but is this in the normal range?
Also not quite sure if this is undercounting meaning that someone who really opens the email does not get counted because he is using Apple and is being excluded erroneously.

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
Sheesh wtf [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) that's crazy💀 but icl that drop is within the expected range. You can check your exact Apple Mail share in Klaviyo's email client analytics, but for most D2C audiences I believe it's in that 50%+ range, so getting rid of those fake opens from attribution naturally cuts a big chunk of credited revenue.

Ik Klaviyo can't reliably distinguish between Apple & a person's action so both go through the same proxy infrastructure. Pretty much the exclusion filter essentially discounts ALL Apple opens, including ones where the person genuinely read the email but didn't click. If that person then goes to the site directly and buys, that sale gets excluded even though email influenced it. Kind of a weird process tbh but that's how I read it.

The truth is probably somewhere between €55K and €80K fr. Neither is perfectly accurate.

To get the most trustworthy number I would just shift to click-based attribution entirely tbh.

user.bio: Owner of Well Copy - $200M Generated Through Email

comments.content:
Also talked to Klaviyo support about this. Excluding Apple Privacy Opens can lead to untercounting. If someone really opens on the Apple MPP device than it does not count so essentially I would therefore say it is BULLSHIT

When a device has Apple’s Mail Privacy Protection enabled, any open that occurs on that device \(whether it is the automatic prefetch or the person genuinely opening and reading the email\) is logged as an Apple Privacy Open = True.

Because Klaviyo cannot distinguish between the automated prefetch and a real human open in that environment, manual opens on MPP-enabled devices will also be treated as Apple Privacy Opens and will be excluded if you filter them out.

What you will still capture as “real” engagement are opens on non-MPP devices and all clicks, so looking at click rate alongside opens is a good way to avoid underestimating engagement.

If you have any further questions or require assistance, please don't hesitate to let me know. I'll be more than happy to help. posts.title: CLAUDE EMAIL DESIGN
posts.content:
Claude Design is starting to cook for email design...

Fed it example emails, had it spit out an MD file of best practices, now I reuse it time.

Hero sections come out clean. Still figuring out product/lifestyle image integration + Figma sync.

Prompt below if anyone wants to mess with it 👇

# Email Marketing Design Standards

This file defines how emails should be designed in this project. Claude reads this automatically at the start of every chat. Update it as our system evolves.

These principles are distilled from 8 reference emails spanning food, supplements, fitness gear, fragrance, beverages, golf and spirits. The brands differ wildly — but the structural rules below hold across all of them. Follow them for any new email.

---

## 1. Canvas & layout

- **Width:** 600px fixed. Every email is exactly 600px wide.
- **Height:** Long — expect 2,400–4,800px tall. Emails are vertical scrolls, not single screens.
- **Single column.** No side-by-side sections at the top level. 2-col product grids are fine inside a section, but the page flow is strictly vertical.
- **Outer horizontal padding:** ~30–75px depending on density. Content rarely runs to the edge except for full-bleed imagery.
- **Vertical rhythm:** large breathing room between sections — 60–120px of vertical space between major blocks. Emails feel generous, not cramped.
- **Safe stacking order \(top → bottom\):**
1. Logo bar \(header, centered\)
2. Hero \(headline + subhead + primary CTA, often over a themed background or image\)
3. Supporting section \(benefits grid, comparison, product list, or story\)
4. Secondary CTA
5. Social proof, badges, or "explore more"
6. Footer \(logo, nav, socials, legal\)

---

## 2. Structural pattern

Every strong email in this set follows a variant of this skeleton:

```
\[Logo\]
\[Hero: big headline + one short subhead + one CTA\]
─── break ───
\[Supporting content: 2–4 benefit tiles, OR comparison table, OR feature list\]
\[Second CTA — same or different language than the first\]
─── break ───
\[Reinforcement: product shot, testimonial, trust badges, or "what's inside"\]
\[Final CTA\]
─── break ───
\[Footer\]
```

Always include **at least 2 CTAs**, ideally 3. They should appear at the hero, mid-scroll, and just before the footer. Never end the email body without one.

---

## 3. Hero

The hero is where most of the design personality lives. Rules:

- **One giant headline.** 50–150px. It should occupy the full width of the content area and dominate the screen.
- **Pair it with a short subhead** \(20–28px\) — one sentence, sells the benefit, not the feature.
- **One primary CTA** below the subhead. Pill or rounded rectangle, full-width of the content column or ~320px wide.
- **Background treatment:** solid brand color, full-bleed photo with gradient overlay, or a textured flat color. Never a plain white hero — the hero always has visual weight.
- **Typographic contrast is the main device.** Pair a large serif/display with a small sans, or an oversized uppercase sans with a lowercase script. Never one font at one size.

Examples from the reference set:
- Display serif italic "Dates?" at 145px over a warm cream bg with tiny overline "Who Needs Sugar When You've Got" at 35px
- All-caps blackletter-weight "STRAWBERRY YUZU" in white on bright red
- Display script "Capsules *Are In*" in white over a dark green product photo with gradient
- Bebas-style "HYDRATION" at 74px in black on white

---

## 4. Typography

### Font choices
- **Pair exactly 2 type families**, occasionally 3. One display, one workhorse sans. That's it.
- **Display:** a serif \(Cormorant, Quincy CF\), a condensed sans \(Bebas, Belgro, Montserrat Bold\), or a utilitarian grotesk \(Acid Grotesk, Inter\) set enormous. Pick to match the brand mood:
- Luxury / wellness → italic serif \(Cormorant italic, Quincy CF italic\)
- Sport / performance → bold condensed sans, all caps \(Bebas, Belgro, Montserrat\)
- Modern / tech / clean → heavy grotesk \(Inter Medium, Acid Grotesk Bold\)
- **Workhorse:** Helvetica Neue, Inter, Funnel Sans, Be Vietnam Pro, Proxima Nova, Lato. Use Regular or Light at 16–24px.
- **Email-safe fallbacks always.** Web fonts are unreliable across clients. Every custom font stack must end in `Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif` \(or `Georgia, serif` for serifs\).

### Scale
- Hero headline: **50–150px** \(bigger than you think\)
- Section headline: **28–40px**
- Subhead / body intro: **20–24px**
- Body: **16–20px** \(never below 16px\)
- Micro / caption / footer legal: **12–14px**
- Button label: **16–22px**, letter-spaced if uppercase

### Styling rules
- **Line-height:** 0.9–1.0 for display headlines \(tight, editorial\); 1.1–1.3 for body; 1.4+ for legal.
- **Letter-spacing:** 0 for body; +0.05–0.10em for small uppercase labels and CTA text; slight negative \(-0.03em\) for huge display type.
- **Mix weights aggressively within headlines.** "Every Man Has Two *FANTASIES*" — normal weight + heavy weight in the same line creates the editorial feel the reference emails lean on.
- **Italics are a core device.** One italicized word inside an otherwise roman headline is a recurring move: *"Delivering Differently"*, *"Is It Really For You?"*, *"Next Get-Together"*.

---

## 5. Color

### Palette construction
Every email uses a **3-color palette**, tightly constrained:
1. **Background / canvas** — a warm off-white, dark brown, deep red, forest green, near-black, or a saturated brand color.
2. **Foreground / text** — high contrast against the background. Usually cream-white on dark, or deep brown/black on light.
3. **Accent** — exactly one. Used for CTAs, highlight swashes, or icon chips. Never more than one accent.

### Tone rules
- **Don't use pure white or pure black** for the canvas. Shift toward cream \(`#FDF8F1`\), bone, warm grey, deep aubergine, or mahogany instead. Pure `#FFF`/`#000` feels cheap.
- **Saturation is allowed, but commit.** Full-bleed cherry red \(`#EE3B3A`\), deep bourbon brown \(`#2A1810`\), olive-lime \(`#D1E143`\). Half-measures look generic.
- **Text on color:** cream/off-white \(`#FDF8F1`, `#FFF4C7`\), not pure white.
- **Dark emails need a warm undertone** — pure grey-black feels corporate. The sport/supplement emails use `#000` but surround it with warm tones elsewhere.

### Accent usage
- CTAs: the accent color background with contrasting label.
- Never rainbow. One accent for the whole email.
- Bright yellow, orange, or lime is the dominant accent pattern for energy/sport brands; cream, gold, or white-on-dark for luxury brands.

---

## 6. Imagery

- **Photography over illustration.** Every reference email leans on real product photography. Use placeholders \(monospace-labeled SVG rectangles\) if you don't have photos — never hand-drawn SVG product shots.
- **Full-bleed hero image with a gradient fade** to the bg color is a recurring pattern. The gradient hides the seam between photo and canvas.
- **Masked product shot in a circle** over a contrasting section bg is another recurring pattern \(see Dates chocolate, Elyon fragrance\).
- **Lifestyle + product.** Alternate between clean product-on-background shots and moody lifestyle imagery to create rhythm.
- **Icons:** simple line icons in colored circular chips \(40–80px\) for benefit grids. Never emoji. Never detailed illustrations.

---

## 7. CTAs \(buttons\)

CTAs are the most important component — every email has 2–3.

- **Shape:** full pill \(border-radius: 50%+\) OR rectangular with small radius \(4–8px\). Match brand personality.
- **Size:** min 56px tall, usually 64–80px. Wide — often 320–450px, almost full content width.
- **Label:** UPPERCASE, letter-spaced \(0.05–0.10em\), 19–25px. Bold or Medium weight.
- **Color:** accent color bg, contrasting label. Or outlined \(transparent bg, 2px border\) for secondary CTAs.
- **Copy:** verb-led and specific. "SHOP STRAWBERRY YUZU", "EXPLORE THE CAPSULE LINE", "ORDER TODAY & GET $20 STORE CREDIT". Not "Click here", not "Learn more" alone.
- **Spacing:** leave 40–60px of clear air above and below a CTA. Never crowd it.

---

## 8. Sections & dividers

- **Alternate section backgrounds** to create rhythm. A cream hero → dark brown benefits section → cream product section → dark footer is a classic flow.
- **Transitions between colored sections** often use a soft curve, diagonal line, or gradient fade rather than a hard edge. Avoid flat rectangular blocks stacked abruptly unless the brand is explicitly geometric.
- **Benefit grids:** 2×2 or 1×4 tiles, each with an icon chip, a short title \(bold, 18–22px\), and a 1-sentence description \(14–18px\). Tiles have subtle borders or soft fills — not heavy cards.
- **Comparison tables** are welcome for competitive/supplement brands. Keep to 2 columns \("Most brands" vs "Us"\), 4–6 rows.

---

## 9. Footer

Every email ends with a footer block containing, in order:

1. **Brand logo** \(centered, ~150–200px wide\)
2. **Short tagline or "Stay connected"** \(optional, 24–32px\)
3. **Social icons row** — Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook as needed. Monochrome icons, ~32px.
4. **Link grid** — 4–6 links in a 2-col or horizontal layout: SHOP, ABOUT, CONTACT, SUBSCRIBE, etc. Bordered or plain.
5. **Legal line** \(12–14px, muted\): "© 2026 Brand Name. All rights reserved."
6. **Unsubscribe + preference links** — always included, always visible, never hidden.

Footers are 500–600px tall. Don't skimp on them.

---

## 10. Copy voice

Across all 8 reference emails, the copy shares these traits:

- **Headlines are punchy and benefit-forward.** "Avoid the Sugar Crash", "Pocket-Sized Full-Spectrum Hydration", "You Didn't Land Here By Chance".
- **Subheads deliver the reason to click in ≤ 20 words.** "Made for the athlete who never stops." "Enjoy chocolate without the blood sugar rollercoaster."
- **Body copy is short.** 2–4 sentences per paragraph, max. Bullet lists wherever possible.
- **Check-mark lists** for feature enumeration.
- **Urgency/specificity in CTAs:** "USE CODE: LOVE20", "$15 off with code SB-X15PW".
- **Second-person** \("you", "your"\) throughout — never third-person brand speak.

---

## 11. Technical constraints

- **Inline CSS only.** Email clients strip `<style>` blocks and `<link>`. Style attributes on every tag.
- **Table-based layouts for real emails.** `<div>` + flex is fine for design mockups / Figma-style hi-fi HTML; when we're producing a sendable email, we switch to nested `<table>`s.
- **No JS, no forms, no iframes.** They won't run.
- **No web fonts as primary.** Link Google Fonts in `<head>` for clients that support them, but always fall back to a web-safe stack.
- **Images need `alt` text** — many clients block images by default and show alt text instead.
- **Bulletproof buttons:** wrap button HTML in VML for Outlook compatibility when producing sendable code.
- **Dark mode:** test that cream/warm backgrounds don't get auto-inverted into unreadable hues.
- **Accessibility:** min 4.5:1 contrast on body text. 44×44px min tap target on CTAs.

---

## 12. Anti-patterns — never do these

- ❌ Plain white background with plain black Helvetica \(generic, untrustworthy\)
- ❌ More than one accent color per email \(looks like a craft store\)
- ❌ Generic stock illustration or AI-generated clip-art
- ❌ Emoji in headlines \(unless brand is explicitly playful\)
- ❌ Centered body copy longer than 2 lines \(centered works for headlines, not paragraphs\)
- ❌ CTA that says "Click here" or "Learn more" alone
- ❌ Gradient backgrounds that span hue wheel \(red → blue → green rainbow\)
- ❌ Drop shadows on everything \(designers call this "bootstrap face"\)
- ❌ Rounded corners everywhere with no shape hierarchy
- ❌ Icons inside rounded-corner cards with a left-border accent \(AI-slop tell\)
- ❌ Footer with only an unsubscribe link — it should have logo, socials, nav, legal
- ❌ Filler sections added just to make the email longer

---

## 13. When making a new email, ask first

Before designing, confirm:
1. **Brand** — logo, palette, existing voice guide? Attach them.
2. **Purpose** — promo, welcome, cart recovery, educational, announcement, re-engagement?
3. **Primary CTA** — what's the one action?
4. **Product hero** — do we have real photography, or do we need placeholders?
5. **Length** — short \(~1,500px, one hero + one CTA\) or long \(~3,000+px, multi-section\)?
6. **Variations** — how many options to explore? What should differ between them \(layout, color, copy, visual style\)?

---

## 14. Output conventions

- File name: `<Campaign Name>.html` at project root.
- Register each email as a named asset with `write_file`'s `asset` param so it appears in the review pane.
- For variations, keep them in one file and use **Tweaks** to toggle between them rather than separate files.
- Always include a 600px-wide viewport meta and a centered stage \(grey page bg, white/colored email column in the middle\) so the email looks like it's in an inbox preview.

posts.title: Site abandon 1st email - dynamic Klayvio only or designed?
posts.content: What's typically best practice for site abandon 1st email? The loom shows what looks like a designed email but I'm not sure if it's native Klayvio only or also Figma designed.

user.name: Florian Ruhstaller
user.bio: Email list manager with big dreams

comments.content:
Yooo what up [@Florian Ruhstaller](obj://user/25feaa3355334940a0919731e28915d7). For site abandonment I'd go native Klaviyo over a custom Figma build. Either can work tho tbh. Reasoning below:

Site abandon is pretty much the lowest-intent trigger in your abandonment stack fr. At this stage, the dynamic product recommendation block is what drives conversion, with it showing them relevant products based on browsing or your top sellers. That's native Klaviyo functionality regardless of what the surrounding template looks like, and it'll do the heavy lifting for you.

Also this is a flow you'll want to test and tweak a lot anyways since the audience is low-intent and harder to convert. Native builds take minutes to change. Figma templates need a designer, HTML export, and QA for every edit. I feel like that matters when ur tryna optimize.

If the brand has a strong visual identity with custom designed templates across other flows, you're gonna want to match that consistency too. But if you're choosing where to invest design resources, site abandon is the lowest priority. LMK ur thoughts!

posts.title: $ vs % Which way to go?
posts.content:
Hey email wizards, wanted to ask how do we decide whether to go with $ or %?

I know that I should test. But I think I have heard [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) say something like it depends on the AOV. If it's above $100 it's something and if it's below it should be something else.

But I don't remember whether he said this in the email marketing course or in one of his YouTube videos.

I will eventually test, but I need to make sure how to go about this so I don't screw up my clients' profit margins.

Thanks.

CCing [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) [@Matthias Lindner](obj://user/9d0fa00b9b1546899ae49761154229cb) and [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5) here too in case they have any insights.

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
I'm guessing you are talking about a discount here?

It's gonna depend on your product and your market but in general I would say if 10% OFF is greater than $10 then do $. If 10% OFF is less than $10 then do %.

It all comes down to perceived value. If your AOV is $20-$40 then 10% OFF is literally nothing. But when AOV is higher then making people realise that 10% off is actually a lot of money is very valuable.

As you said, test it!

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content: Exactly as you and Tristan said, if AOV is above $100, usually dollar off will perform better. If AOV is under $100, typically percent off performs better. However, just test it. [Brez](https://milled.com/drinkbrez.com), for example, never does percent off; they only do store credit, which is dollar off, and so a common offer they do is $5 store credit. It all just depends, but typically the AOV play is the best way to start.

user.name: Max Sturtevant
user.bio: Owner of Well Copy - $200M Generated Through Email

comments.content:
Hey [@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703), the rule you're remembering is the Rule of 100, as under $100 AOV percentage feels bigger. Over $100, the dollar amount feels bigger. Our brains evaluate numbers relative to scale.

Since you mentioned margins, dollar amounts are prob safer because they cap your exposure. Percentages scale with price, so on brands with wide price ranges, a percentage on a high-ticket item can eat into margin fast.

The Rule of 100 is a starting point, not email gospel though lol. Do the math for each client. Calculate what the percentage equals in dollars at their AOV and ask which number sounds more impressive.

And like [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5) and [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) said, test it hella! Also make sure to measure revenue per recipient alongside conversion rates.
