posts.title: Pop up forms: Klaviyo vs Alia
posts.content:
Hey everyone,

I recently saw Alia Popups claiming they can help generate 15%+ of revenue from pop-ups.

I’m curious how they actually outperform Klaviyo. If you’re already following Max best practices \(like quizzes, mystery discounts, strong offers, etc.\), what additional value are they really adding to drive significantly more sign-ups?

The main thing I can think of is timing. For example, triggering earlier and therefore capturing more conversions that might have happened anyway. But at the same time, they showcase a lot of big brands using it, which makes me think there’s more to it.

Would love to hear if anyone here has tested it or has insights on what actually makes the difference!

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
I've seen pretty big uplifts in Alia pop-ups vs klaviyo tbf. The main win for me is that Alia will constantly split test the pop-up for you on their managed plan, which takes another thing of my plate and lets the experts do their thing.

I've seen some brands get 15%+ sign up with klaviyo pop-ups, and seen other brands get under 10% sign ups with Alia, and viser verser. It's just gonna vary a lot with your market, your product, your brand, and your traffic. Alia defo isn't some silver bullet that can get any pop-up form to kill.

I would say just implement all of Max's best practices in klaviyo, see what your numbers are, and then hop on a free trial with Alia and compare the numbers. If they aren't significantly better then stay on klaviyo, if they are then switch to Alia.

posts.title: Dynamic vs Static Product Sections
posts.content:
A lot of times we opt for just doing the designed emails through and through and just having fully designed emails, including product sections.

However, you should consider, for some brands, testing doing the static product sections that are designed versus using product sections that are generated within Klaviyo.

By using dynamic sections within Klaviyo, you can create specific product feeds and tell Klaviyo, "Hey, I want you to just highlight the best sellers in the past seven days." You can even go as far as promoting products that a specific customer has viewed recently.

These product feeds give you way less design capabilities; however, they usually have more relevant products.

For some brands, it makes sense to use this, or at least test it, and this test resulted in a 50% better click rate and double the revenue.

Consider trying it out.

posts.title: Tuesday Coffee Hour Call Summary
posts.content:
If you guys didn't see... we added a new weekly call on Tuesday's called Coffee Hour, directed towards agency owners and freelancers to chat about growth, clients, and challenges.

Attaching the summary below... make sure you are there next week!!! \(Link and time is in the calendar section of this Skool community - 11am EST on Tuesdays\)

🧠 1. Overview of the Call
This was a casual, no-agenda mastermind-style discussion among email marketers, agency owners, and ecommerce operators. The focus naturally centered around:
[ul][li]Client acquisition[li]Outreach strategies[li]Scaling agencies[li]Offer structuring[li]Early-stage growth challenges
It functioned as a peer learning environment, where participants shared real-world tactics, mistakes, and frameworks.

🚀 2. Client Acquisition Strategies \(Core Theme\)
A. Outbound + Inbound Combo \(Most Recommended\)
[ul][li]The most consistent approach discussed was combining inbound and outbound[li]Outbound = DMs, cold emails, personalization[li]Inbound = content, ads, referrals
Key insight:Outbound builds skill fast, inbound scales trust.

B. Personalization is the Edge
Top performers emphasized:
[ul][li]Sending screenshots of a brand’s actual emails/site[li]Giving specific improvements upfront[li]Avoiding generic / AI-looking messages
👉 This dramatically increases response rates because:
[ul][li]It proves effort[li]It feels human[li]It shows competence immediately

C. Timing > Copy
A major takeaway:
[ul][li]90% of outreach fails due to bad timing, not bad copy[li]The same message works if: The problem is urgent The brand is ready to invest
👉 This reframes outreach as a numbers + timing game

D. Volume + Iteration System
Best practice shared:
[ul][li]Test outreach in batches of 50[li]Track: Replies Positive responses Calls booked[li]Iterate quickly based on data
👉 Outreach = experiment loop, not guesswork

🤝 3. Referral Systems & Partnerships
A. Referral Incentives
Strong strategies included:
[ul][li]10–15% commission on referrals[li]Discounts on services instead of cash[li]Recurring commissions for partners
👉 Referrals were described as:
[ul][li]Highest quality leads[li]Most scalable long-term

B. Strategic Partnerships
Examples:
[ul][li]Lawyers, accountants, agencies → refer clients[li]Cross-referrals between niche specialists
👉 Key idea:“There’s enough business for everyone — collaborate instead of compete”

📈 4. Content & Inbound Growth
A. YouTube as a Long-Term Asset
[ul][li]One agency generated 50% of leads from YouTube[li]Videos kept bringing clients years later
👉 Insight:Content compounds → outreach does not

B. Personal Brand Increases Reply Rates
[ul][li]Posting content improves: Trust Authority DM conversion rates
👉 People check your profile before replying
C. Paid Ads \(Advanced Stage\)
[ul][li]Meta ads used for inbound leads[li]Works best when: ICP is clearly defined Funnel is dialed

⚠️ Downsides:
[ul][li]High CAC \(especially during peak seasons\)[li]Requires capital and testing

🎯 5. Outreach Tactics That Worked
A. Founder-Level Outreach
[ul][li]DMing founders directly = higher response rates[li]Methods: Search “Founder @ \[brand\]” Use tools or manual research

B. Value-First Approach
Examples:
[ul][li]Sending Loom videos[li]Giving free advice[li]Highlighting missed revenue opportunities
👉 Builds trust before pitching

C. Platform Systems
Tools mentioned:
[ul][li]LinkedIn + Sales Navigator[li]CRM-style tools \(like tagging + follow-ups\)
👉 Key = organized follow-up system

💼 6. Handling Low-Budget Leads
Two main approaches:
Option 1: Paid Entry \(Flow Build\)
[ul][li]Offer smaller one-time projects[li]Build relationship → upsell later
Option 2: Zero-Time Free Value \(More Efficient\)
[ul][li]Send: Templates Looms Guides[li]Do NOT spend time on calls
👉 Best approach = scalable help without time drain

💡 7. Offer Innovation
A. Unlimited Design Retainer Model
Example offer:
[ul][li]~$3,700/month[li]Unlimited requests[li]One task at a time
👉 Works because:
[ul][li]High perceived value[li]Controlled delivery internally

B. Performance-Based Offers
For beginners:
[ul][li]Charge % of revenue generated[li]Removes risk for client
👉 Great for:
[ul][li]Getting first clients[li]Building case studies

🧱 8. Early-Stage \(0 → First Client\) Advice
A. You MUST Get Proof First
Consensus:
[ul][li]No case studies = very hard to close[li]Solution: Work for free OR heavily discounted Build results first

B. Focus on First Dollar, Not $10K
Big mindset shift:
[ul][li]Don’t chase $10K/month[li]Chase: First $1 First $500
👉 This builds belief and momentum

C. Simplicity Wins
Focus on:
[ul][li]One service[li]One ICP[li]One acquisition channel
👉 Complexity kills beginners

⚠️ 9. Common Mistakes
[ul][li]Relying only on referrals[li]Sending generic AI outreach[li]Targeting wrong ICP[li]Taking bad clients for money[li]Over-focusing on revenue goals instead of execution[li]Doing too much free consulting \(time drain\)

🧠 10. Mindset & Long-Term Thinking
A. “Get Good to Get Seen”
Core principle shared:
[ul][li]Skill → results → referrals → growth
👉 Not the other way around

B. Take Action Over Learning
[ul][li]Watching content ≠ progress[li]Execution = learning

C. Avoid Emotional Rollercoaster
[ul][li]Beginners struggle with inconsistency[li]Solution: Focus on small wins Build proof gradually

🔥 11. Key Takeaways \(Condensed\)
[ul][li]Best acquisition strategy = inbound + outbound + referrals[li]Personalization beats volume \(but you still need volume\)[li]Timing matters more than copy[li]Content builds authority and compounds[li]Referrals are the highest-quality growth channel[li]Beginners should prioritize proof over profit[li]Systems \(tracking, CRM, iteration\) separate amateurs from pros

You'd have to send some numbers in here on opens and click rates. The thing is, deliverability is not just do one thing and then it gets better overnight. It's a long-term thing. All you can do is continue to try to get good open rates and click rates and reduce your spam rates and try to get as many replies as you can.

In your welcome flow, push people to reply. In campaigns, push people to reply. Whatever you can to do that, do that. You can use stuff like:

posts.title: Major decrease in openrate after switching sending domain
posts.content: One of my clients switched domains yesterday so I had to change the email sending domain too. Since then both flows and today’s campaign have had a pretty big drop in open rate. Is this normal after a domain change or did I mess something up? Is there somthing i should do?

user.name: Lukas Anderlind
user.bio: Emails for a couple ecommerce brands.

comments.content:
Yes, this is normal because it's a different sending domain with no reputation. If you change a sending domain, you should technically re-warm up your account, because essentially you just reset your reputation and how inbox providers are seeing your domain now. This is someone who just started sending emails yesterday, so you've no reputation, and so you're more likely to land in spam and promos. This is why you have to go through a warm up period.

What I would recommend is:
[ul][li]Leave your core high-engaging flows on, but just the first two emails \(welcome flow, side abandoned browse, cart abandoned, checkout abandoned, and post-purchase flows\). Leave on just the first one to two emails and have those run for like 30 days before you return to the rest of the flows and the rest of the emails in the flows.[li]Tighten up your campaign segmentation. Instead of sending to a larger list, bring it down to something like 14-day engaged, so you're not blasting a ton of people. Send in the numbers that you get when you send to that super tight engaged list here.[li]I can guide you. You may need to break up the list into even smaller lists and start sending campaigns to literally just 1,000 people, then 2,000, then 4,000, and slowly ramp up volume, but that might not be needed. We'll just have to see what the numbers look like on a tighter engaged list, like a 14-day engaged send.
Keep me updated.

posts.title: HUGE attribution dispute with client
posts.content:
What's up everyone. Open to all ideas from agency guys/freelancers about Klaviyo email attribution.

So with my main client, I've been getting a base pay + 5% revshare on email-attributed rev.

Up until now, we've been using Klaviyo's standard attribution settings which is Opened in last 5 days and Clicked in the last 1 day.

Today, they switched up and said Opened Email in 5 days is NOT fair, and they only want to use Clicked Email in the last 1 day for email attributed revenue.

Obviously, this tanks my compensation as it's reduced email revenue in the last two weeks from 50k to 15k. It won't impact past revenue, but will impact future revenue/ new contract.

❓❓❓What would you guys recommend I do for compensation structure/ attribution settings? And how can I justify it to my client? ❓❓❓

*** for reference, I've been killing it for these guys and we have a good relationship, so they are open to a fair middle-ground agreement***

I need to come back to them with a fair justification why Clicked Email in the last 1 day isn't enough. Unless you guys think it is...

Haven't run into this issue with a client before, so really appreciate any and all insight if you've been in a similar situation 🙌 and shoutout to [@Andy Duong](obj://user/fbfb40fa1fb6459b908879ba62a14f13) for the insight he's already given me

user.bio:

D2C Marketing

comments.content:
I have never done rev share deals just because you'll always have one side thinking they're getting underpaid and it's unfair. Never done it, and I probably never will.

That's completely fine for them to do that and respectable, but that changes: even with your same amount of work, you just get paid less and you get fucked over, so just say they have to adjust it.

posts.title: Hitting Promotion Tab
posts.content:
I just finished fixing deliverability, and we've been at 50% average open rates for the past few weeks. But all of a sudden, on today's campaign, I see that it's going straight to promotions instead of primary.

Any insights on why this is happening or how to fix it?

I might be jumping the gun a little too soon, but I want to fix this so it doesn't continue to happen.

For reference, it was a text-only email from the founder that didn't have any discounts or spam language.

user.name: Aaron Lund
user.bio:
@copylund
D2C Marketing

comments.content:
What's good [@Aaron Lund](obj://user/188c6d11daf64ecbbb1f42aaab736c88) so I'm prob gonna need more context here but based on what ur saying, your emails going straight to promotions tab instead of spam or junk isn't inherently a problem \(just yet\). It's still the inbox, and Gmail has that tab for commercial mail. A lot of D2C shoppers actively check it looking for deals. If opens stay at 50%, your audience is finding the emails regardless of tab.

A few possible reasons tho:

[ul][li]Your overall sender reputation is already set as promotional.[li]Gmail categorizes based on sending pattern over time, not any single email. [li]If the brand has been sending designed promotional emails for months, one text-only send doesn't instantly recategorize you. [li]Your "from" address and infrastructure \(so like unsubscribe footers, list headers, branded domain, links in the email\) all signal commerce regardless of how plain the body looks.

One send isn't a pattern yet bro. Gmail's tab categorization has natural variance so what I'd do is just watch your next 3-5 sends before diagnosing anything.

However if it does become a pattern, check whether anything changed recently. This could be the sending domain, DNS/authentication, send volume or frequency, from name or address, or even any recent spam complaints tbh. Any of those can shift how Gmail categorizes you. You can also test the same email from a different subdomain to see if it's sender-specific or content-related.

But given that you just fixed deliverability, don't buy this as an actual issue yet.

posts.title: Re-Engagement Campaigns
posts.content:
Have any of you guys experimented with re-engagement campaigns? And if so, curious what your results have been. The way I approach these types of campaigns is as follows:

[ul][li]Send out campaign as normal [li]Create a segment of people who didn’t click or open the email[li]Resend the same email to this specific segment 1-2 days later, just change up the SL so it appears to be a different email

I’ve mainly tried these with BFCM or sales emails, and feel like it’s a solid way to squeeze out some extra revenue from each campaign without too much extra effort.

user.name: Barrett Wong
user.bio: Ecomm Email Marketer and AI Automation Specialist

comments.content:
What's good Barrett! This is a hella valid strat and it does work but what ur describing is actually a non-opener resend, not an actual re-engagement campaign.

True re-engagement targets subscribers who've been inactive 60-90+ days as a last-shot attempt winback before sunsetting.

Some sauce that'll make your resend hit harder:

[ol:1][li]Segment on "didn't click," not "didn't open." Post-iOS 15, Apple Mail Privacy Protection creates fake opens on emails people never actually looked at, so "didn't open" segments are gonna be unreliable for you now bro. Click-based filtering catches the people who genuinely didn't engage.

2. Swap the hero image or reframe the opening angle while keeping the same offer.

3. Reserve this for promotional sends with a clear offer, which is what you're already doing.

From what I've seen, resends usually recover around 30% of the original open rate and 10-15% of the revenue. And watch overall frequency, because if you're already at 4-5 sends/week, resends double volume fast and your deliverability could potentially get nuked.

Also if you're not running a true re-engagement flow for 60-90 day inactive subscribers, that's worth building too. Lmk your thoughts [@Barrett Wong](obj://user/709d456b8a884b36b752695fba316180)!

user.name: Aven Tedros
user.bio:
Founder of Magtania, specializing in retention & lifecycle marketing for the pet care industry.

Believe you can achieve it, and you're halfway there.

replies.content:
[@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) ayyy glooks bro i appreciate the sauce 🙏 and yea you're right this isn't a full-on re-engagement campaign like you mentioned above. i'll need to take a closer look at creating a full-on re-engagement flow, i've built out winback flows before but that's obviously for people who are a little bit further down the funnel.

would you build out a re-engagement flow after the core pre and post purchase flows have been built out? or do you think it's important to build it out alongside the core flows?

user.name: Barrett Wong
user.bio: Ecomm Email Marketer and AI Automation Specialist

replies.content:
[@Barrett Wong](obj://user/709d456b8a884b36b752695fba316180) Honestly brodie that's after the core flows in most cases, unless your list health forces your hand sooner.

Pre and post-purchase flows are the revenue backbone bc those hit customers at high-intent moments and drive the bulk of flow revenue. Re-engagement works on subscribers who've already gone cold \(with real value but smaller impact\). There's a good reason to wait because re-engagement flows need data to build properly. Setting the right inactivity threshold depends on knowing how your audience actually engages. I feel like if you build it too early you'd just be guessing imo.

The only real exception to this tbh is if you're taking over a brand with an aging list and a chunk of cold subscribers because atp re-engagement becomes urgent. In that case, at minimum build a simple sunset flow to protect sender reputation while you're working on core flows. The full re-engagement sequence could come later.

Also, winback targets customers who bought once but haven't repurchased. Re-engagement targets subscribers who've gone cold on email engagement regardless of purchase history. The distinction is huge here because those are different audiences but have similar mechanics. You've alr built the muscle with winback so re-engagement should feel pretty familiar.

posts.title: Easiest Way To Win Long Term
posts.content:
One of my favorite things to do that almost nobody does is take your winning campaigns and add them into your flows. You send campaigns multiple times per week and you're constantly testing new angles.

Meanwhile you only update your flows once every six months? Why?

Every single month look at your top-performing non-discount emails. If there's one or two of them that do particularly well, find where you can use those angles or just that email to go somewhere in your flows.

Take this example: this testimonial email absolutely crushed. Why not just add a bar up at the top that reminds of the welcome discount and then B test this with the current email 3 in the welcome flow that might be underperforming?

Odds are if you have a campaign that performs well as a non-discount email, adding the welcome discount and putting that in the welcome flow will probably perform really well too.

You can do this for any flows. If you do an awesome educational email as a campaign on how to use our product and it gets good engagement, why don't you adjust it and add it to your post-purchase flow?

Think smarter not harder folks!

[@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703) This will depend on the brand a bit but I use a simple structure for my clients welcome flows.

Email 1 = deliver incentive
Email 2-5 = any value/education/objection handling
Email 6-7 = Discount reminder and extension

This means I swap in winning campaigns to anything Email 2-5. In most cases you'll want to leave in some specific emails \(e.g. our story, highlighting hero product/s\), but if there's an email which is underperforming then just A/B test the content with winning campaign and see what wins.

posts.title: Post Purchase Trigger Splits
posts.content:
Hey everyone - I’d love some input on structuring a post-purchase flow in Klaviyo.

I have 4 core products for a wellness brand, and I want to tailor post-purchase emails based on what each customer actually bought.

My initial thought was to use trigger splits for each product, but I’m running into a logic issue: if someone buys multiple products \(say A + B\), and they hit a split for just Product A, they’d only get messaging for A and not B.

One idea I considered was creating branches for every possible combination \(A, B, C, D, AB, AC, etc.\), but that quickly turns into 15 different paths- which feels messy and hard to maintain.

So my question is:

How are you all handling post-purchase personalization when customers buy multiple products?

Are you using trigger splits, dynamic content blocks, separate flows, or something else entirely?

Would love to hear what’s worked best for you in practice 🙏

comments.content:
Hey Morgan great question. I would look into the data and see how many people are actually buying multiple of these products, because it might be a very, very small amount. Typically, we just do the splits based on product A. They only get the messaging for A and not B.

Alternative option is you just set up different flows for each product, and then they receive each email. Say somebody bought product A, B, and C instead of having the same post-purchase flow. You could have three different post-purchase flows for each one, and if somebody bought all three, they'd enter into all three of those flows and receive three emails, each one dedicated to each product. Problem with that is they get more emails.

Alternatively, you could do what you said and do splits based on if they have both items or they bought both items. Any of those work, but I would look in the data and see how many people that is actually happening for and is it worth the time to do it? I just go with the main top combinations and then do splits just for those and educational emails for those.

posts.title: Why You Need To Enable Extended ID Tracking*
posts.content:
Hi everyone,

Here's a huge value-add that will take less than 5 minutes to set up.*

Usually, Klaviyo will track customers for up to 7 days. Enabling Extended ID Tracking will allow Klaviyo to track customers for up to a year!!

Why is this valuable?

"\[Without Extended ID Tracking\], if a shopper visited your site and you captured their email or phone number, once their cookie expired, on a return visit you still couldn’t identify who they were. As a result, if they abandoned their cart, you had no way to re-engage or follow up effectively." - Director of Product Marketing @ Klaviyo

So why is it valuable?

It improves the performance of your Abandonment Flows eg. Site, Browse, Cart, Checkout

Here's how to set it up:

[ol:1][li]Head to settings \(bottom left\)[li]Head to data [li]Enable Extended ID Tracking [li]Follow instructions

Let me know if you found this useful 👍

[https://www.klaviyo.com/blog/conversations-extended-id-shopify-pixel-sync](https://www.klaviyo.com/blog/conversations-extended-id-shopify-pixel-sync)

*If you're selling to EU/UK customers, make sure you update your cookie notice and privacy policy before enabling this

posts.title: Stop Building Winback Flows Like This...
posts.content:
A common mistake that I see is people building a win back or replenishment email flow and setting their time delay within the flow, like the example in the first screenshot.

If I were to set live that example in the first screenshot, it would take 45 days then for the people to start receiving the emails, which is not ideal.

Instead, you should use a segment-based trigger.

For example, we could use the win back eligible segment in the second screenshot below and have the flow fire when somebody enters this segment.

If I were to turn a flow live that fires whenever somebody joins this win back eligible segment, then I could turn this flow live today.

People will enter into the segment today and enter into the flow today, and then you don't have to wait for results to start generating.

Make sure you set up your flows like this.

posts.content:
Hey [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) , [@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) , and other email wizards lurking here...

Is there a way to measure repeat purchase rate in Klaviyo / Shopify?

I want to check out my client's repeat purchase rate and, if possible, optimize it.

They dont have a save and subscribe for their skincare products, and I think it'd be a good idea to propose they add this.

Other than that, is there any other way to monitor and optimise repeat purchase?

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
I’m very bullish on subscriptions. Defo recommend it. Subscriptions work because they make the default action to buy again… and again… and again.

Obvs you need a good product to get repeat purchases.

There are tools, like Hiro, specifically built for this. You can do it in Klaviyo \(with segments\) as well though.

[ol:1][li]Create a segment [li]Call segment ‘repeat’[li]What someone has done, place order at least 2 over all time[li]Create new segment [li]Call segment ‘one time’[li]What someone has done, place order once over all time[li]‘One time’/‘repeat’ = your repeat purchase rate

Also, for getting repeat purchases; I really think that being aggressive is necessary. RFM \(Recency, Frequency, Monetary\) — the higher the RFM, the more valuable the customer.

Therefore, when your customer has recently spent money with you, you should go for an upsell or crossell.

However I'd actually push back on the 45-day delay. If it's a daily serum in a 30ml bottle, customers are already out by day 30-35 and your email arrives after they've reordered or switched brands. If it's a larger product lasting 60-90 days, then 45 days is wayyy too early imo. You gotta match the trigger to actual consumption rate per product, and you might need different flows for different product types. It could be worth checking out Klaviyo's "Expected Date of Next Order" too because it predicts reorder timing from actual customer behavior instead of a fixed delay.

The highest-leverage thing for repeat purchase rate though is your post-purchase flow \(as we know\). The first 30 days after a purchase is peak customer attention. How to use the product, what results to expect, when to reorder kind of content will prime people for repeat purchase BEFORE they even finish their first bottle.

Lastly, repeat purchase optimization starts before the first purchase even ships. If the customer doesn't know how to use the product properly, they get subpar results and never come back. The best retention pull is making sure every first-time buyer actually sees results from their first bottle. Everything else just really builds on that.

posts.title: Weekly vs Monthly Discount strategy
posts.content:
Hi everyone,

Let’s say a brand is doing around $100k per month from email, mainly by running a discount every weekend \(so around 4 per month\).

Now imagine this brand switching to fewer promotions. For example, only one discount event per month, or only during bigger moments like Easter, Mother’s Day, etc.

How do you think this would affect the email revenue?

On one side, I think it could go down, because new subscribers \(for example someone who buys early in the month\) might not be as engaged anymore when the next promotion happens 30 days later.

On the other side, maybe the demand just becomes more concentrated. So instead of buying during different weekly promotions, customers all buy during one bigger campaign.

Curious how you have seen this in practice. Does revenue usually go down, stay similar but more concentrated, or maybe even increase? \(Aside that it's obviously better from a branding perspective\)

Thanks a lot!

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
I haven’t ever worked with a brand doing that many discounts, so take what I’m about to say with a grain of salt.

I’d imagine that in the short run you’d see a dip in email performance but in the long run it’d be much better for the brand.

There’s a few reasons I think this:

[ol:1][li]Ecom is already a low margins game 

When you constantly discount, your email attributed rev might look good, but you’re giving away a ton of margin.

2. Expert opinions

Partly from experience & what I’ve read… best practice for running a sale is once every 3 months \(or once a quarter\).

Taylor Holiday \(CTC\) who runs a massive ecom agency speaks about this quite a bit.

That being said, there are a few brands who are constantly discounting & it seems to work for them eg. MyProtein in the UK.

Very interesting question though mate — I could have written a lot more 🤣. I’m eager to see what other people have to say

comments.content: It really varies case to case. Typically, you'll see less revenue in the short term. But, in the long term, you'll see better benefits. And then, when you do have sale events \(whether that's once a month or whatever it is\), those will really pop into well. posts.title: Profile Property Update
posts.content:
Hey everyone, just wanted to ask you if you all use the 'Profile Property Update' in your flows - and if 'yes', would would be the benefit of this?

Looking forward to your reactions.

user.name: Marcel Paulusma
user.bio: Hi there!

comments.content:
Yooo [@Marcel Paulusma](obj://user/c927017210a8453db18633245d783635) yeah I use these. I do it for cross-flow suppression.

Without it, someone who starts checkout could technically get hit by your browse abandonment, cart abandonment, AND checkout abandonment flows all in the same session and ruin the customer experience. A customer's perception of your brand is cooked after that.

That property update stamps "InCheckoutAbandonmentFlow" on the profile the second they enter, so your other flows can filter them out. The same thing works for campaigns too, just exclude anyone mid-flow so they're not getting bombarded at all.

Keep in mind too that you need to clear that property when someone exits the flow, otherwise it stays on the profile forever and permanently blocks them from future flows. And if you're using flow filters to check for placed order, anyone who buys gets kicked out of the flow BEFORE reaching the property reset step. So it never fires which is obv a massive L.

Use conditional splits instead of flow filters to check for purchase, then routing through a property removal step before exiting.

The buyers vs non-buyers split below is a good touch too. First-time buyers need trust and social proof in abandonment copy, repeat buyers just need a nudge.

posts.title: INSIGHTFUL POP-UP FORM AB TEST

In the first screenshot shows the results of testing pop-ups forms with different close form functionality.

Top Variation: Uses an X in the top right corner, standard for closing forms.

posts.title: strange request from client
posts.content:
My skincare client also happens to have a telehealth company and he wants to promote it to his skincare list.

These two businesses are completrly unrelated.

He was asking me how I woukd go about this, and I am thinking of doing what Barton Publishing does when they want to promote affiliate products to their list which is by starting their email with something like:

"Please see the following important health information from our trusted partner, Trugenics.

In hope and healing,

Joe Barton"

But nw he is asking what segment to send it to, there are literally no segments yet in his skincare comoany that shows interest in what his telehealth company has to offer.

So I am thinking sending it to the 30-day and 60-day engaged and then, based on the response, I will create an "interested in telehealth" segment. Does this make sense, [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) ?

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
Interested to hear what Max thinks but personally I don't think it's a great thing to do. If people feel like your just trying to make the most out of them as a customer and sell from other brands too then it could make the relationship feel very transactional.

I'd say try a plain text email to a small segment of repeat customers along the lines of "We know you love us so we thought we'd let you know about our sistering brand...". Could also add a "Click here if you're not interested in hearing about telehealth" to reduce overall unsubs and collect data on if people care.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
Hey [@Suraj Punjabi](obj://user/b2b091f2ef5e4a35b032e02d35240703) I'd zoom out a bit first because ngl the bigger risk here is actually damaging the skincare brand's email channel.

I say that because when someone subscribes to a skincare list, they opted in for SKINCARE. So when you promote a separate business it's simply just off-topic to the subscriber. That's gonna mean higher spam complaints and higher unsubs, which both hurt deliverability. You're risking the core business to promote a side business.

Like Tristan said, curious to learn Max's thoughts here, but two questions I'd ask before doing anything are these below:

First: is there a genuine connection anywhere? Skincare and telehealth aren't necessarily unrelated. If the telehealth company offers virtual derm consultations, prescription skincare, anything that directly serves skincare customers, then it won't come off as some sort of random cross-promo. It would come off as you adding value which would change everything.

Second: is the skincare brand actually founder-led? Because if the audience follows and trusts the person, there's way more wiggle room for content like this. If it's a faceless brand, an off-topic promo would be a a much harder sell imo.

If there's no connection and no personal brand to lean on I would just push back on the client. The deliverability risk isn't worth it man.

But if there's a real connection or strong founder trust then you can do it, just make sure to skip the "trusted partner" kind of framing.

If you do it, start with 30-day engaged only. Be measured with how often you hit that segment going forward.

posts.title: Pop-Up Testing...
posts.content:
Sharing a quick \(and interesting\) A/B test result

We tested Mystery Discount vs. 15% Off in a pop-up form over the weekend.
[ul][li]Important context here: 15% off is their original offer, and the A/B test was purely a headline change to position it as a “mystery discount” instead of revealing the amount upfront.

This one went against what we’d typically expect.
[ul][li]Usually, the mystery discount variation wins, but in this case, 15% off clearly outperformed.

Context that likely influenced this:
[ul][li]Audience skews older \(late 30s to 60s, both male and female\)[li]Less tech-savvy and generally more hesitant to give out email/personal info[li]More responsive to clear, upfront value vs. curiosity-driven hooks

Notably, Klaviyo was able to identify a winner for mobile \(highest traffic segment\) within ~15 hours, and quickly shifted traffic toward the 15% off variation.

Key takeaway:
[ul][li]Mystery discounts aren’t universally effective. For certain demographics, especially older audiences, clarity > curiosity when it comes to conversion.

Next steps:
[ul][li]We’ll test discount framing and perceived value, specifically:% vs. $ \(e.g., 15% off vs. $20 off\)To understand whether the format of the offer impacts submit rate as much as the value itself

posts.title: Easiest Way To Increase Click Rates
posts.content:
A simple and easy way to increase click rates is by adding "Shop Now" in category buttons into your email footer.

We want to do this because sometimes people are not interested in the products or product in the main content of your email. If they scroll to the bottom and there's nothing else for them, then they will just leave.

When you have buttons in your footer, sometimes people will just click and naturally buy.

Oftentimes the footer will get 25 to 50% of the email's total clicks, which is pretty crazy.

As a note, do not put the buttons in the hero section of the email, like some people do. You want the category buttons in the footer.

If you put them at the top, it just distracts the customer and overwhelms them right when they open the email.

By having them in the footer, it lets people take in the content of the email and catches them while they are done browsing.

posts.title: One of the best tests you can do...
posts.content:
Time delays in your abandonment flows!

In this example... a browse abandon time delay resulted in nearly a 50% increase in placed orders.

It's pretty rare for a shorter time delay to not win for abandonment flows so keep that in mind.

Takes 30 seconds to set up...

[ol:1][li]Drop in a conditional split at the top of your flow[li]Set it as a 50/50 random sample[li]Duplicate all emails on both tracks[li]Add a different time delay for both sides at the top of the flow

Voila! High leverage AB test.

posts.title: When does a split test end?
posts.content:
I'm currently split testing pop-up forms. And I would like to know when can i declare one a winner.

Should I wait until each of the variations has received 1000 views? Should I wait a week? Or should I wait until Klaviyo declares the "Win Probabiity" "statistically significant?

Please help.

I have shared two screenshots of two different pop-up forms split tests. The one that says "SMS only" is targetted when existing email subscribers visits the page and we offer them a small discount to subscribe to SMS marketing.

Hope this makes sense.

CC: [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d)

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content: I usually wait a week depending on site traffic. But I think it's pretty easy to see winners after 500-1000 views and data probably won't change loads after that point. I'd probably wait a little longer for the SMS one just to get more conviction but I think you can defo conclude the email & sms one as B being the winner.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
It really just depends. Typically, I kind of just go off feel and logic. If it's been a week and the forms have like 10,000 views and one hasn't pulled away significantly, then it's probably not great to keep going. We run A/B tests to get significant results, and if none pull away, then might as well end the test, go with whatever is winning already, and start a new test. I usually go off feel. If one is clearly pulling away even after a couple of days, then I'll just go with that one and end it early, but typically a week is a good starting point. Then again, sometimes with brands that have a shit ton of traffic, I'll end a test the same day, because they just have so much data.

As far as what I'm seeing right now in the test that you showed, mystery discount looks to be winning. Take a look at the placed orders: 33 versus 23. That's one that I'm good to end and move forward with; that's a big win.

posts.title: Doubled my Client's campaign revenue
posts.content:
Onboarded a DTC skincare client last month.

Sales were dwindling.

Email wasn’t pulling its weight.

The moment I onboarded them, I:
- Migrated their 100k+ list to Klaviyo
- Fixed deliverability issues hurting inbox placement
- Set up core flows \(welcome, abandoned, winback, post-purchase\)
- Simplified and rebuilt their pop-up
- Added SMS to capture and follow up on leads

Result?

Revenue from email campaigns nearly DOUBLED.

Together with sms and flow, it’s currently accounting for 50%+ of their total revenue.

This does not include the revenue generated by the pop-up forms I set up, which is around 25k-30k

What sorcery is this?

To be honest, I didn’t do any complicated, lvl 100000 email sorcery.

I just stuck to proven fundamentals that I have learned for the past 6 years in the game.

❌ They were sending cutesy, smart-sounding, image-heavy emails 2x a week.
✔️ I sent plain-text emails built on proven direct-response principles that were clear, persuasive, and that provided real value, 3x a week.

❌ Their pop-up form asked WAYYY too much.
Name, email, address, what you would like to hear, when’s your birthday, what skin issues are you dealing with, blah blah blah.

Felt like filling out a form, instead of signing up for an offer.

✔️ I cut it down to one thing:
Give an email -> get a discount.

❌ They were training their list to only buy during discounts and BOGO ALL the time.
✔️ I sent emails that built know-like-trust by providing real value and only offered discounts when it made sense \(International Women's Day, Spring arrival, etc\)

❌ Their flow emails were just more cutesy-sounding stuff that were triggered at the wrong time!
Like the welcome flow that was triggered 30 minutes later.
So new subscribers sat there with no follow-up.

✔️ I couldn’t stand the cutesy, smart-sounding brand stuff being sent at the wrong time. LOL.
So I just threw ALL their flows in the dustbin and set up my own.

Which is performing WAYYY much better.

Moral:

- Stick to proven fundamentals.
- Don’t try to sound smart and clever.
- Make it easy for people to say yes.

NOTE: I know saying "replacing image-heavy emails with plain-text emails" might seem like I'm hitting the hornet's nest in this group 😅

So, a little bit of a caveat. If you're going to send image-heavy emails, make sure they're built on direct-response principles.

Don't try to sound clever or smart, or try to be funny at the expense of clarity or persuasiveness.

Case in point:

The HIGHEST PERFORMING EMAIL OF THE MONTH for this win was actually a plain-text version of the LIVFRESH myth email that [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) shared in this group.

I shared how I used AI to translate that image-heavy email into a plaintext version in this post:
[https://www.skool.com/email-marketerz/turning-template-into-dr-style-plain-text-email?p=0578e7a3](https://www.skool.com/email-marketerz/turning-template-into-dr-style-plain-text-email?p=0578e7a3)

posts.title: Is this the laziest way to print money from your list?
posts.content:
What's up everyone👊🏻

Hope you all have an amazing day.

I just received this email from Carpe brand. They sell deodorants.

The email was super short and very pattern interrupting as it came probably from their founder.

I thought was worth sharing it with you.

Here's what he says:

SL: I'm not supposed to tell you this

whats up everyone,
wasn't supposed to tell you this but honestly it's too good not to.
our underarm antiperspirant is now clinically tested to last 100 hours!
anyways, I ran out of time to write a real email so here's a code for up to 40% off: \[code\]

Stay cool out there,
Declan

Sent from my iPhone

.......

They just want to spit out the USP of their product.

It starts with a curiosity line:

“Wasn’t supposed to tell you this… but honestly it’s too good not to.”

When you read that, your mind instantly wants to know what is it about.

Because curiosity is the strongest drug in the world.

Then he rewards that attention with the actual fact.

Shows the USP and ends it with credibility.

"our underarm antiperspirant is now clinically tested to last 100 hours!"

That's the benefit of their product. Or a problem solver said differently.

Everyone wants their armpits to stay dry and smell good for a freaking 3 days…

Stop sniffing their shirts, and just hang out with friends without giving a flip about bad smell or sweat marks.

Then he says:

“I ran out of time to write the email, so here’s the code for up to 40% off:”

Although he might be the founder, he "still" took the time to come back, drop a strong fact about the product, and say it himself to his list. Which shows that he "actually cares of his people".

And on top of that, he gives them a discount code, basically giving people a chance to test his 100-hour antiperspirant. - Especially those who have never bought before.

"Sent from my iPhone" - Wth - that might just be written on purpose bcs people who use iPhone have this underlined down their emails which shows that is written from a phone, which shows that is again written from a human to human from their phone.

I'm a huge fan of plain text emails coming from the founder or from the team and they actually print money when done right.

Curiosity . Fact. Reward.

I don’t know what the performance of this email was…

But it definitely grabs your attention.

And it’s worth trying.

The only thing I’d change is the first line.

I’d go with:“What’s up {first_name}”

Feels more personal, and it’s kind of a rule of thumb in email.

posts.title: Always test the offer, never assume..
posts.content:
The past few weeks we run an offer.

I had assumed based on what I heard that money off would work better than % off.

All cool... I turned on the offer with money off and days passed.

I noticed a significant drop. And I was confused of what happened.

Based on our play book and the offer vault we had seen from the past that % off had worked really well with us. And I went and A/B split test money off vs % off.

The % off wiped the floor with the money off offer.

Our conversion spiked.

Note that we run this test for only a few days just to validate the winner.

Then we changed the offer to another % off and we concluded the promo, and happy ending.

Lesson for you and myself: Every brands audience is different so always test before assuming.

One brand's audience might react different to a certain offer comparing to another brand. Always test test test test test.....

P.S. The pop up form is a quiz type one. Has a 5 sec pop up time and its full page format. This one had an image on the background paper ish style with the promo vibe for that season. Usually I leave it plain with just the offer.

posts.title: How To Get Unengaged People To Come Back?
posts.content:
I get this question all the time:

“How do you re-engage inactive subscribers?”

Here’s the truth: most of them aren’t coming back... And that’s okay.

Subscriber churn is inevitable. No one stays interested forever.

It doesn’t matter how great your emails are, some people will lose interest and stop opening.

This is why the real game isn’t about saving lost subscribers... It’s about constantly growing your list so you don’t feel the hit when some churn.

Instead of stressing over re-engagement, put your energy into bringing in new subscribers. That’s where the ROI is.

If someone hasn’t opened an email in 90 to 180 days, they’re pretty much gone. Think about it... 3 to 6 months of ignoring every email you send... that's a lot.

Let’s not sugarcoat it: Re-engaging past subscribers is HARD.

If I send to 50,000 unengaged profiles and manage to bring back only 10,000, that’s a win. But that still means 40,000 are dead weight and dragging your deliverability down.

How to Re-Engage Without Hurting Deliverability 👇

I don’t waste time chasing people who don’t care anymore. But I do have a system for low-effort re-engagement that keeps things clean.

1. Only Send to Your Engaged List \(95% of the Time\)

For most brands, I only send to people who’ve opened in the last 120 days.

If you’re outside of that window, you’re not getting emails. No point in tanking deliverability by blasting to people who don’t care.

2. Send One “All List” Email Per Month

1-2 times a month, I open up one send to the entire list, including unengaged profiles.

This is usually for a big sale, product launch, or restock.

Most won’t open. But some will. And that’s enough to re-engage without overcomplicating things.

3. Suppress Unengaged Profiles Once A Month

Keep your list clean and lower your Klaiviyo bill by suppressing your unengaged folk once a month and lowering your plan. You can always bring people back for big sale periods like Black Friday,

🎁 BONUS: Send This Email TODAY To Unengaged Non-Buyers

Sender Name: Founder First Name | Brand Name
Subject Line: “Hey, quick thought…”

Hi there,
It’s \[Founder Name\], the founder of \[Brand Name\].
I wanted to personally reach out and say thanks for checking out \[Brand Name\].
A lot of people come across us because they’re looking for \[specific problem your product solves\]—and I totally get it. That’s why I started \[Brand Name\] in the first place. \[Brief 1-2 sentence personal story about the brand’s origin or mission.\]
If you’re on the fence, no pressure. I just want to share a little about why customers love us:
\[Unique Selling Point #1\]\[Unique Selling Point #2\]\[Unique Selling Point #3\]
And - I just reactivated your welcome discount for 10% OFF. Just use code \[Discount Code\] at checkout.
Whenever you’re ready, I’d love for you to give us a try. Here’s a link to check out our bestsellers: \[Shop Bestsellers »\]
Thanks for being here—it means a lot.
\[Founder Name\]
P.S. If you have any questions or want a recommendation, just hit reply. I actually read these myself.

-------

TLDR; focus less on unengaged profiles and more on growing your list. Send campaigns to your engaged list and 1-2 times per month send to your whole list, some unengaged people will re-engage.

posts.title: Finding a NEW Winning Product with email, your approach?
posts.content:
Hey everyone! Got a situation I'd love your take on.

A client is about to launch a supplement line and hasn't decided which product to lead with. We're using email to figure that out before going all in on one SKU.

Here's the testing strategy I've put together:

1️⃣ Discovery
• Survey email asking customers which health goal matters most to them, incentivized with a reward
• Thank-you page survey post-purchase
• One-question post-popup survey

2️⃣ Testing Campaigns
• Collection email — all SKUs in one send, track which drives the most sales
• 4-way A/B split — each SKU as the hero in its own email, 25% of the list each, tracking clicks + conversions per product

3️⃣ Post-Purchase
• Upsell email right after purchase with the collection email, framed as VIP-exclusive. ,Track which drives the most sales
• One-click upsell via Shopify app

The goal is to let the data tell us which product to double down on the winning product.

What would you change or add? Have you done something similar to find a new winning SKU through email? 👇

posts.title: Click Rate suggestions
posts.content:
My client's click-rate is abysmally low.

Is there any way for me to bring it up?

We only use plaintext email.

And any pics we use will be a before/after images.

I know this is kinda vague, so if you need more context to answer my query, please let me know.

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
As you said, need a bit more context. But in my opinion, click rates are a vanity metric that I do not care about. All I care about is revenue. For example, you could have really low click rates but the people who click could be very high converting, and your placed order rate is fine. Also, naturally, as you send more emails, your click rates go down.

As long as you follow best practices like:
[ul][li]Having buttons high up in the email[li]Not having too many buttons that are conflicting[li]Keeping your email simple
Then I don't give too many shits about click rates. Some accounts just have low click rates. For this account, for example, there's going to be no way that you AB test your way to a 1% click rate. That's just not going to happen. If you want to artificially boost up your click rates, you can just by tightening your list. You could just send to a super super engaged list and get a 1% click rate, however you're going to be sacrificing revenue because you're sending to a smaller list. That's why I hate people stressing about click rates and optimizing for them because they often just shorten their list and leave money on the table because they're trying to make their click rates look good. No, they don't matter. Three things go into click rates:
[ol:1][li]Do you follow best design practices with button placement and simplicity[li]The content of your email - does it get people to click? Is it enticing enough to get them to click[li]The list that you send to
That's all that goes into it. But don't get too caught up in it if you're following the best practices.

posts.title: HIGH AOV
posts.content: Max your video of AOV brand came in really good time LOL. I'm currently dealing with AOV brand and doing pretty decent revenue around 30% but pop up conversion is 1.4% from PC and 3.8% from Mobile but it converts 18% with welcome flow. I would like to position my pop up form like you did and also build educational flows/campaigns. The pros of getting our products is around 5-10k in comparison to others and also monthly billing is reduced for 20% and also we offer fixed $150 discount so I just don't wanna overcomplicate in pop up so what are your thoughts how I should position pop up?

comments.content:
Yooo what's up man! Wanted to chime in bc this is up my alley but [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) could give you the final confirmation.

So what you need to know first is that at this AOV, the popup's job isn't to sell. It's actually just to capture the email lol. Nobody is impulse-buying a $5-10k product from a popup. Your welcome flow is where the real selling happens, and at 18% conversion it's clearly working. The bottleneck is really just getting more people into it.

Your instinct to keep the popup simple is right, but the question is which ONE thing gets the most opt-ins, not how to fit everything on there.

$150 off a $5-10k product is only 1.5-3%, so that's not really moving anyone off the fence.

Save it for the welcome flow where it works as a bonus on top of everything else. The $5-10k savings vs competitors is your strongest value prop overall, but it needs context and trust to land. That's a welcome flow job across multiple emails, not a popup job.

The 20% reduced monthly billing might actually be your best popup angle because if customers are paying monthly, that's tangible and ongoing. So something like "See how our members save 20% on monthly payments" is pretty specific enough imo to be intriguing but simple enough for a popup. If that doesn't fit your model, a clean lead magnet works well at this price point.

On the desktop bit, 1.4% is low but desktop always underperforms mobile. Before changing the offer, just do a check of the basics: does clicking outside dismiss the popup? Are buttons and inputs big enough? Does the design feel premium enough for a $5-10k product? Sometimes the gap is UX, not positioning. Lmk your thoughts though bro [@Vukasin Milanovic](obj://user/b4d875d4382c47668bbb091b9e9a48f3)

They had some flows but I made new welcome flow, cart abandonment and now I'm working on other ones...\(also I built 1 campaign which they weren't doing at all and did 4k\) but I really liked the idea of doing a lot of education about products so I will focus a lot on that with campaigns because I had around 50% open rate and also with other flows I'll put education mostly. [@Vukasin Milanovic](obj://user/b4d875d4382c47668bbb091b9e9a48f3) $31k in 13 days vs their previous $20k/month means the infrastructure is clearly working. And your instinct to test instead of rip and replace is spot on bro.

On the education hesitation, it's not about replacing what's converting, it's more so just about reaching the people who aren't.

At $5-10k AOV, a lot of those people aren't saying no, they're just not ready yet fr. They need more trust and proof before committing to that number. The way to test it is this: don't touch your current welcome emails at all. Add educational content AFTER the existing sequence ends. Current flow stays identical for quick buyers, slower-decision people get more runway. Track over 60-90 days since purchases at this AOV take time.

Your abandoned cart flow is actually where education fits most naturally because someone who added a $5-10k product to cart is high intent. They were close but something held them back. At this price point, that's almost always a trust or comparison hesitation. After your initial cart reminder, try adding a "here's why customers choose us" or some kind of testimonial email. You're answering the exact objection that stopped them.

And don't sleep on campaigns too 😂. $4k from one send with zero campaign history means that list is sitting on untapped revenue. At 50% open rates your audience is hungry for content. Build a consistent calendar and that becomes your biggest growth lever.

posts.title: A Flow Most Brands Neglect..
posts.content:
What's going on guys.

For out-of-stock flows for subscription brands, most send something like "Unfortunately, we've run into an unexpected delay. We apologize for the inconvenience."

It's super corporate, cold, and now you've just made the subscriber more anxious about their subscription.

That email doesn't just deliver bad news; it reminds them they're paying for something. If that reminder feels confusing or impersonal, then you just created a churn trigger for yourself.

I just rebuilt this flow for a client. And here's what changed:

[ol:1][li]Tone. Sent from the founder, not the brand. Subject line is calm and personal, it's "Quick heads up about your next order" NOT "Important update regarding your subscription." One honest sentence beats three paragraphs of corporate damage control.

2. Subscription clarity. The old copy said "we've paused your delivery" which made it sound like the entire subscription was frozen. In reality, only the out-of-stock item pauses, and other products on the same subscription still ship normally. Getting this wrong creates support tickets, while getting it right builds trust.

3. One-click Skip and Delay buttons right in the email. This is the move most brands miss. When a subscriber sees an OOS notification, they're in a "something's off with my order" kind of mindset. If the only option is just a generic "manage subscription" link that dumps them into a portal, most won't bother, and they'll just cancel on the spot. Skip and Delay buttons give them instant control without leaving the email, and that control is what prevents the cancellation impulse.

4. Mission-driven close. Instead of ending with an apology, just remind them why they subscribed. What their subscription means and what impact they're making. Reframe the moment from "your order has a problem" to "you're part of something that matters and we've got this handled."

An out-of-stock email shouldn't feel like a problem notice. A good one should feel like a brand that respects you enough to be honest, gives you control, and reminds you why you're here.

posts.title: 💥Massive Win... While Warming
posts.content:
Just wrapped up month 1 with a new client and wanted to share the process because the results speak for themselves.

Client runs an e-commerce store doing solid revenue — but their email was basically dead. Everything was landing in promotions, deliverability was wrecked, and they had zero proper tracking. They were leaving serious money on the table every single day.

Here's what we did:

→ Migrated them off their old ESP to Klaviyo
→ Cleaned the list and fixed sender reputation
→ Built out a proper warming sequence before sending at volume
→ Started conservative — welcome flow + campaigns only until warming was complete
→ Held off on ALL other flows until inbox placement was confirmed

The discipline of the warm-up is what most people skip. They want to blast the list immediately and wonder why open rates tank.

Results after 30 days:
✅ $501,159 in email attributed revenue
✅ 58.88% of total store revenue driven by email
✅ 54% total revenue growth YoY
✅ 48%+ open rates — landing in primary inbox

And this is with just a welcome flow. We're now rolling out all the other flows.

The ceiling hasn't been hit yet.

posts.title: Discount Codes In AB Cart/Check
posts.content:
Wondering if we should be using Static discounts or dynamic in AB cart/checkout.

Love the mystery discount but how does this work moving forward?

Setting static codes to one use per customer would keep them from abusing it - but then they won't be able to get a discount on future abandonments.

comments.content:
Have separate branches in your flow for new v.s repeat customers.... my returning customers don't get any discount \(though technically they could reuse the code from the new customer flow i guess...\).

I suppose the Q is do you want to keep offering discounts to your customers? I'm not a fan of doing it much beyond the 1st purchase personally

user.name: Michael Gorodi
user.bio: A copywriter based out of Koh Samui, Thailand - just living the island life and enjoying being a student of the craft.

comments.content:
Dynamic codes for flows, static codes for promos.

The logic is this: when you have a promo or a flash sale going on, you kinda want to let people share the static discount code around in the socials and stuff. And hope that you get as much sale before the deadline.

Dynamic works great in flows because you want it to be as personalized as possible.

Things like welcome flow and abandoned cart flows, especially the 1st email, has a personalized element to it. And having a personalized code just for you is great.

Also, we dont want people to share a static discount code that has literally no expiry date in bargain websites for the masses to use, do we?

posts.title: Offers For Subscription Brands
posts.content:
This is the kind of offer for sales you should be running for subscription brands!!! @channel

Say you're running a 20% OFF Spring Sale...

And you offer 20% OFF on subscriptions regularly...

That means with the Spring sale you are giving away 40% OFF subscriptions OR 20% OFF if you buy one time.

Often times brands will just say "20% OFF" but that doesn't show the value of the subscription offer...

Major missed opportunity.

For any sale your run as a subscription brand, you should be separating subscription and one-time and making it clear the extra value you get from subscribing.

Ex. 40% OFF when you subscribe or 20% OFF one-time purchases with code SPRING

posts.title: Welcome Offer Question 🤔
posts.content:
I'm wondering what you guys think of these two options for a welcome offer. Obviously need to test but would like some feedback.

Current Offer: 15% Off of a $40 hat ~$6 Off

Potential New Offer: Buy a $40 hat receive a $35 Blank T-shirt free ~T shirts are roughly $8 to produce

We lose out on $2 of profit per purchase with this offer, but I think the T-shirt offer is much closer to "banger" territory so I think more people will buy increasing total profit AND I think in the long run this will increase our LTV with blanks being a very common repeat purchase item.

Thoughts? Thank you guys!

user.name: Wes Dwyer
user.bio: College student looking to launch email marketing for e-commerce business

comments.content:
What's going on [@Wes Dwyer](obj://user/cf33186c223b45c7a418db9b024130d3) good question!

Your instinct is in the right place here man, but free tee wins 100%. Genuinely just because of the perceived value of it. $6 off feels like $6 off. A free $35 tee feels like a steal but it only costs you 8 bucks to produce. That gap between what it costs you and what it feels like to the customer is what makes GWP offers hit so much harder than percentage discounts imo.

The LTV angle is really smart because you're basically just turning your welcome offer into a product sampling play. If the tee is good enough that someone wants more of them, then you've now just created a repeat purchase pathway that 15% off a hat never could.

But there are a few things to test on this though. Make sure that the $2 difference accounts for the added shipping weight too. The tee quality has to be crazy impressive, because the whole LTV thesis falls apart if it's a throwaway.

And think through the execution too on top of that. A GWP is more complex than a discount code. So how does the tee get added to cart? How does the customer pick their size? How does your popup explain the offer clearly? The worst-case scenario is you letting a great offer die because the checkout experience was confusing.

Also you might alr know this, but make sure to A/B test your welcome flow 50/50. Run it 4-6 weeks, but don't just compare initial conversion. You should track both groups out to 60-90 days and compare repeat purchase rate and LTV. That's actually the real test of whether the sampling play works.

I really do think the tee offer wins here but that's just my gut 😂. Let the data confirm it!

user.name: Marcos Morrone
user.bio: Dev

replies.content:
[@Marcos Morrone](obj://user/4ae96b6c0f0944c88ef982e4e8c3051f) Free shipping is a powerful hook, but the 4 second timing is still the likely culprit for that 25% drop in CVR.
​
Think of it this way: this is cold traffic, and at 4 seconds, the page visitor hasn't even decided if they want the product yet, and you’re already asking them to solve a shipping problem they didn't know they had. You're essentially 'gating' a basic perk behind an email opt-in before they’ve even seen the price or the benefits.

​A few ways to keep the 'Free Shipping' hook without killing the CVR:

​Move it to a Sticky Header: If you want them to know shipping is free, put it in a top announcement bar. It’s always visible but never intrusive.

​The 'Teaser' Approach: Instead of a full-screen pop-up, use a small 'bubble' or 'fly-out' in the bottom corner that says 'Get Free Shipping on this order.' It lets them shop while keeping the offer available when they’re ready.

​instead of 4 seconds, you can try to switch to 'Exit-Intent': If they are leaving the site without buying, that could be a good time to 'save' the sale with a 'Wait! We'll give you Free Shipping if you finish your order now' pop-up.

Also, keep in mind the Attribution Trap.
Your pop-up is seeing an 11.4% opt-in and 31M ARS in revenue, which looks great on paper. But because it triggers so early \(4 seconds\), it’s likely capturing people who were already going to buy. They see the 'Free Shipping' offer, sign up, and finish their purchase.
​The email flow/pop up gets 100% of the credit for that sale, making the pop-up look like a hero. But since your overall site CVR dropped from 3.7% to 2.8%, it’s a sign that for every 1 person the pop-up 'converts,' it’s potentially annoying 3 or 4 others into bouncing.

I'd try to test one pop up triggeres when there is exit intent and one with 4 second trigger. See what happens.

Hope this helps. Keep us updated. Good luck.

Hey everyone,

I read a tweet from Max regarding adding images in SMS messages, which can result in more revenue.

Curious what type of images are usually performing for you here. Is it more offer, product or meme related?

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
Nice question [@Pieter and Timo](obj://user/8d3921e72466401f85622a3de923a1d3)! In this case, it really just depends on what the send is doing imo.

Product-in-context images usually hit the hardest from what I've personally seen. Like the product being used in real life, not a catalog shot. You're gonna want it to feel authentic, like something a friend would text you.

For promos it's way more straightforward. A simple graphic with the offer front and center will get the job done. Let the subscriber see the "25% off" text before they even read the rest of copy. The image will do the selling, and the text will stay short.

Memes and casual stuff are great for keeping your list warm between promos. And depending on the brand, they can actually drive sales too. Especially if the humor ties back to a specific product.

I'd mix all three based on the purpose of the send and just save the image sends for when the visual actually adds something \(like promos, launches, and drops\). Quick conversational texts also work fine as plain SMS at a fraction of the cost!

posts.title: Rotating offers in campaigns
posts.content:
Hey guys,

Max mentioned in the classrooms that the 90-day engaged segment usually drives around 80–90% of total campaign revenue.

Right now, we’re rotating \(and testing\) offers quite a lot, with about 8-10 offers in rotation. For example:
[ul][li]weekend 1: BOGO[li]weekend 2: store credit[li]etc

I’m wondering if this is actually the best approach, or if it would make more sense to focus on a smaller set of proven offers \(say top 3–4\) and rotate those more consistently, for example monthly.

Thanks in advance!

user.name: Pieter and Timo
user.bio: Scaling our ecom brand

comments.content:
Hey [@Pieter and Timo](obj://user/8d3921e72466401f85622a3de923a1d3) your instincts are right on this one tbh.

The main issue with 8-10 offers is that you're spreading your data so thin that you can't actually learn what's working. Each offer only comes around once every couple months, and by then your audience has shifted enough that you can't tell if the offer drove the result or if something else did. You're basically just testing without getting any real answers.

I think 3-4 core offers is the sweet spot here but instead of rotating randomly, just give each one a job. You could have one for urgency, one for increasing AOV, one for reactivating people going cold, and one flexible slot for seasonal or launch moments.

The specific offers are gonna depend on your margins and product, but each one should exist for a reason.

Also if every campaign is offer-driven, then you might be training your list to only buy on discount. The best-performing brands I've seen mix in plenty of non-promotional sends \(like content, social proof, new arrivals, behind-the-scenes stuff\) so that when an offer does land, it actually feels like an event. The mix I'd recommend is roughly 60-70% value content, 30-40% promotional. That protects full-price purchasing behavior while making your offers hit harder when they do go out. Lmk your thoughts!

posts.content:
For some context, the list is not exactly 0. It's around 40k. I worked with this brand when my friend owned it and he actually built it from nothing to 130k months before he sold. I stayed on for emails but the new owner tanked the rev which tanked my take because I was doing performance based. And he never paid me lol.

Anyways the new owner reached out to my friend who built the brand to ramp it back up again and is taking me on for emails. The list was pretty engaged when I was running it and was clearing 25-30% attribution during the glory months. There have been absolutely 0 marketing emails for like 5 months, and when I start back up with campaigns, I'm gonna have to do some interesting segmentation. Normally I'd do winbacks, 90 day engaged etc. but there's been no data for a while so I'm not sure what trajectory to take. Does anybody have any suggestions on how to properly segment this list so I'm not getting smacked with spam, bounces and unsubs?

Should I see how the flows perform for 15-30 days before I run campaigns and segment from there?

user.name: Brandon Teyf
user.bio: Founder of Got Mail Media, specializing in email and sms marketing for health & wellness and luxury boutique brands.

comments.content:
There's a thread about a topic when I asked a similar question when I wanted to re-engage suppressed profiles, here's what I ended up doing.

[ul][li]Split list into 5k chunks [li]Ran each chunk through NeverBounce to remove dead emails [li]Wrote a plain text founder email saying 'we miss you'. You could word it more like 'sorry for blanking you'[li]Sent the email to each chunk on a drip send

Worked well for me and some of the profiles in this list were up to 10 years old.

In your case I would say yeah, run high-engagement flows for a little bit to build up some opens before sending campaigns.

posts.title: Your POV on segmentation + Tip to get great copy data:
posts.content:
Fam, I am onboarding a new client and what I typically do first as part of the research is surveying the purchasers and non purchasers. I incentivise them with discount code + entry to a giveaway to get as much feedback as possible. My goal with surveys is:

[ul][li]Understand why non purchasers didn't purchase and key objections[li]Enrol them into purchasing after submitting the form with high incentive[li]Understand why customers purchased[li]Feedback on the product/price[li]How they use the product[li]\(FUN PART\) I ask them as many simple questions that I can turn into stats/infographics to position the brand as top dawg pro max. E.g. 9/10 customers report our product solve their problem. I also use this data and add it after I get key feedback in non purchasers survey like hesitation etc, to create social proof and trust in survey itself so they are not just feeling heard and saying what they didn't buy, I'm also getting them through a mini sales funnel they didn't expect. 

Now, brand I do this for atm is around for 3 years, and they have around 70k purchasers.

I'd love to send a survey to everyone but honestly I'm a bit sceptical on how to go about it, as from purchasers in last 180 days 40k are engaged.

So I'm thinking:

[ul][li]Do I send to everyone and see what's going to happen \(they are sending 4 campaigns a month atm to 180 engaged and getting 55% OR but CRS is on average 0.13% and almost no sales from campaigns a month\)[li]Send to purchasers engaged in the last 180 days

Curios on your POV Fam [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d)

user.name: Jan Uroda
user.bio: Looking for 7+ figure founders who are genuinely interested in serving the world to make more impact.

comments.content:
Yo, right on, brother, great idea. I love surveys and then being able to leverage this data. People love numbers and buying from numbers.

I would start small, send to people who bought between 30 and 60 days ago, or whenever the honeymoon phase is, where people are still excited about their product. They're more likely to respond and more likely to give positive feedback. You only really need to send to 10,000 people, and you might get enough people to respond. Maybe start with just a smaller group, see how many responses you get, and then you can move to bigger if you want to, but definitely start with newer people first.

posts.title: High ticket welcome flow
posts.content: So I nearly always add a 'your discount expires tomorrow' email to a welcome flow \(even if it's a static code\) and usually it's after 10-14 days. But I've just onboarded a high ticket brand with AOV around $6,000, not sure how long to wait until creating urgency around this code as the decisions process will be a lot longer. What do you guys think?

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
Yoo what's good [@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)! The first thing I'd figure out is how does this brand actually close sales. If $6k purchases usually involve a consultation or a long sales cycle, the welcome flow's job is to drive that booking, not push a discount to checkout. That's gonna change everything.

But assuming it is direct-to-checkout, the whole flow needs to be longer and different at this AOV. I'd say around 30+ days and heavy on trust-building imo. Got to answer why is this worth $6k? The craftsmanship, social proof from real buyers, the brand story, content that answers the objections someone has before spending that kind of money.

Also on the urgency email, if it's a static code that doesn't actually expire, I'd question whether the "expires tomorrow" part belongs at this price point at all tbh. Buyers spending that much bread can usually spot fake or manufactured urgency. If you want real urgency, just use a unique code that genuinely expires.

At this AOV, the behavioral triggers are going to outperform any timed sequence. Someone browsing a product page three times tells you 10x more about purchase readiness than "it's been 14 days." I'd say just let the welcome flow build trust in the background, and then let their behavior trigger the conversion emails.

posts.title: Tip: "Random Discount Codes"
posts.content:
Most stores run codes like WELCOME10 or SAVE15.

Clean, easy to remember...and that's exactly the problem.

When a customer sees WELCOME10, they know it's permanent...there's no reason to buy now... they'll come back when they're ready, and that code will still be there.

Test this instead: use a code that looks random. Something like "HI-4XY7G"

It's slightly harder to type for the customer, yes...

But now when you write "your custom discount code expires in 24 hours," the customer believes it.

The code looks one-time and generated for them and the urgency becomes real.

Instead of "use code WELCOME10 for 10% off," you write "your custom discount code HI-4XY7G expires in 24 hours."

Use this in your welcome, abandonment flows, your win-back flows, and any campaign where urgency is doing the conversion work.

Results vary by brand, so run it as an actual split test before rolling it out everywhere.
