posts.title: Popup Strategy Question- Effectiveness and Tradeoffs
posts.content:
Hey everyone,
Quick question about popups and conversion
I added a popup on my site offering 10% off for first purchase. I can see people are signing up, but they’re not converting. When I tested it myself, I noticed the email with the discount code goes to the Promotions tab in Gmail and not the primary inbox.

I’m considering showing the discount code directly on the last step of the popup instead of sending it by email. On one hand it might reduce friction and help conversion, but on the other hand it could lead to low quality signups or people just grabbing the code without real intent. Would love to hear from your experience what kind of popup setup actually drives real purchases and not just email signups
Another thing I’m struggling with is pricing and brand perception. Up until now I barely used discounts because I’m trying to build a more premium brand. Now that I introduced a 10% first purchase offer, I’m worried I might be training customers to expect discounts and hurting the perceived value of the product.

It also creates weird situations. If an existing customer reaches out and wants to buy again, it feels unfair not to give them the same price as new customers. On top of that, some existing customers might just sign up again with a different email, which breaks the data and makes it harder to track real returning customers
Would love to hear how you approach this. Do you see first time discounts as a must in ecommerce or something that depends on the brand, and how do you balance between conversion and brand value over time

Thanks a lot 🙏

user.name: Nitzan Brown
user.bio: Owner of We’re Creatures perfumes

comments.content:
It's probably best for user experience to have the discount code at the end of the pop-up, so it's right there; however, you probably need to fix your deliverability a little bit. If you give people the discount code at the end of the pop-up, then they have no reason to go check their email and get you opens.

What I would do is I would tell people at the end of the pop-up, "Hey, discount code is in your inbox. Check your spam and promos tab." Then just do that, and then in the email, when you deliver it, request that people reply to the email. Maybe say, "Reply yes to be eligible for future offers," something like that, or just say, "Reply this and let us know what you're looking for out of the product," something to get replies to help your deliverability and try to get you in the primary inbox. It's getting harder and harder over time to get out of the promo tab, so don't trip about it too much.

For pricing and brand perception, literally every brand discounts, so take that with what you will. It's your choice as a brand owner, though. You can do some sort of free gift if you want, instead of percent off or dollar off. Some sort of free gift can work well. Maybe it's like a keychain or something with purchase. You can try to advertise that so it's like a bonus and it's not discounting. Maybe that's the happy medium.

posts.title: Should I panic?
posts.content:
I onboarded a client late last month and started sending flows and campaigns earlier this month.

But Subscriber Growth seems to be going down.

Is this something I should panic over?

The previous email marketing team was sending emails 1-3 times a week. Image-heavy email. And was sending promo emails quite often.

Pop-up forms are doing well in capturing new subscribers. But exclusions far outweigh the new subs.

Is this a bad sign? If so, how do we navigate this issue?

CC: [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d)

user.name: Suraj Punjabi
user.bio: Direct Response Email Copywriter.

comments.content:
Keep a close eye on your unsubscribe reports. Every brand is different, but I will attach a screenshot of a good rule of thumb for frequency of campaigns. Actually from the goat himself [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) .

I did have the same issue with a brand I stopped working for a few months ago. All the campaigns were $ off or % off and the customers just got super used to discounts so when you try to throw some education or literally anything else than a sale, it's kinda natural that they won't perform that well. You have to train your audience. [@Esper Manuputty](obj://user/768aea91949b4d5f955d34bf931b9dce) made a sick .pdf guide from Max's info that you can plug into chatgpt or claude or whatever to help you actually make a solid campaign calendar and not rely on discount emails for revenue.

Another thing that is really important is segmentation. Please please do not blast the entire email list for every campaign. I made the same mistake starting out and learned the hard way. Make sure to have at the very least a 90 day engaged segment and a suppress list. This will limit the amount of bounces, unsubs and spam complaints. There are definitely more segments to build out, but start with these.

90 day engaged:
[ul][li]Someone can receive email marketing because person is subscribed[li]AND[li]Someone has Opened Email at least once in the last 90 days[li]OR [li]Someone has been Active on Site at least once in the last 90 days[li]OR [li]Someone has Placed An Order at least once in the last 90 days

Suppress:
[ul][li]Someone can receive email marketing because person is subscribed[li]AND[li]Someone has received email at least 5 times over all time[li]AND[li]Someone has opened email zero times in the last 365 days[li]OR[li]Someone has bounced email at least 3 times over all time[li]OR[li]Someone has marked email as spam at least once over all time

Your client will probably have questions as to why the numbers tanked, but come prepared with an answer and be confident in your response. In my opinion it is probably due to the high frequency of sale/discount email campaigns which I'm guessing your sending a lot less frequently now. The good part is your list is growing. Keep an eye on the pop-up as well. Make sure you're a/b testing it as well.

posts.title: You May Already Know This but it's Still a Banger!
posts.content:
What's up guys! As we know, most back-in-stock flows are usually just one email. They'll have a nice branded design, product photos, an "it's back!" headline, and that's it.

That first email is fine.

It does its job. But the people who didn't convert on it will need something different.

A complete shocker from the brand.

What's been working really well for me is simply adding a second email to the flow. Genuinely just a plain text email from the founder. The vibe has to read something along the lines of "hey, I know you've been waiting on this — it's back and ready to ship."

I believe this works super well because the first email will feel like a brand talking AT you. Whereas the second one feels like a person talking to you. That shift alone is going to re-engage people who tuned out the first send.

A few things you can do to make sure it lands correctly:

[ul][li]Send it from the founder's actual name and email \(use support as the reply-to\) [li]Keep it short, ideally around 4-6 sentences max [li]Acknowledge the wait. If something was out of stock for weeks, lean on that. It'll build trust[li]Close with something human, not salesy

Here's what one of these looks like in practice \(the screenshot attached, brand covered\).

Everyone here is already super smart, so this may have been on your radar. It's a simple addition to the flow, but it catches the people that Email 1 missed.

posts.title: Klaviyo segmentation
posts.content:
Hi guys, I have a question about Klaviyo segmentation.

We want to segment customers by LTV, but using real net revenue after returns/refunds, not the revenue shown in Klaviyo before returns are taken into account.

Is it possible to send that value into Klaviyo via Shopify metafields or another custom property?

For example, I checked one customer — in Klaviyo, her revenue is showing as 58k, but in Shopify, her real post-return revenue is only 7,683 PLN.

We’d like to use this value to differentiate flows in Klaviyo.

Has anyone done something similar, and what would be the best setup?

Thank you for the help.

comments.content:
Hey what's up Matt. This might be one of Klaviyo's most annoying gaps tbh.

The reason you're seeing $58k in Klaviyo vs 7,683 PLN in Shopify is because Klaviyo counts revenue at the time of purchase and never subtracts refunds. Shopify does, so the numbers will always be a bit off for customers who return a lot.

To your direct question, you actually can push real net revenue into Klaviyo as a custom profile property, but Shopify metafields don't automatically sync there. I believe you'd need either a dev to set up a webhook that updates a "Net_LTV" property on the Klaviyo profile whenever a refund happens, or a no-code route like Shopify Flow connected to Klaviyo's API. Once that property exists, you can then just segment by it and use it in flow splits.

Before going that route though check Klaviyo's predictive analytics. There's a metric called Historic CLV that already accounts for full refunds, and you can segment by it out of the box.

The only catch is that it only covers fully refunded orders, not partial refunds, and you need at least 500 customers with orders plus 180 days of history for it to activate. If your returns are mostly full refunds, Historic CLV might get you close enough without any dev work. If it's a mix of full and partial, then the custom property route is the way to go imo.

posts.title: Klaviyo issue
posts.content:
Hey everyone :\)
Happy to be here. Even just going through the course, I’m already realizing how much email revenue potential I’ve been leaving on the table.

I run a perfume brand with a pretty unique concept. We create fragrances inspired by illustrated characters. Kind of a mix between scent, art, and storytelling.

I’ve built an email list of around 1,600 people. About 800 are customers, and around 800 came from a US pre-order waiting list.
Now I’m stuck with a Klaviyo issue.

I don’t want to pay for those ~800 waiting list profiles as active profiles since they’re not relevant right now. But when I try to suppress them, Klaviyo won’t let me.
On top of that:
[ul][li]I can’t contact support because I’m not on a paid plan[li]And I can’t upgrade without paying based on all active profiles, including the ones I’m trying to remove
So I’m stuck in a loop.
I even deleted the waiting list, but those profiles still count as active.
Has anyone dealt with this before or found a workaround?

Appreciate any help 🙏

user.name: Nitzan Brown
user.bio: Owner of We’re Creatures perfumes

comments.content:
Hi Nitzan! First some good news: This is a very solvable problem :\)

To clarify, suppressing profiles in Klaviyo does actually remove them from your active profile count and your billing. So suppression is exactly what you want here.

Since you deleted the list itself, the profiles are still floating in your account \(because deleting a list only removes the grouping, not the actual profiles\). So to suppress them, you need to re-identify them. Try creating a segment with conditions like "has placed order zero times" combined with "date added" around when your waiting list was built. If the waiting list was collected through a specific form, you might also be able to filter by signup source for a more exact match. But before suppressing, double-check the segment to make sure it only contains the profiles you want gone, because you don't want to accidentally sweep up checkout abandoners or other non-customers who might still convert.

Once you have the right segment, you can bulk suppress it from the three-dot menu on the segment or through Account Settings > Profile Maintenance. After suppressing, you'll then need to manually downgrade your billing plan to reflect the lower profile count because Klaviyo doesn't auto-downgrade unless you've enabled that setting.

If you're still hitting a wall with suppression, it would help to know the specific error you're seeing, and that will make it easier to troubleshoot.

And before you suppress all 800, keep in mind those people signed up for a pre-order waiting list, which means they raised their hand. So depending on how long ago that was, it might be worth sending a small test batch \(of 100-200 profiles\) a "we're live" kind of email before suppressing the rest. If the engagement is decent, then you've just converted warm leads instead of losing them. If it tanks, suppress and move on.

Feel free to let me know your thoughts and how the fix goes!

user.name: Aven Tedros
user.bio:
Founder of Magtania, specializing in retention & lifecycle marketing for the pet care industry.

Believe you can achieve it, and you're halfway there.

replies.content:
[@Aven Tedros](obj://user/3815b1a10ede4b02ab650aa68e2dd5f6) Hey Aven, really appreciate the detailed reply, thanks a lot man.

do you know if suppressing profiles only works on a paid plan? I’m wondering if that’s why it’s not letting me do it at all.

The one thing all the profiles I want to suppress have in common is that I imported them from an external list, from a Meta lead form campaign.

Another idea I had was to just open a fresh Klaviyo account and sync it again from my Shopify store. Not sure if that would actually fix it though.

And yeah, great idea about testing a “we’re live” email on a small batch of those pre-order leads, thanks!! 🙏

user.name: Nitzan Brown
user.bio: Owner of We’re Creatures perfumes

replies.content:
[@Nitzan Brown](obj://user/8ae83ec2c9804915ae66c2709b4c146b) On suppression part, I honestly can't 100% confirm that the free plan blocks suppression. One thing I'd try is instead of suppressing profiles one by one, go to Account Settings, then Profile Maintenance and just suppress a whole segment from there. That might get around the wall you're hitting.

And knowing they came from a Meta lead form import gives us a way better filter. Even though you deleted the list, those profiles probably still carry a "$source" property that may say something like "CSV Import." Try making a segment where the source matches that and the person has placed zero orders. That should pull up exactly the ones you want.
The fresh account idea does actually work here too.

When you connect a new Klaviyo account to Shopify, it only pulls in profiles that live in Shopify. Your Meta imports wouldn't come with it since they were never in Shopify to begin with. The only actual downside is you'd lose any flows, templates, or history you've already set up. If you're still early and haven't built much, it might honestly be the fastest move. Keep in mind though that Shopify will also sync over people who checked out but never opted into marketing, and those still count as active profiles. So you'd want to suppress those right away.

Both paths get you there. Suppression in your current account is cleaner if you can get it working. Fresh account is the reset button if not.

posts.title: Easy Way to Boost Trust + Opens
posts.content:
Hey guys, a simple one that most brands either overlook or half-commit to:

Stop sending campaigns from "[info@yourbrand.com](mailto:info@yourbrand.com)" or just your brand name.

Switch your sender name to something like "Josh from \[Brand\]" and your sender email to a real person's address at the company. Your emails will feel like they're coming from a human \(which builds trust and drives replies\), and those replies actually feed your sender reputation with ESPs, which helps deliverability long-term.

Also make sure to set the reply-to as the brand's support email so the person whose name you're using doesn't get flooded lol. You'll get the personal feel without the operational headache that way.

I made this switch for a client and watched open rates steadily climb within the first few weeks.

It's not a magic bullet at all, but it's one of the easiest wins you can implement in 2 minutes!

user.name: Aven Tedros
user.bio:

Believe you can achieve it, and you're halfway there.

user.name: Samuel Hanono
user.bio: Founder at Rettain: helping 7-9 figure brands scale profitably

replies.content:
Great question bro, and not everything haha. I just use it across campaigns and any relationship-driven flows \(like a welcome, winback, post-purchase, sunset, basically anything where the goal is to feel like a real conversation\). That's where the trust and reply-rate benefits kick in.

For transactional stuff though like order confirmations and shipping notifications, I keep it as the brand name. Customers expect those to come from the company, not a person. A human name on a shipping confirmation isn't the end of the world but also isn't ideal imo.

It's all about consistency too. So if you go with a personal sender name, keep it the same person across every touchpoint where you use it. Switching between different names on different flows creates a weird experience for the subscriber.

posts.title: Attribution Question
posts.content:
Hey guys,

I am struggling to come to agreement with my clients about attribution. For most of my clients, there are multiple sources of marketing to acquire the client \(Meta and google ads\).

The issue that clients are bringing up is double attribution. If the customer saw an email, clicked it, then 5 hours later clicked an ad, the attribution would go to the ad and klaviyo. I have advised my clients to get on triple whale or an equivalent tracker because Klaviyo obviously has an incentive to over attribute.

For me, this has been like pulling teeth. Does anyone have any recommendations for a fair method of attribution to put me on the right track? Also, what window of attribution are you guys operating on? I have mine set to defaults.

user.name: Brandon Teyf
user.bio: Founder of Got Mail Media, specializing in email and sms marketing for health & wellness and luxury boutique brands.

comments.content:
Yo yo! Props to you for bringing this up because this is probably the most important conversation you can have with your clients. I'd say you wrestling with this puts you ahead of the pack.

I'd personally frame it like this:

Before anything else man, you should first tighten your Klaviyo attribution windows. The defaults are where most of the inflation lives, and the 5-day open window is the biggest reason for that. Post-iOS 15, Apple's Mail Privacy Protection generates opens on emails people never actually looked at, and Klaviyo actually counts those as touch points. So basically a customer could "open" your email without ever seeing it, buy through a Meta ad 3 days later, and Klaviyo would claim the sale.

I'd move to 0-day open, 1-day click attribution. That way you're only measuring revenue from people who actually clicked your emails and then purchased. Your numbers will drop but whatever's left over form that is real and you can frame that authentically \(which a client would respect tbh\).

Second thing is that the Triple Whale recommendation is solid, but you've got to frame it to your client as a cross-channel lens, not an actual replacement for Klaviyo reporting. No single platform is gonna give you ground truth. What you want here is directional agreement across multiple views. This can be: Klaviyo \(click-only\) for email-specific performance, Triple Whale or Northbeam for blended cross-channel attribution, and Shopify as the baseline sanity check.

Thirdly \(the most important point\) is that you want to be the one who proactively lowers your own numbers. If you wait for the client to install Triple Whale and discover the gap themselves, you're gonna lose all trust overnight. If you're the one who tightens the attribution because you want to report on revenue you actually drove, then you'll become the most credible partner they have.

Lmk your thoughts but given your situation from what you've told me this seems like the best way to roll!

posts.title: This thank you email printsss 💸
posts.content:
Wanted to share a banger for inspo from the man himself [@Max Sturtevant](obj://user/03f98e3139ef4e74a1a648742b9b2c1d) so you guys can get your post purchase dialed in.

It's an easy plain text email you can set up coming from the founder. Just a genuine thank you message with P.S. section on the bottom that's positioned as a subtle upsell.

Have seen this work wonders for accounts.

If you aren't already aware, the moment someone buys from you \(aside from the welcome series\) is probably one of the biggest times your customer is engaged. So getting an easy touchpoint in along with a subtle push is huge. Open rates go as high as 70% in some cases I've seen. Even better if it comes from the founder.

Specifically have tested this email with a hyperlink like the screenshot attached vs a dynamic product block on the bottom. Both work are great to try it out.

And if you want to get the rest of your post purchase series optimized, you can also consider having splits between first time, 2nd time, 3rd time, and 4+ \(VIP\) buyers with the language personalized to where they are in their journey.

All of these are super low lift, plain text. Can obviously test it against branded designs but plain text from the founder always seem to hit lol

For 2nd and 3rd time buyers you can also intro a discount to drive more impulse buys while they're still warm.

Anyways, there's my brief yap session about post purchase flows. Lmk if you have any questions!

posts.title: Evoking Better Emotions in Billing Order Emails
posts.content:
What's up guys!! When it comes to subscription billing reminder emails, there's a ton of rightful emphasis on having skip & delay buttons \(which is a non-negotiable\)..

But here's what most brands get wrong with the actual email copy:

It reads like a warning from collections. Like "Hey, just a heads up we're about to charge you."

That tone there makes the customer feel like they forgot something, not like they chose something.

The fix is to flip the frame entirely.

So instead of reminding them about a charge, just remind them of why they subscribed in the first place. Lead with the mission, the impact, and the benefit they're getting.

Here's what that looks like in practice for one of my clients, a plant-based dog food brand. The billing reminder opens with what the customer has accomplished since subscribing: healthier nutrition for their dog, real CO2 savings, supporting a kinder food system \(second screenshot\).

The result of this was a 28% placed order rate, $91K in revenue attributed to this single flow over the last 30 days \(the first screenshot\).

A small copy tweak, but a big retention lever for sure!

comments.content:
What's up Samuel. That's a good question tbh. I believe the real answer depends on something most people skip over, which is: where does the discount actually live?

If that 52% off is hardcoded on the site, then you can't truly test different offer levels from Klaviyo alone. You can swap popup messaging all day, but if the cart still auto-applies 52% at checkout, you're just testing copy against a fixed experience, not actually testing a different offer.

So the first question I'd bring back to the brand: Can the site-level discount be made conditional? If it can, then you set up your Klaviyo popup A/B split, then tag each variant to a profile property, and just have the site apply the matching discount.

But if not, then you're testing positioning instead of offer levels. Basically the same 52% off, but you test the framing like the urgency, value-anchored, social proof, mystery-wrapped, and measure submit rate and downstream conversion by variant. Still valuable though, just a different kind of test.

Another thing as well bro. "Up to 52% off" as the default site-wide experience is extremely aggressive ngl. The most valuable test might not be mystery vs. 10% vs. 20%, it might just be whether a significantly lower discount paired with stronger value positioning still converts at a rate that makes the unit economics better. A 30% discount converting at 80% the rate of 52% is a massive margin win imo. Lmk your thoughts!

posts.title: Save On Your Klaviyo Bills ‼️
posts.content:
Super simple suppress segment to save on your Klaviyo bill...

[ul][li]Person can receive email marketing[li]Person has received at least 4 emails [li]Person has clicked email zero times over all time [li]Person has opened email zero times over all time 

Alternatively... you can change "all time" to something like 365 days and suppress people who did engaged in the past but haven't since \(this is the more standard route\).

Klaviyo also made it super easy to suppress profiles from segments now...

Literally just create the segment, click the 3 dots on the right, and click suppress current members.

Then head over to your settings > Billing and lower your plan to as low as you can go.

And boom! You just saved some profit.

posts.title: Welcome Flow Tip 💡
posts.content:
Resending the first welcome email to people who didn't open it.

After Email 1, you can add a conditional split about an hour after if they've opened or clicked the email. If they didn't, resend the same email with a different subject line. If they did engage, they continue to Email 2 like normal.

The welcome email has your discount code and it's the most important email in the entire flow. If it got buried in their inbox, the resend gives them another shot at seeing it.

Super simple setup too 🧠

posts.title: TWO RULES FOR EVERY ABANDONMENT EMAIL
posts.content:
1\) Dynamic product block at the absolute top.

Not below a big hero image.

Not halfway down the email. At the very top.

A thin header line, something like "Your order is ready to ship" then immediately the dynamic abandoned product section, then the CTA button.

When someone opens the email and the exact product they were looking at is right in their face, it converts better.

Every email with a dynamic section follows this rule.

2\) Aggressive copy.

Not passive. Drop the soft language.

"Forgetting something?" sounds like extra work for the customer.

It's weak and it doesn't convert.

Use language that makes the purchase feel close and easy:

"Your order is ready to ship" "You're one click away" "We've got your order ready."

This framing converts significantly better across every abandonment flow.

Make it feel like the purchase is practically done, they just need to finish.

This example attached is perfect.

posts.title: March Email Design | L7D Stats + Value add
posts.content:
Sharing a welcome flow email for one of my clients with last 7 day stats.
Simple and clean design with a high click + order rate
Key factors that I think make this email work very well:

46% Open Rate
14.6% CTR
9.2% Order Rate

[ol:1][li]Immediately adding the discount at the top so they don't have to scroll[li]Immediately other people using the product \(social proofing\)[li]Benefits of the product with big callouts and not a lot of small text \(makes it easy and breezy to read through\)[li]Adding a clean, aesthetic box that stands out with their welcome code, reinforcing it if they missed it in the top section, and presenting it like a gift rather than a boring code.[li]Adding a single, easy-to-relate testimonial at the bottom.

Overall just simplifying the design and the message, making it ultra clear what they can expect from the product without having to read too much.

Just need to split test for the open rate increase, but working on deliverability— when I started with them, all their emails were going to spam but now we're up to 63% open rates last 20 days.

These guys just launched 30D ago, so revenue per recipient looks insane right now.

If you guys have any tips or recommendations for welcome flows in general, let me know!

posts.title: Offer Framing!
posts.content:
Brez literally doesn't do 10% OFF or even $10 OFF...

All of their sales are $ OFF, but framed as "Store Credit"... but it's literally just a discount code just like $10 OFF!

If you saw two brands and one of them was giving $10 OFF and one of them was giving $10 store credit... which are you more drawn to?

Personally I'm more drawn to the store credit.

When someone sees "$10 OFF" their brain thinks "the product is $10 cheaper"

When someone sees "$10 Store Credit" their brain thinks "I’m getting $10"

It also just stands out. And as an added bonus it sounds less salesy.

Would love to see some AB test numbers trying this out!

Next sale you do test $10 OFF vs $10 store credit and/or set up the test in your abandonment flows that have offers.

posts.title: You should be split maxxing.
posts.content:
One of the flows we set up for a client targets people who submit the popup form but are already on the email list.

Instead of sending them through the welcome series again \(which they've already seen\), we send them a "You're already on the list / welcome back" email.

The results are insane :\)

Why does this work so well?

These people are already familiar with the brand. They just need a nudge instead of a full education sequence.

The setup is super simple too and can be applied everywhere. Anytime you can split by "has this person placed an order over all time" you should be doing it. Repeat customers vs first-time in checkout, cart, browse flows, etc.

The conditional split is the most underused feature in Klaviyo 🤓

posts.title: Keeping a sale going?
posts.content:
Recently started working with ski wear brand who's objective is just to sell through loads of old stock.

They are very established with a decently big \(but old\) email list and basically just haven't sold as much as they should have this season. My job is to use the email list and deeeeppp discounts \(up to 70%\) to get through as much stock as possible before the ski season finishes in April.

Any good strategies to keep hype around a sale when it's running for a long period of time? I'm used to running sales for a week or two max where it's easy to use urgency. I'm thinking mystery boxes, bundles, flash periods. Would love to hear some insights.

user.name: Tristan Jones
user.bio: Helping ecom brands with email & sms

comments.content:
Try making multiple offers \(that actually are different\) and run them in a short periode off time \(and communicate clearly how long it lasts, and build urgency through that\) - people convert based on different offers...they want different things ;\)

It worked really well during BW/CM for us - Max has some good videos for sale urgency and relavance in his BW/CM YT videos

user.name: Max Sturtevant
user.bio: Owner of Well Copy - $200M Generated Through Email

comments.content: Would also add that on the last day of the sale... specifically have multiple touch points go out so you maximize as much revenue as possible. So an AM send, PM send, final hours send, and a resend to anyone who has engaged with the sale but hasn't purchased. Having a countdown timer in these last minute emails always helps drive urgency too. I would also say on any evergreen send in between when the sale starts and the final day you also should make sure to have a banner on the top so it's top of mind!

posts.title: 7000 sign-ups & €2.5k in sales with lead ads
posts.content:
Hey guys, I want to share a great way how we grow our email list by releasing a free challenge & run lead ads towards.

The brand was in the health/supplement niche and we created a simple free online challenge that people could join.

The main goal was to launch a new product after the free challenge and get as many new email sign ups as possible before with lead ads.

We didn't expect to be profitable at all on the lead ads but to get at least some revenue from the ads, we created a low ticket offer \(€3-5\) after they signed up to upgrade the free challenge to VIP with some extra free assets/bonus.

Free challenge -> Lead ads -> Email OPT -> €3 or €5 VIP upsell -> 7 day challenge -> new product launch

We had 7000+ sign-ups and €2.5k in sales. We’re almost breakeven on ads while growing the list only with the upgrade to VIP and didn't launched the new product.

Bit more effort to set it up, but when working it feels like a GTA V money hack.

Hope this helps guys ✌️

comments.content:
[@Tristan Jones](obj://user/a0f3397bfc48414289ceccf55deba6f5)

Def right on more education. High ticket mean it's going to be a much longer consideration phase. So a lot of your emails need to answer objections before they even ask them. Anything related to quality/durability, warranty, customer support, financing options, lots of and lots of testimonials, etc.

I'd also say the early flow emails tight \(daily or every other day\). The "longer" part should be the flow itself. So anywhere bet 7-8 emails on this one is good

A few other things that I've seen work really well for high ticket:

- Plain text founder emails hit much harder for these kinds of brands
- Post-purchase flow is huge here too. So if you want referrals and reviews - you can position it as a "$400 off for someone you know" angle. We use it for Anthros and it crushes because high-ticket buyers know other high-ticket buyers.
- Do they have a "book a call" thing going on? If they do make sure to add that in your abandonment flows. Sometimes people just need to talk to someone before spending that much.

Also Max covered a lot of this on yesterday's office hours call using Anthros as the example \(they sell $2k+ office chairs\).

posts.title: The Greatest Subject Line Of All Time
posts.content:
I gatekeep this as much as possible because it is my favorite and best hack in email marketing...

But sharing it with you guys here.

It is the abandoned cart / checkout email #1 subject line of "Your order is ready to ship 📦"

Most people use something like "forgetting something?"

But that just has NO urgency and doesn't remind people they were so damn close to buying.

The your order is ready to ship option makes it seem so close. Changes the psychology. Makes the customer be like oh shit I mean I was so close I pretty much already got it.

Works so well.

You don't even need to change the content of the email \(but bonus points if you change the headline to be your order is ready to ship as well\).

posts.title: Improving Retention For A Furniture Brand 🤔
posts.content:
So I have this d2c furniture brand in Germany as a client and wanted to get everybodys opinion. Because truthfully their retention rates are not great...

I am gonna give some stats for YTD 2026:
[ul][li]Mid-six figures total revenue
[ul][li]Attributed email revenue: 28%[li]Flows make up 83% of that[li]Campaigns 17%[li]In fact 65% of total email revenue comes from the welcome flow[li]10 campaigns have been send in the last 30 days. Unsub rate is a little high between 1-1.5%. Open rates 45%, click rates 1.8%, placed order rate 0.09%[li]Popup has an abysmal 1.3% opt in rate. I have tested this quite a bit and the current version is a mystery discount with a micro-comittment. [li]Core flows are all build out[li]Returning customer rate is only 13%[li]AOV around 150€[li]13k active profiles in the engaged 90 days segment

For context:
[ul][li]They sell basic furniture with decent but not great quality at an affordable price[li]It seems that the customers don‘t really form a great bond with the brand[li]I worked with another more luxury furniture brand before and it was the complete opposite. Campaigns performed way better, higher returning customer rates, better opt-ins. Those customers I guess had way more connection with the brand.

What area would you guys focus on to improve results?

user.name: Matthias Lindner
user.bio: Email Marketing for Ecom | Germany + Austria + Switzerland | mlmails.de

comments.content:
I would probably start with the pop-up and the unsubscribe rate. By fixing these two things, you can start sending more campaigns per month and therefore increase the impact email has on the total revenue generated from it.

Pop-up

Can we know what you’ve already tested? Or what the current offer is?

Mainly asking because with an AOV of $150, an offer that usually works quite well is “$X OFF”, but I’m not sure if you’ve already tested that or how much of a discount the client is able to offer.

Alternatively, you could try something more interactive and engaging, like the three mystery boxes to choose from, where each one contains a different offer/discount.

Another option could also be free shipping. I’m not sure how large the fornitures are, but I imagine the shipping costs aren’t exactly cheap, so this could potentially be a strong lever.

Unsubscribe rate

I’d say it’s quite high, and it really limits the number of campaigns you can send in a month. Which segments are you currently excluding?

At this point I would probably exclude:

[ul][li]Bounce once \(OAT\)[li]Marked as spam once \(OAT\)[li]Received more than 3 emails in the last 3 days

I would also exclude anyone who is currently in abandonment flows.

It’s a bit drastic, but it could at least help stabilize the unsubscribe rate, and once things normalize you can gradually widen the segments again

user.bio: I’m on focus to reach the best version of myself

replies.content:
[@Christian Celotti](obj://user/5da96b39a5fb4506b09f39c0c148f4c2) Thanks Christian. We send all campaigns to 90 days engaged and then one or two campaigns per month to the whole list. Excluded:
[ul][li]bounced[li]marked as spam[li]unengaged[li]frequency monthly \(I put a thing in the email preferences where recipients can select if they only want one mail per month to help with unsub rates.\)

For the popup I have tested all the "normal" options floating around in the Inbox community. The offer is 10€ off with a minimum purchase of 100€.
Mystery discount performed better than explicitly stating the discount amount.
Three mystery boxes is an interesting idea.

I do have to say I was able to convince them to implement Alia popups in the past. With Alia the opt in rate came up to about 5% with a "what are you shopping for" micro-comittment.
But the brand owner did not like Alia, thought there was no advantage to Klaviyo popups and cancelled it during the free trial...

posts.title: Max's Daily Insights Day 1 🧠
posts.content:
Random flow that will sneakily get you sales... and is way better than a birthday flow...

First Purchase Anniversary

First Purchase Anniversary Flow Segment:
[ul][li]Someone has placed order once over all time[li]Placed order at least once in the last 181 days[li]Placed order zero times in the last 179 days

This segment creates people who placed their first order exactly 180 days ago, and it will update every day.

You can then fire a new flow that sends this person a discount for their 6 month anniversary.

\(I typically recommend 6 months because 12 months is too long of a time\)

Hey [@Jake Kelly](obj://user/aaa0a40836a34ff6b1f88994e21d811d) , Couple of things you can check out:
[ul][li]Did you recently updated your Shopify theme? -> If yes, check if the ATC triggers are still working. You might need to update those[li]Double check your flow trigger for post purchase, cart & site. It seems like no emails are send. If you open 1 email in the flow > click on view details >   recipient activity > Skipped emails > Fails flow filter > you can see why the emails are not getting send[li]Double check if you have smart sending for flows set-off per email. When someone bought from a campaign/email it could be possible that the post purchase flow emails getting skipped as they already got an email in X time

Hope this would help!
